- No. The Elohim will not hire swords for a war we would not fight ourselves.
- Your price is fair for mercenaries, but we are not buying mercenaries.
- Forgive us, rider; this costs us more than it gives.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, Hippus. Ride home, and let the plains rest.
- We accept. May your companies find worthier contracts than this one.
- So be it. Tell your clans the Elohim keep no grudges, only records.

#### Refuses peace
- Your riders would only come back under a new contract. Not yet.
- Not while your raiders hold our villages. No.
- Your peace is only the pause between two contracts. We cannot accept it.

#### Rejects a demand
- We will not pay a toll on roads our pilgrims walked before your fathers tamed their first horse.
- No, Hippus. You have mistaken us for a client.
- Our coffers belong to the poor. Find another paymaster.

### Elohim → Illians

#### First contact
- We are the Elohim. We witnessed the Compact your god broke, and we lost our shrines to his ice. Do not expect us to forget it.
- The lost men of Letum Frigus, awake again. We pray the world will not have to sleep for it.
- Greetings, Illians. Our monks carried the dying through your god's winter. We would rather not do it a second time.

#### Declares war
- You would climb into the empty throne of Mulcarn. The Elohim will not watch another god break the world.
- We saw the Godslayer placed in Finner's hands. Whoever goes looking for that blade will find the Elohim standing in the way.
- The White Hand froze half of Erebus while we buried its dead. Your second winter ends here.

#### Refuses to talk
- We remember the White Hand. Not a word until your frost leaves our fields.
- Your envoys bring snow in on their boots. Send them home.
- No. A people who would make a god of a man has nothing to tell the Elohim.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Illian. Come and stand by the fire; we hear your halls are always cold.
- We will hear you. Even the servants of winter may seek warmer counsel now and then.
- Greetings. It is good to speak with Letum Frigus in a season of thaw.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- The frost along our border is new, Illian. Explain it.
- You remember everything, they say. So do we: the ice, the hunger, the broken Compact. Speak.
- What does the winter want from us now?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. May this be the warmest thing ever to pass between our peoples.
- We accept, and pray it helps your people more than it helps your ambitions.
- Very well. A fair bargain, even from the north.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Illians? We will keep it near the hearth, in case it is cold.
- Thank you. Perhaps not every heart in Letum Frigus is frozen.
- We are grateful, Illian, and surprised; winter is not known for its gifts.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We will not give anything that brings you one step nearer to godhood.
- We must refuse. The Elohim lost too much to the last winter to feed the next one.
- This we cannot accept. Bring us something that does not smell of frost.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the thaw hold a while longer.
- We accept. Go back to your caverns, and let the world stay awake.
- So be it. Our monks will be glad to stop burying the frozen.

#### Refuses peace
- You still reach for heaven. There is no peace while that hand is raised.
- Mulcarn broke one compact already. We will not trust his heirs with another.
- Not yet. The winter must end, not merely pause.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the White Hand? We paid it once, in lives, through the whole Age of Ice. Never again.
- No. The Elohim do not kneel to men who would be gods.
- Your threats are cold, [CT_NAME], but our answer is colder: no.

### Elohim → Infernal

#### First contact
- Demons of Agares, walking in Erebus. The Elohim have waited a long time for this day, and we are ready for it.
- We know what you are. Our order was born tending the wreckage of the gods' wars, and you are the worst of that wreckage.
- So hell has found a door. We will be standing on this side of it, for as long as it takes.

#### Declares war
- There is no good deal to be made with demons. We will not try again. The Elohim march.
- Our warrior monks carry no weapons; against the things of hell they need none. Prepare yourselves.
- You crawled out of Agares' pit to drag the living down into it. The Elohim will push you back.

#### Refuses to talk
- The last time we signed a treaty with a demon, it smiled. We will not sign again.
- Every word you speak is a hook. We will not bite.
- No. Go back to your fire.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Our peace holds, demon, and it holds because we watch it day and night. Speak.
- We will hear you, but our monks will stand between us, and they are not afraid of you.
- You are here, and we are at peace. Let us keep both of those things brief.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You smell of sulfur and lies. Say it and go.
- Even standing in our hall, you are an abomination to us. What do you want?
- We remember the last treaty with your kind, and what was waiting at home afterwards. Speak quickly.

#### Accepts a deal
- We accept, and every word of it is written down and witnessed three times over.
- Agreed. Not because we trust you, but because this harms no one.
- Very well. If there is a hidden price, demon, our brothers will find it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from hell. We will have it blessed before it crosses our threshold.
- We thank you, warily. Your kind does not give; it only lends.
- Thank you. We will give it to the poor, and pray it does them no harm.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Nothing that passes from your hand to ours is ever only what it seems.
- We refuse. Every gift of Agares comes back one day to collect.
- The Elohim do not bargain with souls, not even by accident. No.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, for now. But every abbey will keep its lamps lit, and every monk will keep watch.
- We accept, because the living need rest. Not because we forgive.
- So be it. We will sign, and then we will go home and look behind every door.

#### Refuses peace
- We made peace with demons once before, and we are still burying the cost. No.
- You do not want peace; you want time. We will not give you any.
- Not while your gates stand open in our world. Never while they stand.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand tribute? We give alms to the living; we give nothing to the damned.
- No. Hell takes enough without our help.
- Our answer is the same today as it will be at the end of the world: no.

### Elohim → Khazad

#### First contact
- Greetings, children of Kilmorph. The Elohim keep no gold, only shrines; you will find us poor customers and good neighbors.
- They say the Khazad did not notice the Age of Ice for three generations. We noticed it every day. Perhaps we can teach each other something.
- We are the Elohim. We know the outside world once cheated your people with illusions. You will find no illusions here, only honest monks.

#### Declares war
- You would dig through a holy place for the ore beneath it. The Elohim will not allow it, dwarf.
- Your vaults are full, Khazad, and still you come for our sacred sites. We must stand against you.
- Kilmorph taught you to honor the earth. You are breaking it open where no pick was ever meant to go.

#### Refuses to talk
- You weigh every word for gold, and we have none to offer today. Go.
- Not while your sappers are digging beneath our abbeys.
- No talk, dwarf. Your siege engines speak too loudly already.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Khazad. Stonework and faith both last for ages, when they are done well.
- Come in, dwarf. Our halls are open to the sky; we hope it does not trouble you.
- Greetings. We hear your vaults are full; may your hearths be just as full.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You counted the offerings at our shrines as if they were yours. Speak.
- Your merchants have been hard on our pilgrims. What do you want?
- Speak, Khazad. We have no patience today for haggling.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. We will not cheat you, dwarf; your people have been cheated enough.
- We accept. Honest weight for an honest price.
- A fair bargain. Kilmorph herself would find no fault in it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from a dwarven vault? Thank you; we know how rarely those doors open.
- Thank you, friend. Generosity from the Khazad is worth more than the gold itself.
- We are grateful. May your mines run deep and your halls stay warm.

#### Turns down a deal
- No, dwarf. Even monks can count, and this does not add up.
- We must decline. Our shrines are not for sale at any weight of gold.
- We cannot accept. Come back with a fairer measure.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back under the mountain, and leave the holy places of the surface in peace.
- We accept. Neither of us gains anything by digging more graves.
- So be it. Let your hammers ring on anvils, not on our gates.

#### Refuses peace
- Your sappers have not left our foundations. Not yet.
- You would use the peace to fill your vaults for the next war. No.
- Not while your engines still stand outside our abbeys.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute for the Khazad vaults? They are full enough already, dwarf.
- No. You were cheated once and swore never to be cheated again. Neither will we.
- The Elohim give to the poor, and no dwarf with a vault is poor.

### Elohim → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- Greetings, children of the confederation. You welcome every race to your cities, and we welcome every pilgrim to our shrines. We should be good friends.
- Hail, Kuriotates. We hear centaurs and giants sit beside men in your councils. That is a sight the world needs.
- We are the Elohim. A nation that gives asylum to the hunted is one we will gladly call a neighbor.

#### Declares war
- Your settlements have swallowed the land around our sacred sites. We cannot let them be governed from a distant throne.
- The hand of your throne is gentle until it closes. We have seen it close on our people, and we must pry it open.
- You say you are building an edifice for the ages. Not on our holy ground, Kuriotate.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your centaurs are still riding through our groves. We will talk when they leave.
- Not today. Your court's courtesy cannot cover what your armies have done.
- We will not speak while our shrines fly your banner.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, friend. How fare the great cities, and all the peoples in them?
- Come in, Kuriotate. Our monks always learn something from your envoys; last time it was a lamia's lullaby.
- Greetings. Our pilgrims speak well of the hospitality of your settlements.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your royal surveyors were measuring our sacred sites for your next settlement. Speak.
- Even a gentle throne can be a greedy one. What do you want?
- Speak, Kuriotate. We are disappointed in you.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. May it draw our peoples closer together.
- We accept, with thanks to you and to every people under your banner.
- A fair bargain, as we have come to expect from the Kuriotates.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, friend. Generosity seems to come easily to a nation of so many peoples.
- We are grateful. We will share this with the pilgrims who pass through your lands.
- Thank you, [CT_NAME]. You give like a host who expects no return, and that is rare.

#### Turns down a deal
- We are sorry, but we cannot. This would cost our pilgrims too dearly.
- No, friend. Not even for the Kuriotates.
- We must decline, though we thank you for the offer.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, gladly. This war never suited either of us.
- We accept. Let the centaurs and the monks go back to their proper work.
- So be it. May your great cities and our small abbeys stand side by side again.

#### Refuses peace
- Your settlements still sit on our shrines. Remove them first.
- Not yet. We have seen your nation draw into its shell like a turtle and wait. We will not wait with it.
- Your court's machinations would bend this peace to its own use. No.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Asylum you give freely; why do you demand your gifts?
- The Elohim open their shrines to all, but their storehouses only to the needy.
- We will not, Kuriotate. Bullying does not suit you.

### Elohim → Lanun

#### First contact
- Greetings, children of the sea. Our pilgrims have sailed on your ships and paid the fares you asked, which were not always gentle.
- We are the Elohim. We already know one word of your tongue: culva, love. Let it be the first word between us.
- Hail, Lanun. Danalin once heard your prayers. We pray he hears them again.

#### Declares war
- Your captains have taken pilgrim ships as prizes. The Elohim must stop them.
- You sold ships to both sides of every war since Patria fell. This time you sold to the wrong one.
- The Overlords whisper to some of your captains, and they have listened. We will not let those whispers reach our shores.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your word changes with the tide. We will wait for a calmer sea.
- Not while your ships hold our pilgrims for ransom.
- No, captain. Sail on.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, captain. We hope the sea has been kind to you.
- Come in, Lanun. Leave the rum at the door, but bring your stories.
- Greetings, friend. Our novices still talk about the last time your sailors came ashore.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders took a pilgrim ship last season. Speak.
- We know how fleeting a Lanun's word can be. Why should we listen to it today?
- What does the sea want from us now, captain?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and witnessed. A captain's word is law on his ship, they say; let it be law here too.
- We accept. May the winds favor this bargain.
- A fair trade, captain. Done.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Lanun, and not even stolen? Thank you, truly.
- We are grateful. The sea gives rarely, and you give more often than it does.
- Thank you, captain. We will pray for your ships in every storm.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Too much of this would end up in the holds of pirates.
- We must decline. The Elohim are poor sailors and poorer gamblers.
- That is not a fair wind, captain. We decline.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to the sea, and leave our pilgrims ashore.
- We accept. Let your ships carry trade, not war.
- So be it. May every one of your captains keep the word you give today.

#### Refuses peace
- Your captains would honor this peace as far as the next port. No.
- Not while our pilgrims are still pulling oars in your galleys.
- Not yet, Lanun. The tide has further to run.

#### Rejects a demand
- You want plunder without the trouble of a raid? No.
- The Elohim pay no tolls on the open sea.
- No, captain. Charm us all you like.

### Elohim → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- Greetings, Summer Court. Before Sucellus departed, he gave our order its charge; we are glad to meet those who kept faith with him through the winter.
- We are the Elohim. Seven firs grew where the Compact was signed, and our monks have tended them ever since. We think the Ljosalfar will understand such work.
- Hail, elves of the forest. Our pilgrims walk softly beneath your trees, and they carry no axes.

#### Declares war
- Your Fellowship would kill a man for cutting one sacred tree. We will not let it kill our pilgrims for walking past one.
- Your rangers shot our brothers from the branches as if they were zealots with torches. The Elohim must answer that.
- You guard the groves with treants and arrows, and now you have taken our shrines as well. We are coming for our charge.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your archers are still perched above our roads. No talk.
- Not this season, Ljosalfar. The forest has heard enough from both of us.
- We will speak when your bows are unstrung.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, elf. How fare the groves of the Summer Court?
- Come in, friend. For too long the Winter Court were the only elves the world remembered; it is good to see you.
- Greetings. Sucellus' name is heard in your woods again, and that gladdens us more than we can say.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your treants have closed our pilgrims' road. Speak.
- The forest is not yours alone, Ljosalfar. What do you want?
- You carry yourselves as if every sacred tree were your own. Speak, and be brief.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. May this bargain grow like a seed in good soil.
- We accept. The Summer Court trades as it rules, fairly and with patience.
- A fair trade, with the forest as our witness.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, elf. We will plant a fir in your honor beside the seven.
- We are grateful. The Summer Court gives like spring, all at once and without counting.
- Thank you, [CT_NAME]. This is a gift worthy of a people who kept faith through the ice.

#### Turns down a deal
- We are sorry, but no. This would leave our shrines unguarded.
- We must decline, even for the Ljosalfar. Our charge comes first.
- Not this one, friend. Perhaps in another season.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the forest heal, and let our pilgrims walk beneath it again.
- We accept. Sucellus would not want his children and his keepers at war.
- So be it. Hang your bows in the branches, and we will tend the wounded of both sides.

#### Refuses peace
- Your rangers still hold our pilgrim road. Not yet.
- No peace while our shrines burn in your woods.
- You would wait out this war the way an elf waits out a century. We cannot afford your patience.

#### Rejects a demand
- The forest is generous, but you are not the forest. No.
- We will not give away what Sucellus charged us to keep.
- The Summer Court asks; it does not demand. Remember who you are.

### Elohim → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- Greetings, heirs of the Open-Skiers. Our monks carried word of your fallen cities through the Age of Ice; we rejoice to see you walk under the sun again.
- We are the Elohim. We hear your golems never tire. Neither do our pilgrims, though they complain a great deal more.
- Hail, golem-makers. Kilmorph held her hand over you through the long winter; we hope she will not mind if we offer ours as well.

#### Declares war
- Your golems have trampled our pilgrims' fields. A servant is only as gentle as the hand that sends it, and yours was not gentle.
- You set tireless clay against the living. The Elohim will stand before it, and it will learn that faith does not tire either.
- Our shrines are not quarries for your artificers. We must stop you.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your golems are still marching. We will talk when they are standing still.
- Not now. Your forges are louder than any words we could offer.
- No, Luchuirp. Wind down your war-engines first.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, friend. How fare your workshops, and your clockwork servants?
- Come in. Our novices are eager to see whatever marvel you have built this season.
- Greetings, Luchuirp. It is good to see the heirs of Kradh-Ke-zun above ground again, where they belong.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems dug through a shrine wall, and no one called them back. Speak.
- We know you are busy, artificer. So are we. What do you want?
- Speak, Luchuirp. We are not pleased with your servants of stone and clay.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Well made, like everything that leaves your workshops.
- We accept. A fair trade between those who build and those who keep.
- Done, and gladly. Your people have never traded in illusions.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, friend. We know how much patient work goes into everything you make.
- We are grateful. A gift from a people who lost so much to the winter means a great deal.
- Thank you, [CT_NAME]. May your forges stay warm and your golems never crack.

#### Turns down a deal
- No, artificer. We cannot spare this, not even for the finest golem in Erebus.
- We must decline. This would serve your forges of war, not your fields.
- Forgive us; the measure is not true, and you of all people can see it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Send your golems back to the fields and the mines, where they belong.
- We accept. Let your forges make plowshares again.
- So be it. Neither of our peoples was made for war.

#### Refuses peace
- Your golems still stand in our cloisters. Not yet.
- You would only use the quiet to build more of them. No.
- Not while your war-engines hold our roads.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Build what you need, artificer, as Graoin's people always have.
- The Elohim pay no tribute to clockwork, nor to its makers.
- You have the cleverest hands in Erebus. Use them, not our alms.

### Elohim → Malakim

#### First contact
- Greetings, children of the sun. Your Empyrean values wisdom over law, and so do we. We think we will understand each other.
- We are the Elohim. Our pilgrims have long crossed your deserts by night, and blessed your wells by day.
- Hail, Malakim. The desert taught you endurance and Lugus taught you light; the Elohim would gladly learn from both.

#### Declares war
- Your Radiant Guard scorches every shadow it finds, even the ones that sheltered the weak. We must stop it.
- You have mistaken our shrines for darkness to be burned away. They are not, and we will defend them.
- The sun is meant to warm the world, not to sear it. The Elohim stand against your blazing armies.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your light is too fierce for counsel today. Return when it has dimmed.
- Not while your Vicars preach against our abbeys.
- No. Even the sun must set, Malakim.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, friend of the dawn. What brings you out of the desert?
- Come in, Malakim. Your Empyrean and our order both prize wisdom; let us use a little of it today.
- Greetings. We hear the Empyrean gives an equal voice to the small and the great. That is a teaching we treasure.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You cast a long shadow for a people of the sun. Speak.
- Your Vicars call our monks blind. What do you want with the blind?
- Speak, Malakim, but do not preach to us.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. May the sun shine on this bargain and on both our peoples.
- We accept. Wisely offered, and wisely taken.
- A fair exchange. Let it be judged on its merits, as your Empyrean would judge it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, friend. Your generosity is as warm as your deserts.
- We are grateful. Such a gift brings light into our abbeys.
- Thank you, [CT_NAME]. May Lugus see your kindness and repay it.

#### Turns down a deal
- We are sorry, but no. This would leave our pilgrims parched.
- We must decline, though gently. The scales are not even.
- No, friend. Judge it on its merits and you will see why.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the sun rise over a quieter land.
- We accept. Light and wisdom were never meant to be enemies.
- So be it. Our monks will be glad to walk your deserts again.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your Radiant Guard holds our shrines.
- You would only wait for another dawn to strike. No.
- Not yet, Malakim. Your armies still blaze along our border.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. The sun gives freely; why do its children demand?
- The Elohim give to those in need, and the children of the sun are not in need.
- Your Empyrean judges each case on its merits. This one has none.

### Elohim → Mercurians

#### First contact
- The Compact was signed before our order's eyes, and you refused it, angel. We have not yet decided whether to bless you or mourn you.
- We are the Elohim. You fight hell's armies, and we tend those they leave behind. Let us not quarrel over whose work is harder.
- Greetings, Mercurians. We have heard you care little for mortals. Our monks care for little else.

#### Declares war
- You kill demons and leave the villages burning behind you. Someone must answer for the villages.
- An angel who broke the Compact now breaks our people. The Elohim will not allow it.
- Your war with hell is no excuse for trampling the innocent. We will stand against you.

#### Refuses to talk
- You have no time for mortals, angel. Today we have none for you.
- Not while your host is camped in our cloisters.
- No. Your hammers have spoken loudly enough.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, angel. We are always glad of allies against the pit.
- Come in, Mercurian. The wounded from your last battle are mending in our abbeys.
- Greetings. We know your war leaves you little time, so we will be brief.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You broke the Compact we witnessed, and now you break our peace as well. Speak.
- Your rage does not frighten us; we have watched gods at war. What do you want?
- Speak, angel, and leave your hammer outside.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. May it hasten the end of your war with hell.
- We accept. Against the demons, the Elohim stand with you.
- Done. Go and fight; we will tend whatever you leave behind.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, angel. We did not think your kind remembered mortals at all.
- We are grateful. It is a rare thing for a warrior of heaven to stop and give.
- Thank you, [CT_NAME]. This will heal many who were hurt in your war.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We will not pay for a war that leaves our villages in ruins.
- We must decline. Your crusade can find its arms elsewhere.
- Forgive us; it is too much, even for the fight against hell.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your true war, angel, and leave us to our works of mercy.
- We accept. The pit laughs while we fight each other; let us stop.
- So be it. Hell is the enemy of both our peoples, and it always was.

#### Refuses peace
- Your host still tramples our shrines. Not yet.
- You say mercy is for the innocent. So were our abbeys, and you burned them. No.
- Not until you treat the living as more than a battlefield.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. The Elohim have given enough to your crusade already.
- You demand as though heaven had sent you. You left heaven, angel.
- Our alms are for the wounded, not the wrathful.

### Elohim → Sheaim

#### First contact
- We are the Elohim. You work to end the world, and we have spent ages keeping it whole. One of us will be disappointed.
- Greetings, Sheaim. We have read your prophecies. We have also tended the dying of every so-called end of the world, and the world is still here.
- Peace to you, though we doubt you want any. Our shrines will stand long after your gates are shut.

#### Declares war
- Every gate you open tears the world we were charged to keep. The Elohim will close them, one by one.
- You call it Armageddon. We call it madness, and we will stop it.
- You want the end of all things. Then let it begin with the end of your cult.

#### Refuses to talk
- We do not bargain with those who pray for the end.
- Not while your gates spill horrors onto our fields.
- No. Every word you speak is only a count toward doom.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- We will hear you, Sheaim. Even you must want something before the end.
- Welcome, though we wonder why those who await the end of the world bother with treaties.
- Greetings. Our monks have prayed for you; perhaps it has helped a little.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your planar gates hum along our border. Speak.
- You long for the end, and we long for you to leave. Speak quickly.
- What does the apocalypse want from us today?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Perhaps a little trade will make you fonder of this world.
- We accept, and pray it buys the world a few more years.
- Very well. Even the end of days must eat, it seems.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. A gift is a strange thing from those who want everything gone.
- We are grateful, Sheaim. Perhaps you love this world more than you admit.
- Thank you. We will use it to mend what your gates have broken.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We will not hasten the end, not even by a single day.
- We must decline. Whatever you buy will only feed your gates.
- We cannot accept. Your bargains are all down payments on the apocalypse.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the world last a little longer.
- We accept. Perhaps one day you will find this world worth keeping.
- So be it. Close your gates, and we will rest.

#### Refuses peace
- Your gates still stand open. Close them first.
- You want a peace that lasts until the end, and the end is all you want. No.
- Not while your cultists pray for the stars to fall.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. The end of the world will have to pay its own way.
- The Elohim give to the living, not to those who wish there were none.
- You ask as if tomorrow did not matter. It matters to us. No.

### Elohim → Sidar

#### First contact
- Greetings, Sidar. You traded pieces of your souls for time; we spend ours tending others. We shall see whose bargain was better.
- We are the Elohim. Our pilgrims sometimes feel a shadow walking beside them on the road. Was it you?
- Hail, grey ones. We share your hatred of the undead, if not your way of outliving death.

#### Declares war
- You gave away your souls, and now you would take our shrines. We will not let you.
- The Sidar walk unseen through our lands and take what they please. No longer.
- You stand apart from the world until you want something from it. Today you wanted too much.

#### Refuses to talk
- Talk to us when you are fully here, Sidar.
- Not now. Your shades still drift through our cloisters.
- No. We will not bargain with what we cannot see.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Sidar. You look a little more solid today.
- Come in, grey friend. Our monks are glad of anyone who hunts the restless dead.
- Greetings. We hope the ages have been kind to you, however many of them there have been.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You pass through our abbeys as if they were mist. Speak.
- We feel your eyes on us everywhere. What do you want?
- Speak, shade. Our patience is only mortal.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. May it last as long as you do.
- We accept. Fair, and fairly offered.
- Done. We are glad to deal with the Sidar while they are still here to deal with.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. We did not think shades still remembered generosity.
- We are grateful, Sidar. Perhaps some piece of your soul remains after all.
- Thank you, friend. We will remember this longer than you might expect.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. What you offer fades, and what you ask does not.
- We must decline, Sidar. Our charge is to keep things, not to let them drift away.
- Forgive us; we cannot spare this, not even for those who have all the time in the world.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to your hidden cities, and let the world forget this war.
- We accept. Neither of us wants more of the dead to walk.
- So be it. May the undead be your only enemy from now on.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your shades hold our shrines.
- You would wait a century and strike again. No.
- Not yet, Sidar. Our dead have not been laid to rest.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. You traded your soul for endless years; you can live without our gold.
- The Elohim do not give to those who no longer need anything.
- You have all the time in the world, Sidar. Spend some of it earning what you want.

### Elohim → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- Greetings, Winter Court. Sucellus gave us our charge before he died, and you gave him up for Esus. We shall see what each choice made of us.
- We are the Elohim. We know the stories told about your court, and we pray they are exaggerated.
- Hail, Svartalfar. Our monks mended many who fled your purges in the ice. We hope there will be no more of them.

#### Declares war
- You punished elves for still loving Sucellus, and we were charged by Sucellus himself. Did you think we would forget?
- Your assassins have killed our pilgrims in their beds. The Elohim answer openly.
- The Winter Court spread its cold through the whole elven nation. We will not let it spread through ours.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your words are daggers with honey on the blade. We will not take one.
- Not while your shadows linger in our abbeys.
- No. The Winter Court has never spoken without a knife behind its back.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Svartalfar. Our doors are open, and our monks are watching them.
- Come in. We hope the Winter Court brings honest words today.
- Greetings. Even in winter, warmth can be shared.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Twelve assassins in our halls, perhaps? Our monks found three. Speak.
- You betrayed Sucellus and your own kin. What could you want from us?
- Speak, dark elf, and keep your hands where we can see them.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and our brothers have read every line for hidden knives.
- We accept. Let this be the honest bargain your court is not known for.
- Very well. Even the Winter Court can trade fairly, it seems.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. Our brothers will look it over for poison, but we are grateful.
- We are surprised, Svartalfar, and grateful in equal measure.
- Thank you. A gift from the Winter Court is rarer than an early spring.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your bargains always come with a second blade.
- We must decline. We know the ways of the Winter Court too well.
- We cannot accept. Find someone who has not heard of your court.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let this winter end.
- We accept. Go back to your court, and leave our pilgrims alone.
- So be it. May both elven courts find rest some day, and no more blood.

#### Refuses peace
- Your assassins are still among us. Not yet.
- You would sign and then sharpen your knives. No.
- Not while you hunt those who still pray to Sucellus.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. The demands of the Winter Court are not our concern.
- We gave nothing to the Winter Court while the ice lasted, and we give nothing now.
- Your academies of persuasion have failed you this time. No.

## Grigori

### Grigori → Amurites

#### First contact
- The Amurites. You worship magic instead of gods. It is a step in the right direction, if a short one.
- Greetings, Children of Kylorin. We once sent a gift into your lands aboard a Lanun ship, and the ice swallowed it. Consider this greeting our second attempt.
- We are the Grigori, a people who govern themselves without heavenly help. You, we hear, are governed by professors. We are not sure which of us is braver.

#### Declares war
- You call no god your master, yet your archmages rule like high priests. We will remind your people what freedom means.
- Your mages have shown they will burn anyone who stands near a mana node. We happen to stand near several.
- You taught your people that power deserves worship for its own sake. We are about to teach you otherwise.

#### Refuses to talk
- Send your committee home. We will talk when your war-mages stop arguing over which of our towns to burn next.
- No. Your envoys file their objections in triplicate, and we have no time to read them.
- I have read your last proposal, all forty pages of it. The answer is still no.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, scholar. Of all the nations of Erebus, yours comes closest to thinking for itself.
- Come in, Amurite, and bring a book. Ours are better than our wine.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. Tell me what your schools have learned lately. No prayers in it, I trust.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You treat other nations like students who failed an examination. Speak, and spare us the lecture.
- Your adepts have been testing spells along our border, on our farmers by the look of it. What do you want?
- Speak, Amurite, and do not hide behind your archmages' committees.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A reasoned bargain between reasonable peoples.
- Done. See how quickly things go without a faculty vote?
- We accept. Your terms were long, but sound.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift, freely given, and no tenure attached? Thank you, Amurite.
- Thank you. Generosity from a people who guard knowledge so jealously is worth twice the price.
- Grateful. You may be the most sensible nation in Erebus that still carries wands.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even without a god's help, we know when we are being swindled.
- The Grigori gain nothing by this, scholar, and you know it.
- I checked your arithmetic, and so did our clerks. The answer is no.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. The gods enjoy watching mortals burn each other; let us bore them instead.
- Agreed. Go back to your studies, and we will go back to our lives.
- So be it. Magic and reason ought to be allies, not enemies.

#### Refuses peace
- Your war-mages are still among our towns. Withdraw them, and then we will talk of peace.
- You want peace now that your fire is running low. We will wait until it runs out.
- Not yet, Amurite. A lesson half learned is not learned.

#### Rejects a demand
- You want tribute? Earn it, the way we earned what we have.
- No. We never bowed to gods, and we are not about to bow to headmasters.
- A demand, from scholars? Go and research the meaning of no.

### Grigori → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- The Grigori believe every man should think for himself. Your court believes every man should think what he is told. This will be interesting.
- Greetings, Balseraph. I count the strings on your courtiers, and I wonder whose hands hold them.
- We walked away from the gods so that no one would pull our strings. You seem to have found new hands for yours.

#### Declares war
- You take free people and make puppets of them. To the Grigori there is no worse crime. We are coming to cut the strings.
- Your taskmasters have carried our citizens off to Jubilee. We are coming to bring them home, and whatever else we find.
- Freedom of the mind is the only thing we hold sacred. You have offended it once too often.

#### Refuses to talk
- How would I even know I am speaking to you, and not to something sitting behind your eyes? No.
- Not now. Your riddles do not amuse me while your harlequins are dancing in our towns.
- We do not bargain with puppeteers. Come back when your envoys can think their own thoughts.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Balseraph. Leave your puppets outside, if you can tell them apart from your retinue.
- Ah, the masquerade. Come in, and let us see which face you are wearing today.
- Always a pleasure, in a nervous sort of way. What game are we playing this time?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- I can hear the laughter of your court from here. Speak, and make it short.
- Your mimics have been wearing our soldiers' skills like stolen cloaks. What now?
- Speak plainly, Balseraph. In prose, if you can manage it.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Now read it back to me once, without the rhymes.
- Done. Strange how easy that was, with no strings attached.
- We accept, and I trust it will mean the same thing tomorrow as it does today.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from Jubilee with no hidden clause? I am almost disappointed.
- Thank you. I will have it looked over for strings, of course.
- Grateful, truly. Your court can be reasonable when it forgets to be mad.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. I have seen what happens to those who sign a contract with your court.
- The Grigori gain nothing and you gain everything. Charming, but no.
- No. Find someone more amusing to cheat.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Release our people, and keep your puppets at home.
- Agreed. Go back to your festivals, and leave our minds alone.
- So be it. A truce is the only game I will ever play with your court.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while a single Grigori is still dancing in your court.
- You want peace the way a gambler wants a fresh hand. No.
- Not yet. Your freaks still hold our towns.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. My mind is my own, and so is my treasury.
- Try making us want to give it. You will find our minds harder to bend than your courtiers'.
- A demand in a jester's voice is still a demand. No.

### Grigori → Bannor

#### First contact
- So you are the Bannor. Your god promised salvation and asked only for unquestioning obedience. We would rather keep the questions.
- Greetings, Bannor. Some of our best citizens were once yours. They came to us with no faith left, and found they did not need it.
- We are the Grigori. You fight for Junil, and we fight for ourselves. We shall see which army sleeps better.

#### Declares war
- Your priesthood decides who is damned, and now it has decided on us. Very well; we have decided on you.
- You march to bring Law to the world. We march to make sure the world can still say no.
- Your Confessors have burned enough heretics. Today the heretics fight back.

#### Refuses to talk
- Talk to a crusade? It only listens to its priests.
- No. Come back when you are able to disagree with your god.
- Not while your Confessors still preach in our streets.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Bannor. You fight the Ashen Veil, and for that alone we are glad to see you.
- Come in. We may disagree about heaven, but we agree about hell.
- Leave your Confessor at the door, [CT_NAME], and we will get along famously.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your priests call us heathens. Well, you are speaking to the heathens now. What do you want?
- Your priesthood has added us to its list of nations that must repent. Speak.
- Speak, Bannor, but do not preach.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. See, even the faithful can strike a sensible bargain.
- Done, and no obedience required.
- A fair deal, honestly offered. Your drill extends to commerce, it seems.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. Charity without conversion; how refreshing.
- A gift from the Bannor, and no sermon with it? I am touched.
- Grateful, friend. Tell your priests the heathens said thank you.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We will not pay for another crusade.
- We would gain nothing here but your priesthood's approval, and we have never needed it.
- No. Your terms demand faith, and we keep ours for people, not doctrines.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your priests will call it a victory; let them.
- Agreed. Go back to fighting the true darkness, if your priests can still find it.
- So be it. We play into the hands of the gods when we fight each other.

#### Refuses peace
- Your priests have declared us damned. Peace means nothing until they take it back.
- You would only use the quiet to raise another crusade. No.
- Not yet, Bannor. We want your Confessors out of our towns first.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute for Junil? Let him come and ask in person. Oh, but the Compact forbids it, doesn't it?
- No. We have never obeyed without question, and we will not start now.
- A demand dressed up as a sermon is still a demand. No.

### Grigori → Calabim

#### First contact
- We are the Grigori, a refuge for those who want to own their lives. You own your people's lives outright. We will not get along.
- Greetings, Calabim. I hear your people walked into their chains of their own free will. Freedom needs a better teacher in your lands.
- Your nobles live forever on borrowed blood. Our people live once, on their own. I know which I respect.

#### Declares war
- Your herds of men are men. Today the Grigori come to tell them so.
- You made cattle of a free tribe through flattery and fear. We will make a free tribe of your cattle.
- Your Broods have hunted along our borders. They will find our adventurers are not easy prey.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not bargain with farmers who herd people. Begone.
- Not now. Your envoys keep looking at our clerks' necks.
- No. We will talk when your pens are empty.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Calabim. Please do not drink the servants.
- We are at peace, which means our people may walk past your castles without fear. Let us keep it that way.
- Speak, and we will keep this cordial. Our guards will keep it short.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your herds keep running to our cities. Speak.
- Every refugee from your lands tells the same story. What do you want?
- You smile with too many teeth. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A clean bargain, which is more than your herds ever get.
- Done. Let us keep it bloodless.
- We accept. Even a vampire can count.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. I will pass it on to your refugees; they are the ones who paid for it.
- A gift from the Calabim? I will not ask whose blood earned it.
- Grateful, however strange it feels to say so to you.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Our people are not for sale, nor is anything that might buy them.
- You offer silk and ask for throats. No.
- The Grigori gain nothing here except a neighbor with a fuller belly.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your refugees stay with us, though.
- Agreed. Go back to your castles, and keep your hunger behind your own walls.
- So be it. Our people will sleep easier tonight, and with their doors unbarred.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your Broods still hunt in our lands.
- You want peace to fatten your herds again. No.
- Not yet. Free one city from its Brood, and then we will talk.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. We have no bloodpets to give, and no gold either.
- Tribute to vampires? We have never even paid tribute to gods.
- You may take nothing from us that we do not choose to give. And we do not choose.

### Grigori → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- We are the Grigori. Your goddess fell and dragged your people down with her, and still you pray to her. We admire the loyalty, if not its object.
- Greetings, orc. You were men once, until a goddess fell on your city. We know how you ought to feel about gods, even if you don't.
- The Clan of Embers, I presume. Both our peoples were shaped by the wars of the gods; you stayed in the fire, and we walked out of it.

#### Declares war
- Your raiders burned our farms in the name of a goddess who burned yours. Enough.
- The Clan has torn down the cities of men for long enough. Today men tear back.
- Bhall has no hold on us, and neither do you. We march.

#### Refuses to talk
- Not while your goblins are in our granaries.
- No. Your warlords only listen to axes.
- Come back when your torches are out.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, orc. Sit, eat, and leave the axe by the door.
- The Clan, being civil. I suppose stranger things have happened, though I cannot think of one.
- You have been a good neighbor lately, which surprised everyone. What do you need?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders are on our border again. Speak.
- You still burn captives for a goddess who barely notices. What do you want?
- Speak, orc, and quickly.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Trading suits you better than raiding.
- Done, and not a single village burned. I am impressed.
- We accept. You count better than your reputation says.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, orc. Generous and peaceful; I like this side of your people.
- A gift from Braduk. Has someone been teaching you manners?
- Grateful. No one here will believe it, but grateful.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You would use this to raid someone, and that someone would probably be us.
- We gain nothing here but a better-armed neighbor.
- Not a chance. Even an orc can see this is lopsided.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go home and argue with your priestesses for a while.
- Agreed. Your goddess may be disappointed, but she will cope.
- So be it. Rebuild Braduk, and build it with fewer pyres.

#### Refuses peace
- You would raid again before the ink was dry. No.
- Not while our towns are still smoking.
- Not yet. Your warlords have not learned the lesson.

#### Rejects a demand
- I paid no tribute to the gods, so why would I pay it to the children of a fallen one?
- No. If you want it, you will have to come for it, and our adventurers are bored.
- Your axe is very large. Our answer is still no.

### Grigori → Doviello

#### First contact
- You survived the ice without kneeling to Mulcarn. So did we. The difference is that we did not have to become wolves to do it.
- Greetings, Doviello. Both our peoples refused a master in the Age of Ice. I wonder if we have anything else in common.
- We are the Grigori. You say only the strong deserve to live; we say everyone deserves to choose. We will probably disagree.

#### Declares war
- You prey on the weak and call it nature. We call it an invitation. Here we come.
- Your pack has hunted our villages for the last time.
- You only respect strength. Very well, let us show you some.

#### Refuses to talk
- You think diplomacy is a trick of the weak. Then talk to my adventurers instead.
- No. Wolves do not negotiate, they say, and today neither do we.
- Not while your pack is howling at our walls.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Doviello. You are honest about what you want, which is rarer than you might think.
- Come in. You smell of the wastes, but you speak plainly, and I like that.
- Ah, the pack leader. What is it you need?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Speak, and keep your teeth to yourself.
- Your raiders have been testing our borders. What now?
- You sized us up as prey. Was it a disappointment?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Straightforward, the way your people like it.
- Done, and no blood spilled. Your shamans will be appalled.
- We accept. Good hunting.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the pack? Thank you. I did not know wolves shared.
- Grateful, Doviello. I will be honest: we did not expect it.
- Thank you. It takes a strong people to be generous, and you have proved it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We would only be feeding the pack that hunts us.
- We gain nothing from this, Doviello. Not even a good fight.
- No. Strength is not the same thing as a good offer.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go home and lick your wounds, and we will lick ours.
- Agreed. You fought hard; tell your pack it was well done.
- So be it. Even wolves know when to stop circling.

#### Refuses peace
- You would only come back stronger. No.
- Not while your pack still thinks of us as prey.
- You wanted a fight. You have one, until it is finished.

#### Rejects a demand
- Only the weak pay the strong, and we are not weak.
- No. Come and take it, if your pack is hungry enough.
- You ask for tribute like a beggar with fangs. No.

### Grigori → Elohim

#### First contact
- Greetings, Elohim. Your first master left Sirona's service to tend men the gods had trampled. Why, then, do you still tend the gods' shrines?
- We are the Grigori. You witnessed the Compact, and we wanted it to go much further. Let us compare notes.
- Pilgrims, are you? Then you should visit us. We have no shrines at all, which you may find restful.

#### Declares war
- You guard the gods' holy places as if the gods deserved them. We have decided they do not.
- Your shrines anchor the gods' hold on this world. We are going to loosen it.
- You keep the sacred sites from our adventurers, as if they belonged to the gods and not to men. We will open them.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not hear another sermon on peace from a people at war.
- No. Pray on it, if you like.
- Not now. Your monks are disarming our soldiers with their bare hands, and I am too irritated to talk.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Elohim. You are the only devout people I can spend an hour with.
- Come in, pilgrim. We have no shrine for you, but the wine is good.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. Still tending the gods' gardens? Sit, and tell me what grows.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You call our adventurers grave robbers. Speak, and be specific.
- Your monks have been preaching humility in our marketplaces. What now?
- Speak, Elohim. Serenely, if you must.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. You bargain like saints, which is to say fairly.
- Done, and no god required.
- We accept, and we will not tell anyone how easy it was.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. Charity with no altar attached; that is the Elohim I like.
- Grateful. If every believer were like you, I would have far fewer arguments.
- Thank you. We will put it to work, not on a shrine.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Our gain would be nothing, and the gods' gain would be your next shrine.
- We decline. Kindly, but firmly.
- No. Not even for monks.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. You never wanted this war, and to be honest, neither did we.
- Agreed. Go back to your shrines, and we will go back to ignoring them.
- So be it. The gods would be glad to see us fight; let us disappoint them.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your monks hold the sites we fought for.
- You want peace because your monks are tired. So are ours, but we are nearly done.
- Not yet. A little longer and those shrines will belong to everyone.

#### Rejects a demand
- You ask in the name of the common good. And which god decided what that is?
- No. You give to the poor, and we are not poor.
- I do not answer prayers, Elohim, not even polite ones.

### Grigori → Hippus

#### First contact
- The Hippus. You measure a tribe's worth in foreign gold rather than in prayers. You will fit in well around here.
- Greetings, horse lords. We hear your companies will ride for anyone who pays. We may be hiring.
- We are the Grigori. We bow to no god, and you bow to no paymaster for long. Let us be friends while it lasts.

#### Declares war
- Someone paid you to ride against us, I suppose. Tell them it was money wasted.
- Your companies have raided our caravans once too often. Our adventurers can ride as well.
- Business is business, as your people like to say. Today our business is with your herds.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not parley with hirelings. Send me your employer.
- Not now. Your riders are still grazing their horses in our pastures.
- No. Come back when your contract runs out.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Hippus. It is always good to see free riders.
- Come in, friend. Hippus companies have guarded our borders well before now, and the Grigori pay their debts.
- Looking for work, or have you come to sell horses?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders ran off our herds. What do you want now?
- Speak, rider. Whoever is paying you this season, it is not us.
- One of your companies changed sides on our border halfway through a contract. Talk fast.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A good bargain, rider.
- Done. Gold is honest, at least, whatever else is not.
- We accept. Shrewd as ever, [CT_NAME].

#### Thanks for a gift
- A Hippus giving without sending an invoice? Remarkable. Thank you.
- Grateful. Remind me to hire your companies the next time we need riders.
- Thank you, friend. That is worth more to us than any contract.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your price is fair for mercenaries, but we raise our own adventurers.
- The Grigori gain nothing here. Find a richer customer.
- No. I know a horse trader's bargain when I see one.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and raid someone else, preferably someone devout.
- Agreed. Now, about that contract we discussed before all this started...
- So be it. Your riders were the best enemies we have had in years.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your riders are burning our granaries.
- You want peace because your employer stopped paying. That is not our problem.
- Not yet. We are winning this one, and you know it.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? We hire mercenaries; we do not pay them for nothing.
- No. You would only spend it on more horses to raid us with.
- Charge us for a service, Hippus, not for the privilege of existing.

### Grigori → Illians

#### First contact
- So you are the Illians, and you mean to become a god. We have known gods. We do not recommend them.
- Greetings, Illians. Mulcarn is gone and you are looking for his replacement. We had hoped the position would stay empty.
- We are the Grigori. We turned our backs on the gods; you, we hear, are trying to grow a new one.

#### Declares war
- The world already has too many gods. We will not let you add another.
- Your god's winter cost the world an age. We will not let you buy it back.
- You call yourselves the lost men. Stay lost.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not bargain with would-be gods. They never keep their bargains.
- If I wished to speak with gods, I would never have left them. No.
- Not now. Your frost is still on our fields.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Illian. Keep your divinity to yourself and we will get along.
- Come in. It is warm here; you may not like it.
- Still mortal, [CT_NAME]? Good. Stay that way.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You look at our people as if they were future worshippers. Speak.
- Your White Hand priests are preaching in our villages. What now?
- Speak, Illian. The cold does not impress us.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Mortal to mortal, while you still are one.
- Done. A fair trade, even from the far north.
- We accept. Cold, but honest.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from Letum Frigus? Thank you. I will check it for frost.
- Grateful. I would much rather have your gifts than your worship.
- Thank you. Generosity is a very mortal habit. Keep it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Anything that helps you toward godhood, we refuse on principle.
- The Grigori gain nothing, and you gain a step toward heaven. No.
- We decline. Find another fool to warm your altars.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Use it to remember that you are human.
- Agreed. Back to your caverns, then, and your ghosts.
- So be it. Let the world stay awake a little longer.

#### Refuses peace
- Your ambitions do not stop at a peace treaty, so neither will we.
- Not while you still dream of a throne in heaven.
- No. A god in the making keeps no treaties.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to a god-in-waiting? We have paid quite enough to the ones already there.
- No. Offerings are for gods, and you are not one yet.
- You must be mistaken; the Grigori make no offerings, to anyone.

### Grigori → Infernal

#### First contact
- Demons. The gods built your hell and now they have let it out. One more reason we do not trust them.
- We are the Grigori. We know what hell is, a prison the gods made. We pity those held inside it, but not those who climb out.
- Greetings, Infernals. Our city is full of ghosts the Ashen Veil made. They have told us all about you.

#### Declares war
- Your Ashen Veil butchered our children on cellar altars. The Grigori have long memories.
- This world was left to men, not to the servants of Agares. Back you go.
- No god will save the world from you. Then men will have to.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not bargain with hell. Hell always reads the contract more carefully.
- No. Go and torment someone else.
- Not today, demon. Not any day.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- We are at peace, demon, and we mean to keep it so. What do you want?
- Speak. Every word you say is being written down.
- Come in, but do not touch anything.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You stink of sulfur and lies. Speak.
- Your cultists left a child on an altar in our lands. What now?
- Speak, demon, and then leave.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Our clerks will be looking for the catch.
- Done. Note that no souls are included. Read it again.
- We accept, but every word stays exactly as it was written.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from hell? We will find out the price later, I suppose.
- Thank you, I suppose. We will keep it far away from the children.
- Grateful, and suspicious, in equal measure.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Hell's bargains are paid in installments forever.
- The Grigori gain nothing here except a claim on our souls.
- No. I can smell the small print from here.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. But your cults stay out of our cellars.
- Agreed. Go and sit in your own fires.
- So be it. We will be watching every one of your gates.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while the Veil still sacrifices our people.
- Peace with hell lasts exactly until hell is ready. No.
- No. We will see you back in the pit first.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demons demanding tribute? The answer was decided long before you asked.
- No. Not gold, not blood, not souls.
- Our souls are our own, and so is our treasury.

### Grigori → Khazad

#### First contact
- The Khazad, who barely noticed the Age of Ice. We noticed it, and we came through it with no god's help.
- Greetings, dwarf. Your people learned to trust no foreigner, and ours learned to trust no god. We might understand each other.
- We are the Grigori. We hear you count your gold carefully. Good; we count our freedoms the same way.

#### Declares war
- Your vaults are full, and now you want our mines as well. Come and take them.
- You learned long ago to distrust the outside world. We are about to show you why you were right.
- Your siege engines are famous. Our adventurers would like to see them up close.

#### Refuses to talk
- We are done haggling with dwarves for today.
- No. Your engines are still at our gates.
- Not now. Go back under your mountain.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Khazad. Honest gold and honest talk, as always.
- Come in, dwarf. There are no illusions here; you will like that.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. What do your vaults need today?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your merchants overcharged our caravans. Speak.
- You say foreigner as if it were a curse. Speak.
- Speak, dwarf, and stop counting our silver while you do.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. The Khazad know a bargain, and so do we.
- Done, and not a single illusion in it.
- We accept. Fair weight, fair price.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the vaults? I will mark the day on the calendar.
- Thank you, dwarf. That is more generosity than your ancestors ever got from the world.
- Grateful. Kilmorph did not send this; you did. That is why it counts.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even a dwarf's arithmetic is not usually that creative.
- The Grigori gain nothing, and your vaults gain everything.
- No. You know as well as we do that it is not fair.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your forges.
- Agreed. Neither of us needs more names carved on the walls of the dead.
- So be it. Trade suits us both better than war.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your sappers are under our walls.
- You would only refill your vaults for the next round. No.
- Not yet, dwarf. You started this.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to fill your vaults? You were cheated once, and now you would cheat us.
- No. Self-reliance, dwarf. Your own people taught it to the world.
- We pay for goods, not for threats.

### Grigori → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- The Kuriotates. You take in anyone who comes to your gates, and so do we. Our refugees may get on well together.
- Greetings. We hear your people call your throne divine. The Grigori have opinions about divinity.
- We are the Grigori. Centaurs, giants, lamia and men under one banner; that is the kind of world we would like to see.

#### Declares war
- Your settlements swallow free land and call it royal territory. We prefer it free.
- Your confederation grows by decree. We will not be decreed into it.
- You say anyone may join you. We say no one must.

#### Refuses to talk
- Not while your centaurs are in our pastures.
- No. Your court is too polite to say anything true.
- Come back with an offer, not a decree.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, friend. Your refugees and ours have a great deal in common.
- Come in, Kuriotate. Tell me how you keep so many peoples content under one roof.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. Still building something to last the ages?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your royal surveyors were in our hills again. What now?
- Your state superstitions are spreading into our towns. Speak.
- Speak, Kuriotate, without the courtly flourishes.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Good for both of us.
- Done. Your bureaucrats are surprisingly reasonable.
- We accept. Fair, and clearly written.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, friend. Generosity suits a confederation of so many peoples.
- Grateful. We will share it with the refugees in our own cities.
- Thank you. No one could call that a superstition.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your settlements would gain, and we would lose.
- The Grigori gain nothing here. Politely, no.
- We decline, friend. Bring us something both sides can live with.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let refugees be the only thing crossing our borders from now on.
- Agreed. Your turtle can come out of its shell now.
- So be it. Two havens should never have fought.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your settlements sit on our land.
- You would only draw back into your shell and strike again later. No.
- Not yet. Your centaurs have not gone home.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Your throne may be divine to your people; to us it is just another neighbor.
- A demand? That is not how you do things, as I recall.
- We earned what we have, and so can you.

### Grigori → Lanun

#### First contact
- The Lanun. Free men on free seas, answering to no one but another captain. I think we will like each other.
- Greetings, captain. A Lanun ship once carried a gift of ours toward the Amurites and vanished in the ice. We do not hold it against you. Much.
- We are the Grigori. We hear Danalin stopped answering your priests. Welcome; we stopped asking long ago.

#### Declares war
- Your pirates have taken our merchantmen once too often. We are coming for your harbors.
- Some of your captains now take orders from the Overlords beneath the waves. We will not let those voices reach our shores.
- Your captains conscript any man they please. They took ours, and we have come to collect.

#### Refuses to talk
- No, captain. Your word is fleeting, and I am tired of chasing it across the waves.
- Not now. Your ships are still off our coast.
- Go back to your ship and stay there.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, captain. Free men talk best over a cup of wine.
- Come in, Lanun. Any good stories from the islands?
- Still free, still sailing? Good. What brings you ashore?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders sank one of our merchantmen. Speak.
- Speak, captain, and do not try to charm us.
- You gave us your word. Where is it now?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Free trade between free peoples.
- Done. I will trust your word for exactly as long as it matters.
- We accept, you old sea dog.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, captain. And not even stolen? Impressive.
- Grateful. The sea was generous to you, and you to us.
- Thank you. We will drink to your ships tonight.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. I have seen better bargains at a pirates' auction.
- The Grigori gain nothing here but a lighter purse.
- No, captain. Not even with that smile.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to the sea, where you belong.
- Agreed. Free peoples should not be at each other's throats.
- So be it. Your ships are welcome in our harbors again.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your ships blockade our coast.
- You want peace to take on fresh water and new crews. No.
- Not yet, captain. The tide is with us.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. We do not pay pirates.
- You cannot charm it out of us, captain.
- A free people pays no tolls, not to the sea and not to those who sail it.

### Grigori → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- Greetings, elves. Your god died and another was raised to fill his seat. You of all people should know that gods can be replaced.
- We are the Grigori. We have heard of a Fellowship that kills its own kind for cutting the wrong tree. We hope that is only a rumor.
- The Ljosalfar. Your forests are beautiful. Your priests, less so.

#### Declares war
- Your Fellowship kills men for the crime of building a home from the wrong tree. We will build its victims a better one.
- Your druids think every oak is holier than a man. We disagree, and we have brought axes.
- You punish mortals in the name of a god of nature. We have come to argue the point.

#### Refuses to talk
- Not while your archers are in our woods.
- No. Your elders take a century to answer anything, so we can wait a little.
- Come back when the Fellowship has stopped killing woodcutters.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, elf. Our foresters have learned to ask permission. Mostly.
- Come in. You live long enough to watch gods come and go; you must have opinions.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. How are the trees?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your rangers shot one of our woodcutters. Speak.
- You look at our cities as if they were a blight on the land. What do you want?
- Speak, elf, and not in verse.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Fair, and with a minimum of ceremony.
- Done. Your patience pays off, for once.
- We accept. Very sensible, for the Summer Court.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, elf. Generosity from the forest is rarer than an ancient oak.
- Grateful. I will plant something in your honor, if that pleases you.
- Thank you. No god asked you to give it; that is why it matters.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We would gain nothing, and your groves would gain everything.
- We decline, quietly, so as not to upset the trees.
- No. Not this season.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your groves; we will mind where we cut.
- Agreed. Let the forest heal, and our villages with it.
- So be it. A long war means nothing to elves, but it means a great deal to us.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your treants are crushing our villages.
- You can wait a century for a better peace. We cannot, so we will finish this now.
- No. Your Fellowship has not answered for our dead.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the forest? The trees have not asked.
- No. The Summer Court has more than enough already.
- We do not pay for the privilege of breathing your air.

### Grigori → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- The Luchuirp. You lost an empire to the ice and rebuilt it with your own hands. That is the kind of story the Grigori like best.
- Greetings, golem-makers. Your servants never pray, never complain and never kneel to anyone. We approve.
- We are the Grigori. Kilmorph taught your fathers to dig, we hear, but the golems were entirely your own idea.

#### Declares war
- Your golems have trampled our fields. We will see how they fare against adventurers.
- You build armies that cannot refuse an order. We find that more frightening than any god.
- Our adventurers have been asking for a real challenge. Your clockwork will do nicely.

#### Refuses to talk
- Not while your golems are still marching on our towns.
- No. Go back to your workshop and tinker.
- We will talk when your war-engines have stopped ticking.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, artificer. What have you built lately?
- Come in, Luchuirp. Our engineers want to see your latest golem; please do not let them take it apart.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. It is good to see a people who trust their own hands.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems knocked down one of our granaries. Speak.
- You are busy, and so are we. What is it?
- Speak, Luchuirp. Our patience does not run on clockwork.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Precise and fair, like your engineering.
- Done. A well-crafted bargain.
- We accept. You build agreements as well as you build golems.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you, friend. One thing made by mortal hands is worth ten handed down by a god.
- Grateful. We will take good care of it; we know how long it took to make.
- Thank you. The Open-Skiers would be proud of their heirs.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. The gears do not mesh on this one.
- The Grigori gain nothing. Recalibrate and try again.
- No. Even a golem could see this is not balanced.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your workshops, then.
- Agreed. Send your golems to the fields, where they do some good.
- So be it. Your craft is wasted on war.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your golems hold our towns.
- You would only build more of them in the quiet. No.
- Not yet. Your engines are still on our side of the hills.

#### Rejects a demand
- Build it yourself. You are rather good at that.
- No. Your people rebuilt a whole nation from a single clan; you can manage without our gold.
- We pay tribute to no one, not even to the finest clockmakers in Erebus.

### Grigori → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim. Your Empyrean judges each case on its merits instead of by a codex. For believers, that is almost sensible.
- Greetings, children of the sun. We do not worship Lugus, but we will not complain about the daylight.
- We are the Grigori. You found a god in the desert. We found that we could do without one.

#### Declares war
- Your Radiant Guard brings light whether people want it or not. We do not want it.
- You call our people shadows. Let us see how shadows fight.
- Your Vicars preach in our towns that we live in darkness. We will show you who is blind.

#### Refuses to talk
- I am in no mood for a sermon about light.
- No. Come back when the sun has set on your temper.
- Not while your armies are camped in our valleys.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Malakim. Your Empyrean gives small nations an equal voice, and we appreciate that.
- Come in out of the sun, friend, and have some water.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. What brings you out of the desert?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You say we walk in shadow. Speak.
- Your Vicars have been preaching to our refugees. What do you want?
- Speak, and spare us the imagery about dawn.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and judged on its merits, the way you like it.
- Done. Fair and clear, like a desert sky.
- We accept. Your Empyrean would approve, and so do we.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. Generous as the sun, and far less likely to burn us.
- Grateful. We will put it to good use, here and now.
- Thank you, friend. No god is needed to see the kindness in this.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Judged on its merits, this one fails.
- The Grigori gain nothing here, however bright the offer looks.
- No. Even in broad daylight, this looks bad.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the sun shine on something else for a while.
- Agreed. The world is wide enough for those who worship and those who do not.
- So be it. Equal voices again, as your Empyrean teaches.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your Radiant Guard holds our towns.
- You would only wait for a brighter dawn to strike again. No.
- Not yet. Our people have not finished being enlightened by your armies.

#### Rejects a demand
- Your Empyrean gives an equal voice to the small and the great. Our voice says no.
- No. The sun gives freely; so can you.
- We do not tithe to Lugus, nor to anyone who preaches in his name.

### Grigori → Mercurians

#### First contact
- You left your god to keep on fighting. The Grigori left the gods to stop. Strange that we should meet.
- Greetings, Mercurians. You broke the Compact because it did not go far enough against hell. We thought it did not go far enough against heaven.
- We are the Grigori. You care little for mortals, they say. We are mortals. Shall we go on?

#### Declares war
- Your crusade tramples whatever lies between you and the nearest demon, and today that is us.
- You think heaven's war gives you a right to our lands. It does not.
- Even angels who have left their gods behind can be wrong. We have come to prove it.

#### Refuses to talk
- You have no time for mortals. Today we have none for you.
- No. Your hammers have said enough.
- Not until your host has left our fields.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, angel. We all fight the Ashen Veil, one way or another.
- Come in. You broke with your lords and we broke with the gods. We have more in common than you think.
- Speak, then. I know you dislike delay.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You treat our people as kindling for your war. Speak.
- Your rage is old news. What do you want?
- Speak, angel, and put down the hammer.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Go and kill demons with it.
- Done, and quickly, as you prefer.
- We accept. Even rebels need supplies.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. I did not think you noticed mortals at all.
- Grateful, angel. That was most unlike you.
- Thank you. Perhaps not every angel is a lost cause.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your war is not ours to pay for.
- The Grigori gain nothing here except a seat in someone else's crusade.
- No. Find another sponsor for your war on hell.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to hell; that is the war you actually want.
- Agreed. The demons are laughing at us both.
- So be it. Two peoples who said no to heaven should not fight each other.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your host occupies our towns.
- You would only come back the next time you smelled a demon near us.
- Not yet. You have not paid for the villages you burned on your way to the pit.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Heaven does not get our gold, and neither do its runaways.
- You demand as if you still spoke for a god. You do not.
- Fight your war with your own resources, angel.

### Grigori → Sheaim

#### First contact
- The Sheaim. You work to end the world for a goddess's bargain. We will not let a god, or her servants, make that choice for us.
- Greetings. You think the end of creation will set you free. We think it will simply be the end.
- We are the Grigori. One day the doors will open, we believe, but they will not be opened by burning down the house.

#### Declares war
- You would end the world to keep a promise to Ceridwen. We are not done with it yet.
- Every gate you open lets in something the gods made. We are going to close them.
- Your Armageddon will have to wait until we are all dead, and we intend to be stubborn about that.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not negotiate with people who want everything dead.
- No. Count down to the end without us.
- Not while your gates stand open.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Sheaim. Still waiting for the end?
- Come in. You seem almost cheerful, for an apocalypse.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. How goes the end of the world?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your gates are spitting horrors across our border. Speak.
- You would bring down the sky to escape your own prison. What do you want?
- Speak, and quickly. We have a world to keep running.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A sensible trade, for people who have a future.
- Done. Odd that you bother, but done.
- We accept. Perhaps you like this world more than you say.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. A gift is wasted on the apocalypse, so it is good you gave it to us.
- Grateful. We will use it to make the world worth keeping.
- Thank you. A strange present from those who want everything gone.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We will not help pay for the end of the world.
- The Grigori gain nothing, and the apocalypse gains a little. No.
- No. Not even a small down payment on doom.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. The world gets a little longer.
- Agreed. Go back to your rituals, and keep them small.
- So be it. Let the end wait its turn.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while a single one of your gates still hums along our border.
- You would only use the time to finish your ritual. No.
- Not yet. We have more gates to close.

#### Rejects a demand
- Why would you need gold, if the world is ending anyway?
- No. Our treasury intends to outlive your prophecies.
- Wait for the end, and then you can have everything.

### Grigori → Sidar

#### First contact
- The Sidar. You traded pieces of your souls for time to learn, and answered to no god for it. We almost approve.
- Greetings, grey ones. You have watched the younger races for ages. What have you concluded about us?
- We are the Grigori. You hide from the world, and we invite it in. Let us see which of us learns more.

#### Declares war
- You stand apart from the world until it suits you. It now suits us to make you stand somewhere else.
- Your shades have been watching our people for too long. We would like you to leave.
- Very hard to kill, you say. Our adventurers love a challenge.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You barely notice us anyway.
- Not now, shade.
- Come back when you are entirely here.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Sidar. You look a little more solid than last time.
- Come in, and tell us what you have learned over the last few centuries.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. Still here, then?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your shades walk our streets unseen. Speak.
- You watch us the way we watch insects. What do you want?
- Speak, grey one.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, for as long as either of us cares.
- Done. A fair trade, now and for an age or two.
