- We accept. Knowledge for knowledge, the only honest coin.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. I am surprised you noticed us long enough to give it.
- Grateful. A gift from those who outlive everyone is worth keeping.
- Thank you, Sidar. There is some warmth left in you after all.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You can wait for a better one; you have the time.
- The Grigori gain nothing. Come back in a century.
- No. We are mortal, and we cannot afford that price.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your hidden cities with you.
- Agreed. Let us both return to what matters.
- So be it. A blink for you, a generation for us.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your shades occupy our towns.
- You would only wait us out. No.
- Not yet. You may have forever, but we have this year.

#### Rejects a demand
- You need nothing, you have said so. So you will get nothing.
- No. Immortality ought to have taught you patience.
- We earned what we have. You have eternity to earn yours.

### Grigori → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Svartalfar. Your court replaced a dead god with Esus by decree. That was halfway to wisdom; you simply chose the wrong half.
- Greetings, Winter Court. We hear you do not betray and kill all of your allies. We would like to stay among the lucky ones.
- We are the Grigori. You keep secrets for Esus; we keep none for anyone.

#### Declares war
- Your assassins have been in our cities for too long. Now our soldiers will be in yours.
- You punished your own kin for praying to the wrong god. We punish no one for that, but we will punish you.
- Your court likes knives in the dark. Let us try daylight.

#### Refuses to talk
- Every word from you has a knife behind it. No.
- Not while your shadows are in our halls.
- No. We have read your history, all of it.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Svartalfar. Please leave your knives at the door. All of them.
- Come in. We have nothing hidden here; you may find that confusing.
- Ah, [CT_NAME]. To what do we owe the danger?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- We found your assassins. Speak.
- You smile as if you knew all our secrets. What do you want?
- Speak, dark elf.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and our clerks found only two traps in it.
- Done. Honest dealing; how novel for your court.
- We accept. Keep your end, and we will be watching.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Thank you. We will check it for poison, of course.
- Grateful, and surprised in equal measure.
- Thank you. Giving in the open; Esus would be scandalized.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There is a blade in this bargain somewhere.
- The Grigori gain nothing here but a target on our backs.
- No. Not with your court, not this time.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your shadows at home.
- Agreed. We will be watching.
- So be it. We will count our citizens every morning, just to be sure.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your assassins are in our cities.
- You would sign it and then sharpen your knives. No.
- Not yet. Your court has not paid for its knives in the dark.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Persuasion takes more than knives.
- Demands from the Winter Court? We are not your kin, to be cowed by them.
- We give nothing to those who would stab us for it.

## Hippus

### Hippus → Amurites

#### First contact
- Amurites! When Kylorin hunted his wayward pupils across Patria, it was Hippus lances that rode them down. Remember who your friends were.
- Well met, Amurite. Your portals and conjured beasts once made our horses look like toys. The portals are gone, and the horses are still here.
- The Hippus greet you, wizard. We have chased the hills of Nimarail clear of your scholars before; let us hope we never need to again.

#### Declares war
- A war-mage casting a spell stands very still. Our riders have always liked that about your kind.
- Nothing personal, Amurite. Someone paid well, and your schools have soft walls.
- Our grandfathers charged down the warrior mages of Patria for Kylorin. Today we do it for ourselves.

#### Refuses to talk
- Words are your weapon, wizard, not ours. Save them.
- No. Your archmages would take a season to agree on a reply anyway.
- Idle talk with spellcasters? Not while our lances are still warm.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the scholars! Need an escort for your siege-mages? They ride like sacks of grain, but we will get them there.
- Well met, [CT_NAME]. Your mages and our horses together could take any city in Erebus. Shall we talk prices?
- Welcome, Amurite. Have your schools finally learned to ride? No? Then you still need us.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You look at our riders the way your archmages look at a failed student. Say your piece.
- Your fireballs scared off half our herds last season. You owe us horses. What do you want?
- Speak quickly, wizard. Our mounts do not like the smell of your magic.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. You bargain hard for a bookworm.
- Agreed. Gold from a wizard spends the same as gold from anyone else.
- A fair deal, Amurite. Our companies will remember it when you need riders.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift? From an Amurite? I will have the riders check it for curses, but thank you.
- Generous, scholar. The Hippus repay a kindness, in hoofbeats if need be.
- You honor our clans. Next time you need a mage hunted down, the first ride is free.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? You would not offer that to a pack mule. Try again.
- No, wizard. Your magic may be priceless, but your gold is not, and this needs more of it.
- After all the mages we rode down for your founder? You can do better than this.

#### Agrees to peace
- Fair enough. We have taken our plunder, and your wizards can go back to their books.
- Peace, then. Tell your archmages they fought well, for men who cannot ride.
- Done. We are always ready for a raid; if you know any good targets, send word.

#### Refuses peace
- Your granaries are still full and your mages are slow. Why stop now?
- No. We have not been paid to stop, and you have not offered enough.
- You started this with fire. We will finish it with hooves.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand from scholars? Write us a thesis on it, and we will use it to light our fires.
- No. If your mages want our gold, they can try to conjure it.
- You aren't as persuasive as your schools think you are. Let us see how well you make your case on the field.

### Hippus → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- So this is the mad court! Your coin bought Hippus riders once, to fetch your court some dwarven slaves. It spent well.
- Well met, Balseraph. We hear your jesters fight like dancers. Ours fight from the saddle, which is better.
- The Hippus greet you. Laugh all you like, but count the riders before you laugh too long.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, clowns. Your festivals are rich, your harlequins are slow, and business is business.
- Your taskmasters took Hippus riders for your puppet shows. We are coming to collect our kin, and your treasury.
- Toy soldiers need a battle, your court says. Very well, here comes the cavalry.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not stand still for a riddle while my riders are under your harlequins' knives.
- No. Your court talks in rhyme, and our horses do not like poetry.
- Talk is for the stage, Balseraph. This is a battlefield.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Balseraph! Still paying in gold, or is it puppets this season?
- Welcome. Our riders loved the last festival in Jubilee, though a few came home wearing strange masks.
- Need riders for your next game, [CT_NAME]? Name the stakes.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your mimics stole the skills of three of our best captains. Speak, and keep your freaks behind you.
- What now, jester? Your laughter is getting on our horses' nerves.
- Speak plainly. The Hippus do not play your games for free.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done, and our clerk read it twice for tricks.
- Agreed. Your court is mad, but its gold is sane enough.
- A shrewd deal, Balseraph. Now pay before you forget you made it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the mad court? I suspect a trick, but I will take it.
- Our thanks, Balseraph. You are an odd friend, but a generous one.
- You honor our clans. We will drink to your court, and keep one eye open.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? You want us to ride for laughter? Pay in coin.
- No, jester. That bargain has more trapdoors than your palace.
- After all the work we did for your court? Can't you do better than this?

#### Agrees to peace
- Fine. The game was fun while it lasted. Shall we play another, with someone else as the target?
- Peace. Keep your harlequins home, and we will keep our lances sheathed.
- Done. Our riders could use a rest from dodging your dancers.

#### Refuses peace
- Your court is still rich, and we have only taken half of it. No.
- You want to change the rules mid-game? Not this time.
- When there is still plunder in Jubilee? Nah.

#### Rejects a demand
- Not sharing makes us bad playmates, does it? Then we are bad playmates.
- No. Hire us, or leave us be; we do not give.
- Ask the puppets in your court to pay you. Our purse stays shut.

### Hippus → Bannor

#### First contact
- The Bannor! A people forever at war. You will need riders, and we have the best in Erebus.
- Well met, crusaders. Your Orders take fighters from every nation; ours come with their own horses.
- The Hippus greet you. Your drill is famous. So is our charge. Let us hope we meet on the same side.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, Bannor. Your garrison towns are rich, and someone has paid us to visit.
- You call everyone who is not under your Law an enemy. Today you are right.
- Your farms are castles, they say. Our riders have never minded a long ride around a wall.

#### Refuses to talk
- You preach before you trade. We do neither with an army at our backs.
- No. Your priests would only tell us we are damned.
- Idle chat is for the Confessors, not for warriors.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Bannor! How goes the crusade? Need some fast riders for the flanks?
- Welcome, [CT_NAME]. Your Orders are the best paymasters in Erebus, as long as the war lasts.
- Ah, the soldiers of Law. Our companies are ready whenever your priests point at the next enemy.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Confessors called our riders godless brigands. Speak.
- You look at us like the next name on your list of the damned. What do you want?
- Speak, crusader, and leave the sermon at home.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, a just and equitable deal, as your people like to say.
- Agreed. You pay on time, Bannor, which is more than most.
- Done. Our companies will ride for your crusade at this price.

#### Thanks for a gift
- You are an honorable friend, Bannor. The Hippus will not forget.
- A gift without a sermon? Our thanks.
- Generous of you. When your crusade next marches, our riders will remember.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? For a crusade? Holy wars cost more than that.
- No. Your priests may accept faith as payment, but we do not.
- After all the battles we fought on your flanks? You can do better.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your crusade; we have other customers.
- Fine. Your soldiers fought well. Our riders would welcome a contract with them, instead of against.
- Done. Now, do you know any good targets? Not you, of course.

#### Refuses peace
- Your estates are still rich and your Orders are still marching. Why stop?
- No. Your priests would just name us damned again tomorrow.
- When your free land is still full of fat villages? Nah.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute for the crusade? We are mercenaries, not converts.
- No. If your priests want our gold, they can pray for it.
- You aren't as persuasive as you think, crusader. We will see how your drill holds up against a charge.

### Hippus → Calabim

#### First contact
- The Calabim. Your nobles say our people smell of horse. Better than smelling of blood, I always say.
- Well met, vampire. You keep herds of men, we keep herds of horses. Ours are happier.
- The Hippus greet you, but our riders will keep their collars buttoned high.

#### Declares war
- Your nobles grow fat on their own people. We are coming to take back what they have stolen, and keep it.
- Nothing personal, Calabim. Your castles are full of silver, and silver is our trade.
- Fast hunters, you say, tireless and keen-eyed? Let us see how you do against cavalry at noon.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not parley with things that eat their own herds.
- No. Your envoys keep eyeing our horses, and I do not mean for riding.
- Idle talk with the dead? Not today.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Calabim. Your gold is good, even if your manners are hungry. What is it?
- Welcome, but no drinks, thank you. We will stay with wine.
- Need riders, [CT_NAME]? We take silver, not blood.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your nobles have been hunting our grooms. Speak.
- Speak, vampire, and keep your teeth behind your lips.
- You look at us like a meal on horseback. What do you want?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Paid in coin, not in throats.
- Agreed. Even the dead pay well, it seems.
- A shrewd deal, Calabim. You have had centuries to practice.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Calabim! I will not ask where it came from.
- Our thanks. Generous, for a people who usually take.
- You honor our clans. Our riders will still sleep with their swords, though.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? You want us to work for that? Even your herds get better.
- No. The Hippus do not sell their riders to be eaten.
- After all this? Find someone hungrier for gold.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your Broods in their castles, and we keep our horses in the fields.
- Fine. We have taken enough silver to make the war worth it.
- Done. Your herds can keep their blood; we have their gold.

#### Refuses peace
- Your castles are still full of silver. Why stop?
- No. Your nobles would hunt our grooms by night again.
- When there is so much to plunder from your estates? Nah.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? Feed on your own people, not on our purse.
- No. Even your threats smell of blood.
- You aren't as frightening as you think, vampire. Let us see you on the field in daylight.

### Hippus → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- The Clan of Embers! Orcs who live by raiding. So do we. Let us agree not to raid each other, at least not first.
- Well met, orc. Your goblins ride wolves, we hear. Wolves tire. Horses tire later.
- The Hippus greet you. Your warriors come cheap and many, and ours come few and dear. Some day we will find out which is worth more.

#### Declares war
- Your raiders drove off our herds. Now our riders come to drive off yours, and burn the camp behind them.
- Nothing personal, orc. Somebody paid us to clear their roads, and your war-bands are standing on them.
- You think the Clan are the best raiders in Erebus. We have come to settle that question.

#### Refuses to talk
- Talk with orcs? Go and chew on your axe.
- No. Not while your goblins are still in our pastures.
- Your shamans can do the talking with your goddess. We have nothing to say.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Clan! How goes the raiding season?
- Welcome, orc. Fancy a raid together? We bring the speed, you bring the numbers, and we split it fair.
- Need riders to carry the loot home faster, [CT_NAME]? We charge by the saddlebag.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your goblins stole three of our best mares. Speak.
- Your torches are too close to our stables. What do you want?
- Speak, orc, and keep that axe on the ground.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Not bad haggling for an orc.
- Agreed. Trading beats raiding, now and then.
- Done. You count better than your reputation says.

#### Thanks for a gift
- An orc giving something away? Our thanks. I will tell the clans, though they will not believe me.
- Generous of you, Clan. Our riders will drink to the fires of Braduk tonight.
- You honor our clans. Hooves and fire make a fine pair, when they ride the same way.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Even a goblin could see it is lopsided.
- No. Our riders are worth more than the leftovers of your last raid.
- Come now, orc, after all the raids we could share? Can't you do better than that?

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. There is fatter prey elsewhere for both of us.
- Fine. You fought well, orc; tell your warlords we said so.
- Done. When you go raiding again, send word. Not here, of course.

#### Refuses peace
- Your camps still have plunder in them. Why would we stop?
- No, orc. Your war-bands are slow, and we are just getting started.
- When there are still herds in your hills? Nah.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? Take it from someone slower than us.
- No. Your axe is big, but our horses are faster than your arm.
- The Hippus give nothing to anyone who has not paid first, least of all to orcs.

### Hippus → Doviello

#### First contact
- The Doviello. Wolves, they call you. Our herds have known wolves for a long time, and our riders know how to deal with them.
- Well met, northman. While your pack fed on the tribes the White Hand cast out, our clans were holding the frostlings back. Remember that when you count heroes.
- The Hippus greet the pack. We both raid, and we both ride hard. The difference is that we get paid for it.

#### Declares war
- Your pack has been taking our foals. Now we come to take your pelts.
- Nothing personal, wolf. Business is business, and the pack is fat this year.
- You respect only strength. Then count our lances as they come over the hill.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not talk with wolves. I hunt them.
- No. Your pack is still circling our herds.
- Diplomacy is a trick of the weak, you say? Then stop asking for it.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Doviello! Good hunting this season?
- Welcome, northman. Your beastmen and our riders would make a fine raiding party. Interested?
- Need horses, [CT_NAME]? We will sell you the ones that do not bolt at the smell of wolf.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your wolves killed two of our herdsmen. Speak.
- You look at our horses like dinner. What do you want?
- Speak, savage, and keep your pack on a short leash.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. The easy way, for once.
- Agreed. You bargain the way you fight, straight for the throat.
- Done. Good hunting to you, northman.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A wolf sharing its kill! Our thanks, and our surprise.
- Generous, northman. The clans will hear of it around every fire.
- You honor us. Our herdsmen will leave your wolves alone for a season.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? The pack wants the whole carcass and leaves us the bones.
- No. We are not lame foals, to be cut from the herd that easily.
- Can't you do better than that, wolf? We have seen what you drag home from a raid.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. There is weaker prey than us out there, and you know where to find it.
- Fine. Our herds can graze without looking over their shoulders again.
- Done. Shall we go hunting together some time? Not each other, I mean.

#### Refuses peace
- Your camps are still full of furs and plunder. Why stop?
- No. The pack would only come back when the snow falls.
- Nah. We smell blood too, wolf.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the pack? Only the weak pay the strong, and we are not weak.
- No. Come and take it, if your wolves can catch us.
- You ask with your fangs bared. Our answer comes on hooves.

### Hippus → Elohim

#### First contact
- The Elohim! Monks who fight without weapons. We fight with nothing but weapons. Perhaps we should trade lessons.
- Well met, pilgrims. Your cities are rich in shrines and poor in cavalry. That is where we come in.
- The Hippus greet you. Your holy places need guarding and our riders need work. A good match, no?

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, monks. Your shrines are full of offerings and your guards carry no swords.
- Someone has paid us well to ride against your abbeys. Business is business.
- You would never pay for our courage, you said. Now you will face it for nothing.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not sit through a sermon on peace in the middle of a war.
- No. Your monks broke two of my best riders' arms with their bare hands, and I am not in the mood.
- Idle chat with pilgrims? Not while there is plunder left in your abbeys.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Elohim. Need riders to guard your pilgrims on the road? We are fast, and we do not stop to pray.
- Ah, the monks. Your abbeys always have room in the stables, and our horses thank you for it.
- What service can the Hippus offer the keepers of holy places, [CT_NAME]?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You called our riders bandits in your chants. Speak.
- Speak, monk, and spare us the sermon.
- You look at us as if we had trampled a garden. Well, maybe we did. What is it?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. You drive a soft bargain, which is how we like them.
- Agreed. Your gold is as holy as anyone's, and spends the same.
- Done. Our riders will guard your pilgrims at this price.

#### Thanks for a gift
- You are an honorable friend, Elohim. The clans will remember.
- A gift, and a blessing with it? Our thanks, monk.
- Generous of you. If anyone troubles your shrines, send for us first.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Even pilgrims can afford more than that.
- No. You want our riders in exchange for prayers and thanks. We want gold.
- After all the pilgrim roads we have guarded for you? Can't you do better?

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your monks hit harder than we expected.
- Fine. Go back to your shrines; we have other contracts waiting.
- Done. Now, about guarding those pilgrims of yours...

#### Refuses peace
- Your abbeys still have silver on the altars. Why stop?
- No. We have not been paid to stop, and you do not pay at all.
- When there are shrines still unplundered? Nah.

#### Rejects a demand
- Alms for the poor? We are not poor, and neither are you.
- No. Ask your gods for it; we hear you keep their houses clean.
- Your monks may move us with their fists, but not with their begging.

### Hippus → Grigori

#### First contact
- The Grigori. No gods, no priests, and coin that spends like anyone's. We will get along.
- Well met. We hear your adventurers can become anything they choose. Can they become cavalry? Ours were born to it.
- The Hippus greet you. Our companies have ridden your borders under contract before; now we get to meet the paymaster.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, Grigori. Your caravans are rich, and your adventurers are few.
- Our contract on your border has been renegotiated, and not in your favor.
- You believe every man makes his own fate. Ours today is to ride over you.

#### Refuses to talk
- No reasoning with us today, Grigori. Our lances are not philosophers.
- Not while your adventurers are hunting our riders.
- Idle chat is for old women and scholars, not for warriors.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Grigori! Need riders on your borders again?
- Welcome. Your coin is good and you never make us swear by a god. Our favorite kind of client.
- What can the Hippus do for free men today, [CT_NAME]?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your adventurers ambushed one of our companies. Speak.
- You think too much and pay too little. What now?
- Speak, Grigori, and make it reasonable, since you like reason so much.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Reasonable, as always.
- Agreed. See, no god was needed to make a good deal.
- Done. You are a shrewd one, Grigori.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Our thanks, Grigori. You are an honorable friend.
- Generous of you. Our companies will ride your borders gladly.
- A gift with no prayer attached. The clans approve.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Reason it through again, Grigori.
- No. Even free men have to pay for horses.
- After all the borders we have guarded for you? Do better.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to business, then.
- Fine. Your adventurers fight well; we might hire a few of them.
- Done. Now, shall we renegotiate that border contract?

#### Refuses peace
- Your caravans are still on the roads. Why stop?
- No. Our employer has paid for another season.
- Nah. Not while there is plunder left in your hills.

#### Rejects a demand
- You preach self-reliance, Grigori. So rely on yourself.
- No. The Hippus take gold; we do not give it.
- Clever words do not work on the Hippus, Grigori. Coin does.

### Hippus → Illians

#### First contact
- The Illians. In the Age of Ice our clans held back your god's frostling hordes, and whole camps of ours died under his frost golems. We remember.
- Well met, winter-men. Our horses do not like the cold, and neither do we. Keep it to yourselves.
- The Hippus greet you. We hear you would make yourself a god. Gods pay badly, in our experience.

#### Declares war
- Your frost golems flattened Hippus camps in the ice. Now our riders come to repay the visit.
- Nothing personal? No, this one is personal. Mulcarn's winter cost our clans too much.
- The frostlings could not stop us then, and your White Hand will not stop us now.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not parley with winter.
- No. Our dead in the snow have not forgiven you.
- Go and talk to your frost golems; they listen better than we do.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Illian. Need riders who can survive the cold? We learned how, the hard way.
- Welcome. Your coin is cold, but it spends.
- What can the Hippus do for Letum Frigus, [CT_NAME]?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your frost is creeping into our pastures. Speak.
- You look at us the way a blizzard looks at a newborn foal. What do you want?
- Speak, Illian, and quickly; our horses are freezing.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Even the north pays its debts.
- Agreed. Cold coin, warm deal.
- Done. Our riders will bring their furs.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the north? Our thanks. Surprisingly warm of you.
- Generous of you, Illian. Perhaps winter has a heart after all.
- You honor our clans. We will drink to the thaw, and to you.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Not nearly enough to ride into the snow for.
- No. Our clans lost too many to your god's winter to work for you cheaply.
- Can't you do better? The cold costs extra.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your winter north of our grass.
- Fine. Our horses want to graze in the sun again.
- Done. Let the thaw last a while.

#### Refuses peace
- Your caverns still hold treasure from the old age. Why stop?
- No. This is for the camps the frost golems flattened.
- Nah. We have long memories and fast horses.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to winter? We paid it once, in blood. Never again.
- No. Freeze if you like; our fires are our own.
- You are not a god yet, Illian. Ask again when you are, and the answer will still be no.

### Hippus → Infernal

#### First contact
- Demons. Our horses scream at the smell of you. Good instincts, horses.
- Well met, Infernal. The Hippus work for gold, and never for souls, at any price.
- The Hippus greet you. Your Gaersteeds are ugly mounts; ours are faster and do not smoke.

#### Declares war
- Even mercenaries have a line, demon, and you are on the far side of it.
- Nothing personal. Hell is simply very bad for business.
- Your hellhounds ran down our herds. Now our riders run down your hounds.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not parley with hell.
- No. Our horses will not stand still anywhere near you.
- Talk to the fires; they are the only ones listening.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Speak, Infernal, but stand downwind of the horses.
- We are at peace, demon. Keep it that way, and keep your hellhounds away from our herds.
- What do you want? We sell horses, not souls.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your hellhounds ran down our foals. Speak.
- You stink of sulfur. What now?
- Speak, demon, and then go back down where you came from.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done, and paid in gold, not in souls.
- Agreed. Our clerk checked every word twice, and the horses sniffed it.
- Done. Now leave, before the mares panic.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from hell? We will have it blessed. Twice.
- Our thanks, I suppose. The horses do not like it.
- Generous, demon. We will not ask what it cost, or whom.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There is no price for our souls.
- That? With hell's small print? No.
- No. Business is business, but not with Agares' servants.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your fires to yourself.
- Fine. Our horses will be glad to stop rearing.
- Done. Go and burn somebody else.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while your hellhounds roam our plains.
- No. Even mercenaries fight for free, against hell.
- Nah. Your gates are still burning.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to hell? Our souls are not for sale, and neither is our gold.
- No. Burn on your own fuel.
- Demand all you like. The plains are wide and our horses are fast.

### Hippus → Khazad

#### First contact
- The Khazad! Our riders know your caravans well. No one outruns the Hippus, dwarf, but we would rather escort you than chase you.
- Well met, dwarf. Your gold is famous across Erebus, and so are our lances. Let us keep them away from each other.
- The Hippus greet you. Your feet may not reach our stirrups, but your purses reach deep.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, dwarf. Your caravans are heavy, slow, and full of gold.
- No one outruns the Hippus. Your merchants are about to learn it.
- Your vaults are full and your legs are short. Business is business.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not talk with a dwarf who keeps black powder hidden in a pouch.
- No. Your musket balls are still in our horses.
- Go and talk to your hammers, dwarf.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Khazad! Need an escort for your caravans? Our rates are fair, and no one will dare ambush you.
- Welcome, dwarf. Our riders will guard your gold as if it were their own. Almost.
- What can the fastest riders in Erebus do for the richest vaults, [CT_NAME]?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your thunder-powder spooked half our herd. Speak.
- You look at us as if we were about to steal your beard. What do you want?
- Speak, dwarf, but keep your powder far from our camp.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. You know a bargain when you see one, dwarf.
- Agreed. Dwarven gold is the best kind there is.
- Done, and fairly weighed, on your scales and ours.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A dwarf giving gold away? The clans will never believe it.
- Our thanks, Khazad. It seems your vaults have a heart.
- You honor us. Your caravans will ride safe on our roads.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? A dwarf with full vaults offers that? Try again.
- No. Our riders cost more than that, and you can afford it.
- Can't you do better, after all the caravans we did not raid?

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your caravans may pass.
- Fine. Your muskets are louder than we like.
- Done. Need an escort home?

#### Refuses peace
- Your caravans are still on the road. Why stop?
- No. Your vaults are still full.
- Nah. Our riders have not been paid in dwarven gold yet.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute from us, to fill your vaults? You have gold enough for a hundred clans.
- No, dwarf. Our purses are lighter than yours, and they are staying that way.
- Come and take it, if your legs are long enough to catch us.

### Hippus → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- The Kuriotates. You have centaurs; we have horses and riders. Let us see which arrangement is better.
- Well met. Your royal shepherds pushed some of our clans out of the valley of Caledor. We have not forgotten.
- The Hippus greet you. Your great cities are rich, and our companies are for hire. You see where this is going.

#### Declares war
- Your centaurs think they are the finest horsemen in Erebus. We are coming to correct them.
- Nothing personal, Kuriotate. Your settlements are wide open and far from your cities.
- For the valley of Caledor, and for every herd driven out of it.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not take counsel from a court that sends shepherds against our clans.
- No. Your centaurs are still grazing in our grass.
- Not now. Your courtesy will keep.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Kuriotate! Your settlements need guarding, and our riders need work.
- Welcome. Your centaurs and our riders should race some day. We would win.
- Still gathering the peoples of Erebus under one banner, [CT_NAME]? Gather some Hippus companies too.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your centaurs scattered our herds. Speak.
- Your surveyors are in our pastures again. What now?
- Speak, and keep your centaurs away from our mares.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Let it draw our peoples closer, as you always say.
- Agreed. Your royal treasury pays well.
- Done, and fair. Even the centaurs would approve.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Our thanks, Kuriotate. Generous, for a rival.
- You honor our clans. Perhaps we will forgive Caledor. Someday.
- A fine gift. We will toast your centaurs. Once.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Your settlements could pay three times as much.
- No. Our riders do not come cheaper than your centaurs.
- Can't you do better? You rule half the continent.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your centaurs fought well, for horses with opinions.
- Fine. The valley is big enough for us both, perhaps.
- Done. Back to your shell, turtle, and we will go back to our plains.

#### Refuses peace
- Your settlements are still unguarded. Why stop?
- No. Not until Caledor is ours again.
- Nah. Your turtle has pulled its head in, and we are going to knock on the shell.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to your throne? The Hippus kneel to no throne.
- No. Your shepherds took enough from us already.
- Come and take it, and bring your centaurs. We will race you for it.

### Hippus → Lanun

#### First contact
- The Lanun. Sea-thieves, our clans call you. Tell me, is there no honor on the seas?
- Well met, captain. Our riders turn green just looking at your ships. Keep to the waves, and we will keep to the grass.
- The Hippus greet you. Your captains once held a Hippus envoy at sea until the price was paid in trade contracts. We still remember the bill.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, captain. You raid our coasts from the sea, so we will raid your ports from the land.
- Your pirates have cost our companies a whole season's profits. We have come to collect.
- On the waves you are kings. Ashore you are men on foot, and we ride.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not haggle with pirates while your ships are still burning our harbors.
- Dragons take you and your seas! No talk today.
- Go back to your ship, sea-thief.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Lanun! Have you any of that good wine left?
- Welcome ashore, captain. Are your legs still wobbling from the sea?
- Need riders to carry your cargo inland, [CT_NAME]? Your ships stop at the shore; our horses do not.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your pirates took one of our transports. Speak.
- You smell of salt and lies, captain. What do you want?
- Speak, and keep your hands off our saddlebags.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done, you salty old dog.
- Agreed. Sea gold and steppe gold spend the same.
- Done. Even a pirate can be a fair negotiator, it seems.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from a pirate! Is it stolen? No matter. Our thanks.
- Our thanks, captain. This is much better than being abducted.
- You honor us. Your sailors are welcome at our fires any night.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? This is extortion, and believe me, we know extortion.
- No. We are not galley slaves, to row for scraps.
- Can't you do better, captain? Your holds are fuller than that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your waves; we have grass enough.
- Fine. Our horses hate your boats anyway.
- Done. Want to raid someone together? You take the coast, and we take everything inland.

#### Refuses peace
- Your ports are still full of loot. Why stop?
- No. Not until you have paid back that season's profits.
- Nah. Your crews are slow on dry land.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to pirates? Come ashore and ask us properly.
- No. Your charm does not work on riders.
- You will get your gold the day your ships learn to gallop.

### Hippus → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- The Ljosalfar. Your forests are bad country for horses. Open a few meadows, and we will be friends.
- Well met, elf. They say your archers are the finest in Erebus. Our riders would prefer to stay out of their range.
- The Hippus greet the Summer Court. You have long memories, and so do our clans, though mostly of who paid.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, elf. Your groves are rich and your borders are thin.
- Your rangers shot our horses from the treetops. Now we will see how your archers do in the open.
- Your forests cannot cover everything. Our riders will find the meadows, and your villages in them.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not talk to trees.
- No. Your archers are still in the branches above our roads.
- Talk is for the slow season, elf, and this is not it.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Elf! How fares the forest?
- Welcome, Ljosalfar. Need riders to patrol the edges of your woods?
- Your archers and our riders would make a fine pair, [CT_NAME]. Have you considered it?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your treants trampled one of our camps. Speak.
- Speak, elf. Our horses are nervous in your shade.
- You look at us as if we had come to cut down your trees. What now?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Wise beyond your years, as your people would say. Though you have a great many years.
- Agreed. Fair, as elves go.
- Done. Our horses will graze your meadows gladly.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Our thanks, elf. Generous as midsummer.
- You honor our clans. We will keep our horses off your saplings, in return.
- A gift from the Summer Court! The clans will sing of it, badly.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? The forest can spare more than that.
- No. Our riders do not work for acorns.
- Can't you do better, elf? You have had centuries to save.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your trees, and we to our grass.
- Fine. Our horses hate your forests anyway.
- Done. Let the woods heal, and the meadows too.

#### Refuses peace
- Your groves still hide their treasures. Why stop?
- No. Your archers killed too many of our horses.
- Nah. We have not finished finding your meadows.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the trees? No.
- The oak does not bend, you say. Neither does the steppe.
- Come out of the forest and ask again, elf. In the open.

### Hippus → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- The Luchuirp. In Patria, golems took our horses' place in the fields. Our clans never quite forgave the golems.
- Well met, golem-maker. Your servants never tire, we hear. Can they gallop?
- The Hippus greet you. Your ancestors built golems and ours bred horses. At least ours enjoyed the work.

#### Declares war
- Your golems are slow and your workshops are rich. Nothing personal.
- Golems put our grandfathers out of work. Our lances will put yours out of work.
- Someone paid us to break your clockwork. Business is business.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not talk to clockmakers today.
- No. Your golems are still stamping through our pastures.
- Wind down your machines, and then we will talk.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Luchuirp! Have you built anything with legs that can outrun a horse yet?
- Welcome, artificer. Need riders to scout ahead of your golems?
- Our horses and your golems could plow half of Erebus together, [CT_NAME].

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems trampled our grazing land. Speak.
- Speak, tinker. Our horses do not like the clanking.
- You look at our horses like outdated machinery. What do you want?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Well crafted, like everything of yours.
- Agreed. Fair, and built to last.
- Done. Our horses thank you, even if your golems do not.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Our thanks, golem-maker. Generous of the Open-Skiers' heirs.
- You honor us. We know how much work goes into your gifts.
- A gift! Not a golem, I hope. They frighten the mares.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Our horses are worth more than your spare gears.
- No. Recalibrate your offer and try again.
- Can't you do better? You have been tinkering with gold for centuries.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Golems to the fields, horses to the plains.
- Fine. Our riders are tired of bouncing their lances off stone.
- Done. Tell your golems they fought well, if they can hear.

#### Refuses peace
- Your workshops are still full of treasures. Why stop?
- No. Your golems are slow, and we are not finished.
- Nah. We have not yet seen how your forges look from the inside.

#### Rejects a demand
- Build your own gold, tinker.
- No. Our purses are not powered by clockwork.
- Come and take it, with something faster than a golem.

### Hippus → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim. Your deserts are hard on horses, but our riders have crossed worse.
- Well met, children of the sun. You have your Lugus, and we have our saddles. Both get a people through hard country.
- The Hippus greet you. We hear your Empyrean gives an equal voice to small nations. Good; our clans are small, and very loud.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, Malakim. Your temples are gilded, and gold is our trade.
- Your Radiant Guard shines very brightly. Bright things make good targets.
- Someone has paid us well to ride across your desert. We will try not to take the sun with us.

#### Refuses to talk
- No sermons about light today, Malakim.
- Not while your armies are camped in our grass.
- Idle chat in this heat? No.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Malakim! Need riders for your desert roads?
- Welcome. Your light is warm, and your gold is warmer.
- What can the Hippus do for the children of the sun, [CT_NAME]?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Vicars called our riders creatures of shadow. Speak.
- Speak, and skip the part about dawn.
- You look at us as if we were a cloud across your sun. What now?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. A good deal, and you would be foolish to turn it down.
- Agreed, and judged on its merits, as your Empyrean likes.
- Done. May your sun shine on it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Our thanks, Malakim. Your light reaches a long way.
- You honor our clans. Generous, as the desert never is.
- A fine gift. Our riders will toast the dawn tonight, just for you.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Even the desert is richer than that offer.
- No. The sun may give freely, but our riders do not.
- Can't you do better? Your temples have gold to spare.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your sun, and we will go back to our grass.
- Fine. It was too hot for fighting anyway.
- Done. Light and lances can share the world.

#### Refuses peace
- Your temples still have gold on the walls. Why stop?
- No. Your Radiant Guard has not stopped shining at us.
- Nah. We have not seen the far side of your desert yet.

#### Rejects a demand
- Shine all you like; you will get no gold.
- No. Your light does not pay our riders.
- Your Empyrean gives equal voice to the small. Ours says no.

### Hippus → Mercurians

#### First contact
- The Mercurians. You fight demons for nothing, we hear. For nothing! You give soldiering a bad name.
- Well met, angel. If you ever need cavalry for your war on hell, we have a price list.
- The Hippus greet you. You broke the Compact to keep on fighting. We understand; peace is bad for business.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, angel. Your host is small and your camps are full of spoils from hell.
- Someone hired us to ride against you. We do not ask whether the other side has wings.
- You care little for mortals, they say. Well, here come a great many mortals, on horseback.

#### Refuses to talk
- Not today, angel. Your hammers have already said enough.
- No. Go back to fighting your demons, and leave us to our plunder.
- You never talk long anyway, Mercurian. Today, do not talk at all.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Angel! Need cavalry against the pit? Our rates for hell are only a little higher.
- Welcome, Mercurian. Our riders will run down hellhounds for a fair price.
- You fight for free and we fight for coin, [CT_NAME]. Shall we discuss which is wiser?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your soldiers trampled our camps chasing a demon. Speak.
- Speak, angel, and be quick about it, as you always are.
- You call us brigands, and we call you unpaid. What now?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Now go and kill some demons with it.
- Agreed. Even a rebel angel can bargain, it seems.
- Done. The Hippus will ride against hell at this price.

#### Thanks for a gift
- An angel giving gifts! Our thanks, and our astonishment.
- You honor our clans, Mercurian. We will put it to more earthly use than you would.
- Generous, for someone who works for nothing.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Riding against hell costs more than riding against men.
- No. Our riders will not face a Balor for so little.
- Can't you do better? Even angels must have some treasure tucked away.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your real enemies; we were only ever a distraction.
- Fine. Our horses were tired of the smell of your burning wings.
- Done. If hell ever pays better than you, we will let you know first.

#### Refuses peace
- Your camps are still full of the spoils of hell. Why stop?
- No. You hit us hard, and our clans want something back for it.
- Nah. An angel on foot is a fine target for a lance.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute for your crusade? We sell our swords; we do not donate them.
- No. You fight for nothing, so you can live on nothing.
- Demand all you like, angel. Our purse answers only to coin.

### Hippus → Sheaim

#### First contact
- The Sheaim. You want the world to end. A bad idea, if you ask us: the dead hire no mercenaries.
- Well met, gate-openers. When your end of days comes, who will be left to buy our horses?
- The Hippus greet you. We ride for gold, and you work for doom. The gold, at least, can be spent.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, cultist. Ending the world is simply bad for business.
- Your gates spill monsters onto our plains. We will close them with lances.
- If the world must end, it will not end with the Hippus standing still.

#### Refuses to talk
- No talk with doom-sayers today.
- Not while your gates are open and spitting horrors at our herds.
- Idle chat about the end of days? Not with warriors.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Sheaim! Still waiting for the end? Meanwhile, do you need riders?
- Welcome. You will not need gold where you are going, so spend it with us.
- How goes the apocalypse, [CT_NAME]? Slowly, I hope.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your planar gates are spilling horrors among our herds. Speak.
- Speak, cultist, and be quick; the world might end before you finish.
- You look at us as if we were already ashes. What do you want?

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. Spend it before the end comes.
- Agreed. Gold now, doom later.
- Done. Pleasure doing business with the apocalypse.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Our thanks. Giving gifts before the world ends; how thoughtful.
- You honor us, Sheaim. Strange, from people who want us all dead.
- Generous of you. Well, you cannot take it with you.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? Not nearly enough to ride into the apocalypse for.
- No. If the world is ending, our price is going up.
- Can't you do better? What are you saving it for, the end of time?

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the world last a little longer; we have contracts to fill.
- Fine. Our horses were tired of shying at your summonings.
- Done. Close a few of those gates, if you would.

#### Refuses peace
- Your temples are still full of treasure you will not need. Why stop?
- No. Not while your gates are still open.
- Nah. Better we end you before you end us.

#### Rejects a demand
- Why do you need our gold, if the world is ending anyway?
- No. Wait for the end, and then take whatever is left.
- Your doom may come for us all, but your tax collectors will not.

### Hippus → Sidar

#### First contact
- The Sidar. It is very hard to raid a city one cannot find.
- Well met, shade. Our horses shy at you; they cannot tell whether you are there or not.
- The Hippus greet you. You traded pieces of your souls for long life. We trade our swords for gold. I think ours is the better bargain.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, Sidar. Your hidden cities are full of old treasures, and we have finally found one.
- You walk through our camps unseen. Let us see if you can walk through a cavalry charge.
- Hard to kill, they say. Our lances are patient.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not talk to fog.
- No. Your shades are still haunting our camps.
- Not now, grey one. Come back when you are solid.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Sidar! Are you actually here, or should I talk to the mist?
- Welcome, shade. Need riders who can travel faster than rumor?
- Still around, [CT_NAME]? Good. Most of our clients do not last that long.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your shades spooked our herds again. Speak.
- You watch our camps from the shadows. What do you want?
- Speak, grey one, and stay where we can see you.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done. It will outlast us, but not you.
- Agreed. Old gold spends the same as new.
- Done. A shrewd bargain, from a people with all the time in the world to think it over.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from a ghost! Our thanks.
- You honor our clans, Sidar. We did not think you noticed us.
- Generous, for those who have given away so much of themselves already.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? You have had centuries to save, and that is all you offer?
- No. Our riders are mortal; they want to be paid in this lifetime.
- Can't you do better? Look again in those hidden vaults of yours.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back into the mist with you.
- Fine. Our horses will be glad to stop jumping at shadows.
- Done. It was a short war, for you.

#### Refuses peace
- Your hidden cities are still hidden. We have more to find.
- No. You would only wait a hundred years and come back.
- Nah. Even a shade cannot outrun our horses.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute from the living to the half-dead? No.
- No. You need nothing, you always say.
- Come and take it, if you can hold onto it.

### Hippus → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Svartalfar. You raid by night with knives, and we raid by day with lances. Both work.
- Well met, Winter Court. Your assassins are famous; our riders are faster.
- The Hippus greet you. We hear you do not betray all of your allies. We would like to be among the lucky ones, or at least well paid.

#### Declares war
- Nothing personal, dark elf. Your halls are rich, and your knives are short.
- Your assassins killed one of our captains in his tent. Now we come for yours in the open.
- The Winter Court prefers a faster tempo, you say. Then dance to a gallop.

#### Refuses to talk
- Talk with the Winter Court? I would rather keep my throat.
- No. Your shadows are still in our camps.
- Idle chat is for courtiers, not for warriors.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Svartalfar! Need riders who strike by daylight, for a change?
- Welcome, dark elf. Please leave your knives with the grooms.
- What can the Hippus do for the Winter Court, [CT_NAME]? Nothing involving poison, I hope.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- We found an assassin in our horse lines. Speak.
- You smile like a knife. What do you want?
- Speak, dark elf, and keep your hands where I can see them.

#### Accepts a deal
- Aye, done, and our clerk counted the knives in the contract.
- Agreed. Trade is quicker than theft, as your people say.
- Done. Pleasure doing business, for once.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Winter Court? Our thanks. We will test it for poison.
- You honor our clans. And surprise them.
- Generous, dark elf. Not a single hidden blade, as far as we can tell.

#### Turns down a deal
- That? There is a knife in this bargain somewhere.
- No. Our riders want gold, not promises from your court.
- Can't you do better? Your court has robbed enough to pay us properly.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your assassins at home.
- Fine. Our sentries will finally get some sleep.
- Done. We will be counting our captains every morning, just in case.

#### Refuses peace
- Your halls still have silver on the walls. Why stop?
- No. Your knives found our captains; our lances will find yours.
- Nah. You would only sign it and sharpen your daggers.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the Winter Court? Our gold stays where your knives cannot reach it.
- No. Persuade us with something other than a dagger.
- Your academies of persuasion would fail us anyway. We do not listen; we ride.

## Illians

### Illians → Amurites

#### First contact
- Children of Kylorin. Your forefather walked into the ice with a glowing blade, and the Thaw followed him out. Did he never come home to you?
- So these are the heirs of the man who broke the long winter. You are smaller than the legend.
- Your schools teach every current of magic, I hear. Enrol a few students in frost; you will want the lesson soon.

#### Declares war
- Kylorin bought your people one warm age with his blade. It has run out, and he is not here to pay again.
- Bring your archmages to the field. Let us see whether fire learned in a lecture hall burns in a blizzard.
- [CT_NAME], your forefather murdered winter's lord. I have come to collect the debt from his children.

#### Refuses to talk
- Write your petition, file it with your council of archmages, and wait. That is how your people prefer things, is it not?
- No. The snow does not parley with the candle it is about to smother.
- Your heralds speak in footnotes. Send them home before they freeze mid-sentence.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, scholar. Even I admit your mages know things worth knowing. Mind the frost on the threshold.
- The children of Kylorin, at a hearth with no fire in it. What have you come to teach, or to learn?
- You worship magic for its own sake, I hear. So do I, when it is mine. Sit.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your archmages squabble over obscure points while the cold creeps into their towers. Say your piece and go.
- I remember whose blade ended my age. Every Amurite face wears a little of his smile.
- You again. Do your headmasters never tire of sending me lecturers?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A child of Kylorin can be useful to the winter after all, which your forefather never was.
- Done. Enter it in your registers; I know how your people love a sealed document.
- A fair exchange. Do not boast of it in your academies; I prefer my bargains quiet.

#### Thanks for a gift
- An offering from the house of Kylorin. How strangely the seasons go round.
- I accept. Your forefather took a world from us; consider this the first coin of the repayment.
- Generous. When the snow comes for your schools, I may let one of them stand.

#### Turns down a deal
- You value this the way your bureaucrats value a seal on a scroll. No.
- Your people are clever enough to know this is an insult. Correct the arithmetic and come back.
- I have studied longer, in colder places, than any of your universities. This bargain fails the examination.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, then. Go back to your lecture halls, and keep the shutters closed.
- Kylorin's children may keep their warmth a while longer. It is a loan, not a gift.
- Your firebows have made their argument, and the frost has made mine. Let the field cool.

#### Refuses peace
- Your forefather did not offer Mulcarn peace. I see no reason to offer it to his blood.
- Peace? I have barely begun to teach your mages what cold does to a casting hand.
- No. Let your archmages draft their treaty in triplicate while the snow buries the ink.

#### Rejects a demand
- You mistake me for one of your junior faculty. I do not hand over my work because a senior asks.
- Kylorin's children have taken enough from the winter. Not one thing more.
- Demand of me again, and I will answer you with a season that does not end.

### Illians → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- The circus that hid from the White Hand all winter long. My priests searched for you, you know. You hid well.
- Masks, bells and painted smiles. You survived the Age of Ice by staying out of my priests' sight. Stay out of mine.
- Jubilee's players, at last on a stage I can see. Do your puppets speak for you, or you for them?

#### Declares war
- The White Hand missed your caravans once. My armies are not so easily fooled by greasepaint.
- The masquerade is over. Let us see what faces freeze beneath the masks.
- Laugh while you can. In the snow, laughter carries a long way, and nothing ever answers it.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not bargain with puppets, and I cannot tell which of you is holding the strings.
- Your jester's tongue has nothing I wish to hear. Go back to Jubilee and rehearse.
- No, [CT_NAME]. The show is closed until the frost lets it reopen.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the masquerade comes calling. Mind your bells; they crack in the cold.
- Your madness amuses me, and few things do. What game shall we play today?
- Come in, come in. I have never seen a harlequin shiver; perhaps today I will.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- I know what lies behind the painted smile. I have seen the faces of those your court made sport of.
- Your mimics and your freaks walk my borders. Call them home, or I will keep them as ice statues.
- Another performance? I did not buy a seat.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and without a single rhyme. You may add one later if you must.
- A sound bargain, for once, from a court of jesters. I will search it for tricks all the same.
- Done. Remember that a bargain sealed in winter does not thaw.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A present from the court of masks. Is there a viper at the bottom of it? No? How disappointing.
- Your generosity is as strange as your manners. I accept both.
- This will keep a few of your taskmasters out of my villages. Accepted.

#### Turns down a deal
- Pretty wrapping around an empty box. I know your court's tricks.
- That is a jest, and not a good one. Bring me something real.
- Your mimics steal what they win on the field. They will not steal it from me at this table.

#### Agrees to peace
- The curtain falls. Take your players home, and leave my snow unpainted.
- Very well. A truce with madmen is still a truce, so long as it is written plainly.
- Peace. I confess the war had grown as tiresome as one of your plays.

#### Refuses peace
- Your court hid through one winter. It will not hide through mine.
- No. The jesters will dance until the frost stops their feet.
- You offer peace with a grin. I will wait until the grin is frozen in place.

#### Rejects a demand
- You would have me pay for a seat at your circus? Hardly.
- Your taskmasters take what they want from the weak. I am not weak, and you are not my master.
- Juggle something else, jester. My treasury is not one of your props.

### Illians → Bannor

#### First contact
- The Bannor. You climbed out of hell just as the world was freezing. The snow must have seemed a mercy.
- Crusaders of Junil. Your priests keep a list of the damned, I am told. I expect to rise near the top of it.
- Your farms are castles and your peasants drill like soldiers. Good. You will last longer in the cold.

#### Declares war
- You call my winter chaos. It is the most perfect order there is: everything still, everything silent.
- Your priests damned me long ago. Allow me to earn it.
- March, crusaders. Junil asked you for unquestioning obedience; the cold asks only that you lie down.

#### Refuses to talk
- I will not hear a sermon from a soldier. Take your Confessors home.
- Your obedience belongs to Junil. Ask him what to say to me; I am not listening.
- No. Bannor envoys never come to talk, only to read out judgements.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Even crusaders need a moment of quiet. Winter is full of quiet, [CT_NAME]. Sit.
- You fought the orcs of Braduk for an age. I can respect any enemy of fire.
- The Bannor at my gate, and no sword drawn. These are strange days indeed.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Order would burn my priests and call it law. I have not forgotten.
- I hear your Crusaders praying for my fall. Pray louder; the wind is drowning you out.
- Speak, Bannor, and be quick. My patience with zealots melts slower than snow, but it melts.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A Bannor bargain, drawn up like a battle order. I approve.
- Done. Junil's people keep their word, they say. So do mine, though for colder reasons.
- Acceptable. Tell your priesthood the infidel was reasonable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the crusaders. Does your priesthood know you consort with the damned?
- I accept, and I will remember that the Bannor once gave and asked nothing.
- Generous. Your years in hell must have taught you the worth of a gift freely given.

#### Turns down a deal
- Your terms are drawn up like a surrender. I am not surrendering.
- No. The Bannor do not bargain; they dictate. I do not take dictation.
- Even your own law would call this unjust. Try again.

#### Agrees to peace
- So be it. Go back to your garrison towns. The snow will keep my borders while you are gone.
- Peace. Strike my name from your list of the damned, or at least move it down a line.
- Enough marching. Even crusaders must rest before the long night.

#### Refuses peace
- Your angel led you out of one hell. I am making you another, a cold one.
- Peace with a crusader is only a pause between sermons. No.
- You were raised to fight forever, were you not? Then fight.

#### Rejects a demand
- A tithe? I am not of your Order, and I tithe to no god at all.
- Your priests may tax their own faithful. I am not among them.
- You demand like a judge. I do not recognise your court.

### Illians → Calabim

#### First contact
- The Calabim. Winter nearly starved your kind out of the world. Strange that you come to greet the one who would bring it back.
- Vampire princes and their herds. I keep no herds; my people run colder than your palate likes.
- You survived the long winter by turning men into cattle. Clever. I survived it by turning myself into something else.

#### Declares war
- Your herds will freeze in their pens, and the Grand Broods will learn to dine on ice.
- Your kind nearly starved in the last winter. This one I will make longer.
- War, [CT_NAME]. Let us see how a vampire fares in a land with no warm throats.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not talk with leeches while they are gorged on my soldiers.
- No. Go back to your broods and count your cattle; you will have fewer soon.
- Your courtiers smile with too many teeth. Send them away.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, ancient one. We are both creatures this warm age does not quite understand.
- Your broods keep their herds docile and well fed. I admire a well-run estate.
- Come in out of the sun. You will find my halls agreeably dark, and cold enough to keep anything.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your hunters have been feeding near my borders. My snow keeps the bodies, and I count them.
- I know what you think of the living: cattle. Consider what the winter thinks of you.
- You come smelling of blood. State your business and leave.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A contract between immortals should be written in something that lasts.
- Done. Your nobles bargain better than they feed, which is saying a great deal.
- Acceptable. Do try not to drain the courier who carries it home.

#### Thanks for a gift
- From the Grand Broods, and not a drop of blood on it. I am touched.
- I accept. The cold and the dead ought to look after one another.
- Noted, and kept. Few of your kind give anything away but the Dark Gift.

#### Turns down a deal
- You offer me the dregs and keep the vintage. No.
- I am not one of your bloodpets, to be soothed with promises. Better terms.
- Your princes may bargain like that with cattle. Not with me.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go home and feed; you look pale, even for your kind.
- The dead and the frozen have time on their side; let us not waste it on each other.
- Enough. My snow is red enough for one season.

#### Refuses peace
- Peace? Your herds are thinning nicely. I will wait until they are gone.
- The last winter nearly finished your kind. I mean to let this one complete the work.
- No. A starving vampire is a humble one, and I want you humble.

#### Rejects a demand
- My people are not your cattle, and my treasury is not your vein.
- Demand blood from your herds. From me you get nothing.
- You thirst for what is mine? Thirst on.

### Illians → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- Orcs of Braduk. You huddled around your burning city all through the Age of Ice. I watched your fires from the dark.
- So Bhall's children survived the winter by hugging the flame. Do you still flinch when the wind changes?
- Mulcarn took the world when your goddess fell. I would have you remember which of them won.

#### Declares war
- Fire and ice again, as in the old days. Bhall lost the first time.
- I will put out the fires of Braduk one hearth at a time.
- Your goddess fell, and mine took the world. Shall we see whether the story repeats, [CT_NAME]?

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not parley with the brood of a fallen fire. Go and warm your hands at your ruins.
- No. Your envoy's breath steams, and steaming mouths do not speak in my halls.
- The snow does not talk to cinders. It buries them.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The Ember Banner at my door. Leave your torches outside, and we can talk.
- You are brutes, but honest brutes. I can work with that.
- Orcs with something to say rather than something to burn. Say it; I am curious.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You come reeking of smoke. My halls remember what fire did to this world.
- Your raiders burn my villages to stay warm. Every hut you torch is another grudge laid down in the ice.
- Speak quickly, orc. Embers do not last long in my wind.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Even an orc can count, it seems.
- Done. Take it back to Braduk and warm yourselves on it.
- Acceptable. A fair deal with the Clan; Mulcarn would have laughed to see it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- The Clan, giving instead of burning? I accept, before you change your mind.
- Fire paying tribute to frost. That is how it should always have been.
- I accept, and I will not ask whose village it came from.

#### Turns down a deal
- You offer embers and expect a hearth in return. No.
- That is a raider's bargain, all take and no give. Try again.
- No. Go back to your fire and think harder, if orcs do that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your sacred flame and keep it small.
- Let it be so. Your fires have melted enough of my snow; let it settle.
- Enough. Even the old war between flame and frost had its lulls.

#### Refuses peace
- Bhall never asked Mulcarn for peace, and Mulcarn never offered it.
- No, orc. I mean to see Braduk dark and silent under the drifts.
- Peace with fire is a thaw, and I permit no thaws.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand of me as though Bhall still had a throne. She does not.
- Raid someone weaker. You will get nothing from me but frostbite.
- Ask again and I will send my answer on the north wind.

### Illians → Doviello

#### First contact
- The wolves of the long winter. We let you hunt, once, and you hunted well. Then you turned on us.
- Doviello. You bared your teeth at Mulcarn when Kylorin held your leash. I have not forgotten.
- You miss the snow, do you not? I can smell it on you. Perhaps we can hunt together again.

#### Declares war
- You bit the hand that let you hunt. Now the hand closes into a fist.
- Wolves who betray their winter freeze with everyone else. Come, Doviello.
- The pack turned on its master once. This time the master culls the pack.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not barter with dogs that slipped their leash.
- No. Howl at the moon if you must talk to something.
- Your pack leader may whine at my gate all night. It stays shut.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Old hunters of the snow. The cold remembers you fondly, even if I do not always.
- You did what you had to, to live through the Thaw. I understand that. Let us talk of what comes after it.
- The wolves come to my fire. Mind it; there is none.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your hunters stalk my outriders the way they once stalked my enemies. I notice the difference.
- Speak, turncoat. You chose the Thaw over us; I hope it has kept you warm.
- Your pack sniffs around my borders. Sniff somewhere else.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. The pack eats, and so do I.
- Done. Strength deals plainly with strength; you know that better than anyone.
- A fair kill, fairly shared. Take your portion.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the wolves. I trust the prey was fresh.
- I accept. Perhaps the pack still remembers the winter that fed it.
- Good. This is how the strong ought to treat the stronger.

#### Turns down a deal
- You offer me scraps from the kill. I am not one of your weaklings, to be fed last.
- No. Even a wolf knows when the share is unfair.
- Bring me something worth the hunt.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your packs; the deep winter will need wolves again.
- The cold and the wolf were allies once. Perhaps they will be again.
- Enough blood on the snow. Go and lick your wounds.

#### Refuses peace
- No. A pack that betrays its master must be thinned.
- Wolves do not beg. Fight, or show me your throat.
- I let you live once because you were useful. You are not useful now.

#### Rejects a demand
- The wolf demands from the winter? The winter answers with hunger.
- Take what you can, as your pack always has. You cannot take this.
- No. The pack eats what it kills, and you have killed nothing of mine.

### Illians → Elohim

#### First contact
- The Elohim. You watched the Godslayer handed to Finner, they say. Tell me, where did they bury him?
- Monks and pilgrims, reclaiming your shrines from the ice. Some of them, I fear, are mine now.
- You tended the dying all through the Age of Ice. You must have seen my priests at their work.

#### Declares war
- Your shrines lie under my snow, and there they will stay.
- I asked politely where Finner lies. Now I will ask your monasteries, one at a time.
- You keep the holy places of the gods. I mean to be a god. Make room, or be buried.

#### Refuses to talk
- No, monk. You came to speak of mercy, and I have none to discuss.
- Your chants will not soften me. Go home and sing them to the dying.
- Silence suits the Elohim. Keep it.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, keepers. Even I cannot fault a people who carried learning through the long winter.
- Your healers tended my people as well as any in the dark years. That is remembered.
- Pilgrims at my door. Do not look so worried; I have no quarrel with gentleness.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You pray for my fall at every shrine you reclaim. I hear it on the wind.
- Speak, Elohim, and spare me the homily.
- You guard secrets meant for killing gods. Do you think I do not know why you look at me so?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your word is said to be the most trusted in Erebus. Let us test it.
- Done. Your monks drive a gentle bargain; I will not abuse it.
- Acceptable. Go in peace, as your people say.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Elohim, freely given. Your order never changes.
- I accept. Your charity once reached even the frozen. It still does, it seems.
- Kind. Tell me where Finner lies, and I will be kinder still.

#### Turns down a deal
- Holy men should know better than to haggle so poorly. No.
- That bargain is a pilgrimage with no shrine at the end. Refused.
- No, keeper. Your vows of poverty need not extend to me.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your seven firs and your shrines; I will leave them standing, for now.
- Very well. Let the healers bury their dead.
- Enough. I find no glory in breaking monks.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Not while your monasteries keep secrets meant to kill me.
- Peace? You never wanted this war. That is exactly why you will lose it.
- Your warrior monks subdue marauders with their bare hands. Let them try it on a blizzard.

#### Rejects a demand
- You preach charity, and then you demand? How unlike you.
- Ask the gods for alms, monk. I am not one of them. Not yet.
- No. The Elohim do not threaten well; it embarrasses us both.

### Illians → Grigori

#### First contact
- The Grigori, who need no gods. How fortunate; I am not one yet.
- A people who turned their backs on heaven. You will find it harder to turn your backs on winter.
- Your adventurers wander everywhere, I hear. Tell them the far north is not for wandering.

#### Declares war
- You teach that men need no gods. I will teach you that men cannot do without the cold.
- Your adventurers wanted a great quest. I give them one: survive me.
- You reject every god, so you will reject the one I am becoming. That is why you must be buried first.

#### Refuses to talk
- I have nothing to say to people who believe in nothing.
- No. Send your adventurers home to their own fires.
- Your counsel is famous, I hear. Keep it.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Freethinkers. I confess you interest me; you bow to no one, and neither do I.
- Your cities shelter anyone who wants to live without gods. Some of my people might like to live without the sun.
- Come in, Grigori. I promise not to demand worship. Today.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You whisper to my people that gods are tyrants. Whisper it again and I will freeze your tongue.
- Your adventurers keep poking about Letum Frigus. They do not come back, and I do not apologise.
- Your creed says no power is worth bowing to. Mine will be. Say what you came to say.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A people who expect nothing from heaven read their contracts very carefully. I like that.
- Done. You bargain like people who expect no help from above.
- Acceptable. Your creed of standing on your own feet has served you well here.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift, from people who refuse the gods their offerings. I am flattered.
- I accept. Do not call it worship; I know you would not.
- Generous. Even godless men know whom to keep warm.

#### Turns down a deal
- You bargain the way the gods once bargained with men: all promise. No.
- Not enough. Your adventurers could steal more than this from a sleeping dragon.
- I decline. Go and be self-reliant somewhere else.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Live your godless lives, while the season lasts.
- So be it. You fought without divine help; I respect that much.
- Enough. Your heroes have earned their rest.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your heroes still carry swords, and I can still hear them.
- The Grigori fight without gods. Let us see how long.
- Peace is a gift of the gods, the priests would tell you. And you have none.

#### Rejects a demand
- You bow to no god, and I bow to no Grigori. Nothing.
- Careful, freethinker. Demands are the habit of gods; you of all people should disdain them.
- No. Find it yourself; your people pride themselves on that.

### Illians → Hippus

#### First contact
- Horse lords. You held back my frostlings in the old winter. Few did.
- The Hippus. You let frost golems trample whole camps rather than beg help of a cousin. Pride like that is nearly Illian.
- Mercenaries now, are you? I may have work for your companies when the snow returns.

#### Declares war
- Your horses will break their legs in the drifts, and your riders will freeze in the saddle.
- The frost golems are coming back to your plains. Your clans will not stand together this time either.
- No one outruns the winter, rider. Not even you.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not haggle with hirelings in the middle of a battle.
- No. Ride back to your plains and count your coin.
- Your envoy came at a gallop. He can leave the same way.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, rider. Stable your horse by the hall; the stalls are cold but sheltered.
- I like a people who know their worth to the last coin. Speak.
- The Hippus at my gate, and not raiding. Times change.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders took from my villages. I take memories, and keep them a long time.
- I know your companies sell their lances to anyone. Who has bought them against me?
- Speak, horse lord, before your mount's breath freezes.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your companies honour their contracts; I will honour mine.
- Done. A fair price, from a fair rider.
- Acceptable. I am almost tempted to hire you.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Hippus, who give nothing without a fee. You honour me.
- I accept. Tell your clans the north remembers.
- Good. This buys you a warm winter. One.

#### Turns down a deal
- That is a mercenary's price, and I am not hiring.
- No. You would charge a dying man for a cup of snow.
- Rein in your greed, horse lord. You haggle like a clan that has never had to share a fire.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Take your herds south while the grass is still green.
- You rode well, horse lord. Go home.
- Enough. Neither of us gains by killing good horses.

#### Refuses peace
- No. The frost golems never offered your grandfathers peace either.
- Your clans broke in the last winter. I mean to break them again.
- Peace? Your contract is not finished, and neither is mine.

#### Rejects a demand
- You raid your own cousins, and now you would raid me with words? No.
- Gold is your god, horse lord. Do not expect me to worship it.
- Earn it with your lances, if you can. You will not have it for asking.

### Illians → Infernal

#### First contact
- So Agares has sent his furnace up into the world. Do not expect the world to stay warm for you.
- Demons, carving cities out of the dirt with their claws. Mind where you dig; the ground here is frozen.
- I have heard of the mire of Mulcarn, below. Did you pass through it on your way up?

#### Declares war
- Fire again. It is always fire. I will show you what the cold does to hell.
- Your gate opened onto my world. I mean to freeze it shut with you on this side.
- You came up to harvest souls, demon. Harvest my answer.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not barter with the pit.
- No, demon. Go back down; you will find it warmer.
- Whatever you offer, it has a soul's price. I am not selling.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, demon. We both find this green age distasteful; let us talk.
- You want souls; I want a throne. Our ambitions need not collide.
- The pit and the frost at one table. The gods would be appalled, and that pleases me.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your heat stains my snow. Speak, and be gone.
- You eye my people as if they were already yours. They are mine, in this life and in the next.
- I know what your pacts cost. Do not bother offering one.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. And I will read every line twice; I know where your kind hides its clauses.
- Done. A bargain between the cold and the fire. Let it hold until it does not.
- Acceptable. Keep your claws off the souls of my dead.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from hell, with no hook in it? I will search for the hook anyway.
- I accept. Even demons, it seems, can tell which way the wind blows.
- Generous. Agares must be in a rare good humour.

#### Turns down a deal
- Demons always give less than they promise. This is less than even that.
- No. I know a soul's price when I see one.
- Refused. Take it back to the pit and polish it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and burn someone else.
- Very well. Your flames and my frost have made a fine bog of the borderlands.
- Enough. Neither of us wins anything here but steam.

#### Refuses peace
- No. I mean to see hellfire freeze.
- Peace with hell? I would sooner make peace with the sun.
- Your fires are guttering, demon. Why would I stop now?

#### Rejects a demand
- Make demands of the damned, demon. They have to listen to you. I do not.
- You will have nothing of mine, in this world or in yours.
- No. Hell takes; I do not give.

### Illians → Khazad

#### First contact
