- The dwarves who slept through my god's winter in their holes. Did you even notice it?
- Khazad. Your old kings kept you underground with tales of a dread god and his legion of giants. The tales were true.
- You count gold beneath the mountains; I count snowfalls above them. We may both be patient people.

#### Declares war
- You hid from one winter under the hills. This one will follow you down.
- Bar your stone doors, dwarves. Ice is very patient, and it splits stone.
- Your vaults would make a fine treasury for a god. Open them, or I will.

#### Refuses to talk
- I do not bargain with miners in the middle of a siege. Go back to your tunnels.
- No. Your ledgers can wait until the snow melts. It will not.
- Hammer on my gates if you like. I am not answering.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Dwarves at my hearth. You, at least, do not complain about the cold.
- Come, Khazad. We are both people who remember the deep places.
- You are welcome, so long as you do not try to sell me anything.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your miners tunnel close to my caverns. Letum Frigus is not your quarry.
- Speak, dwarf. You wear the look of a merchant about to name an outrageous price.
- Your gold-counting bores me. Come to the point.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A dwarven bargain is hard but honest, they say. I find it so.
- Done. Weigh it twice if you must; it is all there.
- Acceptable. You may carve it into your rune halls.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from a dwarf. I will have this recorded; it may never happen again.
- I accept. Did it hurt, parting with it? Your face says it did.
- Generous. The deep halls will be remembered kindly when the cold returns.

#### Turns down a deal
- You price this like a dwarf. That is not a compliment.
- No. Your scales are weighted, and we both know it.
- Too little. Dig deeper into those vaults.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back below and shut the door behind you.
- As you wish. Your black powder makes a fearful noise; let the mountains rest.
- Enough. Your hammers and my ice have cracked enough stone between them.

#### Refuses peace
- No. I mean to see your gold frozen in your vaults.
- You want peace so you can count your losses. Count them now.
- The last winter never reached you. This one will, and it is not finished.

#### Rejects a demand
- Gold for nothing? You must take me for one of your debtors.
- You hoard in your vaults and demand from mine? No.
- Not a single coin. Mine it yourselves.

### Illians → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- The Kuriotates. You were born in the Thaw, on the bones of my winter. I do not hold it against you. Yet.
- Centaurs, lamia, giants and men, all under one crown. Do you take in the frozen dead as well?
- Your settlements stretch so very far. How will you hold them when the snow comes back?

#### Declares war
- Your settlements are thin and far apart. The snow will find them one by one.
- You retreat into your shell when war comes, I hear. Then let the frost seal it.
- Your confederation was born in a thaw. I will end it with a freeze.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Send me a centaur, a giant and a lamia; I will still not listen.
- Your ambassadors are many and courteous. All of them are dismissed.
- Your court speaks with many voices. None of them interests me today.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome. Your realm shelters every odd creature in Erebus; I find that useful.
- You take in strangers from the wilderness. Some of mine might like to visit.
- The Kuriotates, polite as ever. Sit and speak.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your realm is a bazaar of half-men and outcasts. Tell me why I should care for its opinions.
- You make citizens of my deserters. That ends.
- Speak, Kuriotate. Your settlements creep too near my snows.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your royal administration is efficient; I approve.
- Done. Have one of your centaurs carry it home quickly.
- Acceptable. Your court bargains well.

#### Thanks for a gift
- I accept this, with something close to gratitude. Your confederation is generous to its neighbours.
- Generous. Your core cities must have more than they need.
- I accept. Your outlying settlements may sleep easier this winter.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That is the offer of a nation that believes itself the centre of the world.
- The Kuriotates welcome everyone, I hear. That does not mean I welcome this offer.
- Refused. Keep it in your core lands.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Withdraw to your core cities, and leave the frontier to the snow.
- Your centaurs fought bravely; let them go home.
- Enough. Your settlements may thaw.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your far settlements burn so prettily against the snow.
- You may retreat to your core lands. I will follow you there.
- Peace? Not until your outlying settlements are mine.

#### Rejects a demand
- Your crown commands its subjects. I am not among them.
- No. The Kuriotates have taken in enough strays; they will not take in my treasure.
- You demand like the king of many peoples. I am lord of one, and the answer is no.

### Illians → Lanun

#### First contact
- The Lanun. My icebergs tore your galleys apart in the old winter. I am glad some of you survived; it makes the story better.
- Sea-raiders. Your god of the waters stopped answering you, I hear. Mine stopped answering too. We manage.
- Captains, each a king on his own deck. Which of you speaks for the rest?

#### Declares war
- The ice will return to your harbours, and your ships will freeze where they lie.
- Your crews vanished into the blizzards once. I will send them more blizzards.
- War, pirate. Run before the wind while you still have water to run on.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. A Lanun's word drifts with the tide, and I am not wading after it.
- Your envoy smells of salt and lies. Send him back to his ship.
- I do not bargain with pirates in the middle of a raid.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, captain. Even I enjoy a sea story, if it is cold enough.
- You traded with every frozen tribe in the last winter. You must know how to talk to me.
- The Lanun, ashore and sober. What brings you?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your ships prowl my coasts like gulls around a carcass. Say what you want.
- You smuggle anyone who pays out of my reach. I know it; speak and go.
- Your word is worth what the tide leaves behind. Talk if you must.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Swear on your own ship, captain; I know nothing else binds you.
- Done. A fair cargo, fairly paid.
- Acceptable. I will count the barrels myself all the same.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Pirates bearing gifts. I shall count my harbours afterwards.
- I accept, and I will not ask what happened to its last owner.
- Generous. Your ships may winter in my harbours. Once.

#### Turns down a deal
- That is a smuggler's price. I am not a fool off the docks.
- No. That is the sort of cargo your crews traded to starving tribes in the long winter. I am not starving.
- The tide is out on this bargain, captain. Try again when it turns.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and pirate someone warmer.
- Very well. My coasts are cold enough without your burning ships on them.
- Enough. Take your fleets home before the ice closes the straits.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your word lasts one tide, and this war will last many winters.
- Peace with the Lanun is just a pause before the next raid.
- Your harbours are icing over, captain. I will wait until the last ship is locked in.

#### Rejects a demand
- Plunder someone else, pirate. My halls are not a merchant ship.
- You will take nothing from me without boarding first, and you cannot board a glacier.
- No. Ask your silent god for it.

### Illians → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- The elves of the Summer Court. The long winter killed your god and most of your people. You look well, considering.
- Ljosalfar. You came out of your last hidden groves into my Thaw. Enjoy the summer; it is brief.
- Your spring never came, did it? I remember. I remember it very fondly.

#### Declares war
- The forests sleep under snow, and the Summer Court sleeps with them. Forever, this time.
- Your god died in the last winter. Shall we see what the next one takes from you?
- I will strip your groves to bare branches, [CT_NAME], and leave them that way.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your court talks in seasons; you will have to wait for winter's end.
- Summer elves at my gate? Go back to your groves.
- Your words wither in the cold, elf. Do not waste them.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Ljosalfar. Do not tremble; it is merely cold, not cruel. Today.
- Elves who outlived their own god. I find that worth talking to.
- The forest folk come calling. Wipe the snow from your feet.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your druids pray to Cernunnos for a summer that never ends. I hear them, and I laugh.
- You hate me, I know. Every elf remembers whose winter it was.
- Speak, elf. Your leaves are already turning brown.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Even the Summer Court has to trade with the Winter in the end.
- Done. Your craft is fine work; I will put it somewhere cold, where it keeps.
- Acceptable. You bargain better than you fight snow.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the elves, to me? Your ancestors must be turning under the ice.
- I accept. Perhaps your court has learned to bend before the frost.
- Generous. Your groves may stay green a little longer.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer what the snow would take anyway.
- Not enough. Elves bargain as if they had forever; you do not.
- Refused. Come back when you understand who wins in winter.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go home and tend your saplings.
- The forests may have their summer. The winter can wait.
- Enough. I have no need to burn trees; I only need them to sleep.

#### Refuses peace
- No. The last winter took your god. This one is for your courts.
- Peace? Your groves are bare. Let them stay that way.
- Your people nearly vanished once. I will finish the work Mulcarn began.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand of winter? Ask Sucellus for it. Oh, but he died in the snow, did he not?
- Nothing, elf. You will get nothing from the frost but frost.
- No. Your court rules in summer only. This is not summer.

### Illians → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- The Luchuirp. Your golems froze in the fields while your cities cracked under the blue ice. I am surprised any of you remain.
- Open-Skiers, back under the open sky. You remember what happened the last time.
- Little builders. Your clockwork men stopped working in the cold, did they not?

#### Declares war
- Your golems failed you in the last winter. They will fail you again.
- I will bury your cities under ice, as the glaciers did before.
- Back into the caves, gnome. The sky is mine again.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Send me a golem, if you must talk; at least it would be silent.
- Your envoy is three feet tall and three times too loud. Go.
- I have no words for a people who hid under the mountain while the glaciers took their cities.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Luchuirp. Your craft is fine, even if it dislikes the cold.
- Builders at my gate. Perhaps you could build me something that does not freeze.
- Come in out of the wind. Your kind feels the cold more than most.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- I have seen your golems stamping about my borders. They will make fine statues.
- You curse my name around your forges. I hear the hammers stop when you do.
- Speak, gnome. Your Kilmorph cannot shield you from the sky.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your work is honest, and I appreciate honest work.
- Done. Now build me something that lasts a winter.
- Acceptable. Kilmorph's children are better traders than they are survivors.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Luchuirp. I hope it was not one of your golems; they rust here.
- I accept. Your cities may keep their roofs a while longer.
- Generous. When the glaciers come again, I may tell them to go around your workshops.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You price your work as if the ice had never crushed it.
- Not enough, little builder. Your ancestors priced their golems like this too, right up until the ice took them.
- Refused. Your golems are clever, but they cannot bargain for you.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your workshops while they still stand.
- I accept. Your golems have done enough marching in the snow.
- Enough. Rebuild your cities, Luchuirp. I have no need to crush them twice.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your cities crumbled once. They will crumble again.
- Peace? Your golems are stiffening, and so are your soldiers.
- Your goddess hid you under the mountain last time. Go back there and wait.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand of me? Go and ask your goddess; she is used to sheltering you.
- No. Your golems can dig it up for you.
- Not a thing, gnome. The ice gave nothing to your ancestors, and I give nothing to you.

### Illians → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim. Your faith in Lugus began in the Shadowed Vale, in a light I tore through the mist. You owe your god to me.
- Children of the sun. You will find the sun does not reach everywhere, and never into my halls.
- Desert folk. You have never seen real snow, have you? I will show you.

#### Declares war
- Your sun has had its age. I am putting it out.
- Lugus blazes in your temples. I will see the frost creep up their steps.
- The light that woke your faith was mine to give. Now I take it back.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your priests talk of light; my halls are dark, and I like them that way.
- Sun-worshippers at my gate in the middle of a war? Go home and pray for a thaw.
- Your Vicars may judge each case on its merits. This one has none.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, children of the desert. Shelter from my wind; your robes are thin.
- The Malakim, come to see the cold for themselves. Look your fill.
- Even the sun must set, and visit the night now and then. Sit.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Radiant Guard stares at my borders as if the sun could melt them. It cannot.
- I know what your priests call me. A shadow. A shadow needs a light to cast it, remember.
- You hate the cold, Malakim. The cold does not care. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your Empyrean prizes fairness; this was fair.
- Done. Take it back across the sands before it melts.
- Acceptable. Let the sun and the snow keep their bargain.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the sun's own people. I will keep it in the shade.
- I accept. Perhaps Lugus has finally learned his place.
- Generous. I may spare a temple or two when the cold reaches the desert.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your Vicars would not call this just, and neither do I.
- That is a bargain made in the heat of the day. Think on it at night, and come back.
- Refused. The desert must offer more than sand.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your sands and your sunrise.
- Very well. Let the sun keep the desert. The north is mine.
- Enough. Even the longest day ends, and so does the longest night. Let this one end.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your sun rose because I let it. I mean to see it set.
- Peace with the Malakim? Not while a single temple of Lugus still blazes.
- Your light is fading at the edges, I see. I will keep pressing.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand of me? Your faith itself is my gift. Be content.
- No. Ask your sun for it; it gives so freely.
- The desert is barren for a reason. I will not water it.

### Illians → Mercurians

#### First contact
- Angels who broke the Compact. So did my god. We have that in common, at least.
- The Mercurians. You hunt demons, I hear. I am no demon; leave me be and we will get along.
- Rebels from the heavens, walking in the snow. Your wings look cold.

#### Declares war
- You defy the gods to fight their wars. I defy them to take their place. One of us is in the way.
- Angels freeze, I am told, if you hold them still long enough.
- You came to Erebus to kill demons. You will die here killing me instead.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You came down from the heavens to fight. So fight.
- I do not talk to soldiers of a god they disobeyed.
- Carve another prayer into your flesh, angel. I am not listening to any of them.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, angel. We are both outlaws from heaven, in our way.
- The hunters of hell, at my hearth. There is no fire here to remind you of your work.
- You care nothing for men, they say. Neither do I. Sit.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You look at me as if I smelled of brimstone. I smell of snow.
- Your host broke the Compact, then judges me for wanting a throne? Speak.
- Go and kill your demons, angel. Why are you at my gate?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Even angels must trade, now that they have joined us on the ground.
- Done. You bargain bluntly; I approve.
- Acceptable. Spend it on demons, by all means.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from an angel. Do they still make such things in the heavens?
- I accept. Perhaps you see that I am not your enemy.
- Generous. I will remember it if the demons come north.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You came down to judge demons, angel. Judge your own offer, and you will find it wanting.
- You offer what the Compact offered your host: less than you thought you deserved. Refused.
- Not enough. A host that spends half its days in hell should know what things truly cost.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and fight the fires of hell; they need you more than I do.
- Your swords belong in the pit, angel, not in my snow.
- Enough. Go back to your crusade.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You chose to fight in the world of men. Then stay and fight.
- Peace with an angel? Not while you stand between me and a throne.
- Your wings are stiff with frost, angel. Fold them, and stay down.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand of the gods you defied. They have more to give.
- No. Angels who disobey their lords have no right to command me.
- Ask the hells for tribute, angel; you spend half your days there. There is none for you in the snow.

### Illians → Sheaim

#### First contact
- The Sheaim, who want the world to end. I want it to sleep. There is a difference.
- Gate-openers. I hear your master once crawled through the mire of Mulcarn. Did it leave a chill?
- You long for the end of creation. Let me show you a gentler end: snow, and silence.

#### Declares war
- You would end the world. I would rule it. You cannot be allowed to win.
- Your gates will freeze shut, and your Armageddon with them.
- The end of the world will come when I say so, not when your rituals do.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Talking to the Sheaim is talking to the end of everything.
- Your envoy speaks of doom. I have heard better from the wind.
- Go back to your rituals. I do not barter with the apocalypse.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, gate-opener. We both find this green world wearisome.
- The Sheaim at my hearth. Do sit, and tell me how the world will end. I like to know.
- You want endings, I want stillness. We may find much to agree on.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your rituals stain the sky over my lands. I do not want your apocalypse; I want my winter.
- Speak quickly. You may end the world before you finish.
- I know what you summon through your gates. Keep it away from my snow.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Strange to trade with those who would end all trade.
- Done. Spend it before the world ends, as you hope.
- Acceptable. Even the end of the world needs supplies, it seems.

#### Thanks for a gift
- The Sheaim, giving things away. Is the end so near already?
- I accept, and I will use it to delay your apocalypse.
- Generous. I will spend it keeping the world alive long enough to freeze it properly.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You bargain as if nothing will matter tomorrow.
- Not enough. The end has not come yet, and I still count.
- Refused. Your price would bankrupt a world that is not ending.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your gates, and keep them shut near my lands.
- So be it. Let the world end some other day.
- Enough. We both want this age gone; let us not hasten each other.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your gates are an affront to my winter.
- Peace with the Sheaim? There is nothing to be peaceful about at the end of the world.
- You want the end, gate-opener. I am giving it to you.

#### Rejects a demand
- Make your demands of Ceridwen, who let your master out of hell. I am not so generous.
- No. You will not need it at the end of the world anyway.
- Nothing. What use is treasure to a people who mean to burn the world it lies in?

### Illians → Sidar

#### First contact
- The Sidar. Shades in grey, watching the world from your hidden cities. My Illians watched from the caverns of Letum Frigus for an age. We know the waiting.
- You traded half your souls for endless time. What did you buy with it?
- Immortals of the grey. You have outlived many winters. You will outlive mine, perhaps.

#### Declares war
- You thought to stay out of the world's wars. Mine finds everyone.
- Fade, shades. The frost will fill the spaces where you were.
- Your cities are hidden. The snow will find them anyway.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You stayed out of the world's affairs for an age. Stay out of mine a little longer.
- Shades who speak? Go back into the fog.
- I do not barter with ghosts while they war against me.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, grey one. You and my Illians are both half-departed from this world. Sit.
- Grey ones, outside your fog? The world must be ending, or near enough.
- Few visit me, and fewer still who understand patience. Welcome.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You destroy the undead, they say, yet you are half-dead yourselves. Spare me your purity.
- Your shades drift through my lands. Speak, or drift away.
- Your grey folk feel nothing, I hear. Then my displeasure will not trouble you. Speak anyway.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Immortals should trade with immortals.
- Done. Let it last as long as either of us.
- Acceptable. You bargain without feeling, which I respect.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the grey people. I did not know you still cared for anything.
- I accept. Perhaps you see that the winter will outlast even you.
- Generous. Your hidden cities may stay hidden from me.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You value things as if you had forgotten what value is.
- Not enough. You gave up the taste of food and the sound of music; surely you can give up a little profit.
- Refused. You have had centuries to learn to bargain, and this is the best you can do?

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. The fog may have you back; I have no use for ghosts.
- You have centuries to regret this war, and I have an age to forget it.
- Enough. Your shades may drift on.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You chose to fight. You will learn what frost does to shades.
- Peace? Your cities are fading, and I will see them gone.
- You stepped out of your grey world. Now you will not step back.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand? Shades who have traded their souls have nothing left to bargain with.
- No. You need nothing, grey ones; that is your whole creed.
- Nothing. A people who cut away their own desires should not be making demands.

### Illians → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Winter Court. When spring never came, your queens ruled for an age. You should thank my god for that.
- Svartalfar. You took Esus for your god when Sucellus died, and the snow made your reign eternal. We are kin of a sort.
- Dark elves of the long night. I know your court; it was at its finest when the world was frozen.

#### Declares war
- You loved the winter while it served you. Learn how it treats those who serve themselves.
- The Winter Court rules only in winter. I am winter now, and I abdicate nothing to you.
- Your daggers are sharp in the dark, elf. My dark is longer than yours.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Unseelie promises are made of mist.
- I do not trade words with a court that lies for sport.
- Go back to your own winter, elf. Mine is not open to guests.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Unseelie. The frost always suited your court.
- The dark elves come visiting. Sit by the cold hearth; I know you like it.
- Your court ruled the long winter's elves. I would hear what you learned.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- I know what your court did to the elves who would not abandon Sucellus. Do not imagine you can do it to me.
- Your assassins prowl my lands. Call them home.
- Speak, Svartalfar, and keep both hands where I can see them.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Esus teaches that miracles must be paid for. Consider this one paid.
- Done. I will count the coin twice; you are elves of Esus, after all.
- Acceptable. A bargain worthy of the Winter Court.

#### Thanks for a gift
- From the Unseelie, unasked. I will wonder for a long while what it was meant to buy.
- I accept. Your court remembers who gave it its long reign.
- Generous. Perhaps the next winter will crown you again.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You bargain as if I were one of your Seelie cousins.
- Not enough. Esus would be ashamed of such a poor trick.
- Refused. Your court has had an age of darkness to practise its lies, and this one is not worthy of it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. The Winter Court and the winter itself should not squabble like Seelie children.
- Very well. Winter has room for one court only, but it can wait.
- Enough. Two courts of the cold should save their knives for the summer folk.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your court grew fat on my god's winter. Now pay for it.
- Peace? I will make your long night longer.
- You have the dark, elf, but I have the cold. I will not stop.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand of me? Your court should be paying tribute to winter.
- No. Esus sells his miracles; go and buy one.
- Nothing. Your court grew fat on the long winter. It is you who should be paying.

## Infernal

### Infernal → Amurites

#### First contact
- The Amurites. Your Kylorin banished my kind from Patria when he shut the portals. Look who found the door again.
- A nation of mages who license necromancy like a market stall. How quaint. Hell grants no licences.
- Children of Kylorin, still warm, still clever, still mortal. I can work with all three.

#### Declares war
- Your archmages will burn first. Hell has a special pit for those who think they understand it.
- You studied the dark spheres from behind your regulations. Now study them up close.
- Ready your firebows, [CT_NAME]. They will make a cheerful light when your schools go up.

#### Refuses to talk
- Talk? I have heard Amurite debates. I would rather be back in the pit.
- No. Send your petition through your proper channels; mine run straight down.
- Your heralds have a lovely smell of fear and ink. Leave before I sample them.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the mages. You want something forbidden, I can tell. Sit, and tell me which branch of it.
- [CT_NAME], your scholars have such appetites. I could feed them, for a price.
- The children of Kylorin come to me willingly. He would be so disappointed.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You punish your necromancers spectacularly, I hear. Do you think it hides what they learned from us?
- Every Amurite who dabbles in the forbidden spheres comes to me eventually. You will too.
- Speak, wizard. My patience burns down faster than your candles.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Write it in your best hand; your souls will be signing the next one.
- Done. Your scholars drive a precise bargain. I enjoy precision, especially in pain.
- Acceptable. Tell your archmages it was a fair trade. They will not believe you.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Amurites. Is it a bribe, or a sacrifice? Either pleases me.
- I accept. Your forefather threw us out; his children bring us presents. Delicious.
- How generous. When your mages come to hell, I will remember who was polite.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your mages know the price of power better than anyone. This is not it.
- You offer me crumbs from your library table. I want the books.
- Refused. Even a first-year student of yours could count better than this.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, for now. Your mages are more useful alive and curious.
- Go back to your schools. Some of your students will find their way to me anyway.
- Enough. I will let your towers stand; they make such fine beacons for the corrupt.

#### Refuses peace
- Kylorin cast us out once. His children will not be so lucky.
- Peace? Your wizards are still burning so beautifully.
- No. I have not yet collected your archmages, and they are the best part.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand? The flames do not give, scholar. They consume.
- Study this answer carefully: no.
- A tribute from hell? Your bureaucrats would need a new form for that, and I will not fill it in.

### Infernal → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- The Balseraphs. Your court raises its children among imps, I hear. We should get on famously.
- A carnival of masks and slaves. Hell has its own carnivals. Yours are almost charming.
- Your summoners bind my servants as nursemaids. Do they know we keep count of every one?

#### Declares war
- The masquerade ends, and the real faces underneath are all mine.
- Your summoned servants belong to hell. I am taking them back, and you with them.
- Laugh, jesters. You will laugh in the pit too; it is required.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your jesters' rhymes give even me a headache.
- I do not bargain with madmen while I am busy killing them.
- Go away, harlequin. I am not one of your puppets, to be pulled about by the strings.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The masquerade comes to hell's door. Come in; we have such interesting masks.
- [CT_NAME], your court keeps slaves and calls summoned devils playmates. I admire the style.
- Mad, cruel and inventive. You would make a fine demon.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your summoners chain my imps to your service. Every one of them is mine, and I want them back.
- Your laughter grates on me. Speak, and stop grinning.
- Your mimics steal what is not theirs. Hell does that too, but better.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and spare me the rhyme.
- Done. A bargain between the mad and the damned. What could go wrong?
- Acceptable. Your taskmasters will find a use for it, I am sure.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A present from the court of masks. Is it poisoned? How thoughtful, if it is.
- I accept. Your court understands generosity as a kind of cruelty. So do I.
- Charming. Send more slaves next time; they are my favourite gift.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. I do not trade with fools unless I am the one doing the fooling.
- You offer me a jester's prize: bright paint over nothing.
- Refused. I know all your tricks; we invented most of them.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your festival. I will come and watch some day.
- Fine. Keep your slaves; I will collect them later anyway.
- Enough. The show was entertaining, but I tire of it.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your court is too much fun to stop now.
- Peace? I have not yet seen what is under your masks.
- You summon my servants and then beg me for peace? No.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand of me, jester? I am not part of your act.
- No. The flames do not juggle.
- Nothing. Ask your imps; they owe you more than I do.

### Infernal → Bannor

#### First contact
- The Bannor. You were ours once, in the ash. Your angel stole you away. We remember every name.
- Your ancestors ran across the plains of ash with my hounds at their heels. Do you still dream of it?
- One of you stayed behind to hold the door, you know. Donal Lugh still fights in the pit. Shall I tell him you said hello?

#### Declares war
- You escaped hell once. You will not do it twice.
- Your angel cannot carry you out again. I will drag every one of you back to the ash.
- Junil promised you salvation for obedience. I offer damnation for free.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Hell does not negotiate with escaped prisoners.
- Your Confessors cannot exorcise me with words. Go away.
- I have nothing to say to the runaways of the ash, except come home.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The Bannor, come willingly to hell's door. What an improvement.
- Even crusaders get tired, [CT_NAME]. Sit, rest, and tell me what you want.
- Your people know the pit better than any. Perhaps you know what we can offer.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Crusaders cut down my demons and call it Junil's will. I call it theft.
- You are runaways from hell. Talk, before I decide to collect you.
- Your priests preach against us at every altar. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A contract with the Bannor, at last. The pit will be laughing for ages.
- Done. Your Order would burn you for this. I find that delightful.
- Acceptable. Junil will not like it, but Junil does not have to.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the crusaders? Junil must be looking away.
- I accept, and I will remember that the runaways sent an offering home.
- How touching. Your ancestors' souls are still warm in the ash. They send their thanks.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your Order's laws have made you poor bargainers.
- You offer what a priest would offer: little, and with conditions.
- Refused. Hell does not take promises, only payment.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. But know that every Bannor soldier who dies will still come to me.
- Very well. Go back to your fortress farms. I know where they are.
- Enough. Rest, crusaders. Hell can wait for you.

#### Refuses peace
- You stole yourselves out of hell. I am not done collecting.
- No. Your Basilicas burn so well.
- Peace with the Bannor? Not while you still pray for my destruction.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand of hell? You fled from us; you do not get to make demands.
- No. Junil can pay your tithes.
- You would demand something from me? Have you forgotten what we did to your ancestors?

### Infernal → Calabim

#### First contact
- The Calabim. Every soul your vampires drink is a soul stolen from my fires. We must talk about that.
- Vampire lords and their herds. You keep cattle; I keep souls. We are almost colleagues.
- You devour men's spirits rather than let them fall where they belong. Thief.

#### Declares war
- You have been stealing from hell for centuries. Today I collect the debt.
- Every spirit you have swallowed will be cut out of you, vampire.
- Your herds belong to me after death. I am coming to take them early.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. A thief who has picked hell's pocket for centuries does not get a hearing.
- Go back to your feeding, leech. We will talk when you are ash.
- Your courtiers smell of stolen souls. Send them away.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the vampire princes. Come, let us discuss the division of the spoils.
- [CT_NAME], your nobility has such refined cruelty. I could learn from it.
- The Calabim, at my table. Shall we talk about how to make cattle of the world?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You eat the souls that should come to me. Do you know what I do to thieves?
- Your Grand Broods grow fat on what is mine by right.
- Speak, leech. And keep your teeth to yourself.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Between your herds and my fires, the world is well managed.
- Done. A vampire who pays his debts. How refreshing.
- Acceptable. Now stop drinking from my supply.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Calabim. It does not quite make up for the souls you swallow, but it is a start.
- I accept. You know how to treat a lord of hell.
- How generous. Feed well, vampire; you will come to me eventually.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You keep the best of your herds for yourself. I know.
- That is a bloodpet's bargain. I am no bloodpet.
- Refused. You owe hell more than this already.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your herds. But their souls are mine when they die.
- We both prefer living prey to dead soldiers.
- Enough. Go and feed, and leave the spirits for me.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You have been stealing from hell too long.
- Peace? I have not yet made you choke on what you have taken.
- Your herds are scattering. I will chase them into the pit.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand? You owe me, vampire. Not the other way round.
- No. Hell does not feed leeches.
- Nothing. You have already taken enough souls from me.

### Infernal → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- Children of Bhall. Your goddess fell because she listened to Agares. Will you listen too?
- Orcs of Braduk. Half your holy city is a pit of fire. I know that pit well; it leads to my home.
- The Ember Banner. When Bhall fell through Braduk, she dragged the best of your city down to us. We kept them. You are what was left.

#### Declares war
- Agares only had to whisper, and your goddess fell. I will not bother whispering to you.
- Bhall's fire is a candle beside hell's. Let me show you.
- Your raids are entertaining, orc. Mine are thorough.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Go and pray at your Sacred Flame. See whether your goddess answers before I do.
- The Clan negotiates with an axe. So do I, today.
- Your priests of Bhall may scream into the fire all they like. I am not listening.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The orcs of Braduk. Your goddess fell to a whisper. Listen to mine.
- [CT_NAME], your clans burn and pillage with real enthusiasm. I respect that.
- Come, orc. Your clans and my legions both hate the Bannor. That is a fine place to begin.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You sacrifice humans to your fallen goddess. Their souls come to me anyway.
- Your goblins have been looting my borderlands. Hell does not share its loot with goblins. Talk.
- You call yourselves the children of fire. You are its leftovers. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Strange; I expected you to try to stab me across the table.
- Done. Burn something in my honour.
- Acceptable. Take it back to Braduk and roast it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Plunder, freely given. Whoever you took it from, I approve of the method.
- I accept. Bhall's children know who holds the real fire now.
- How generous. Your souls will be warm when they come to me.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer me the share a war chief leaves for the goblins.
- The damned on the plains of ash have made me better offers than this. Try again.
- Refused. Hell is not a village for you to plunder.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go home to Braduk and stoke your little flame.
- Very well. You will burn yourselves out without my help.
- Enough. Your clans and my legions have common enemies left to burn.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Bhall fell all the way down, orc. You have only started.
- Peace? The Clan has never kept a truce longer than its own hunger. No.
- Your war camps are burning nicely. I want to see the Sacred Flame go out.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand of hell? Your goddess listened to Agares once. Ask her how that ended.
- No. Go and pull your tribute out of a Bannor village, like an honest orc.
- Nothing. Your clans take; they do not demand.

### Infernal → Doviello

#### First contact
- The Doviello. You cull your weak the way wolves do. In hell we would call that a promising start.
- Northmen of the wastes. Your shamans fetch heroes back out of Camulos' vault. I know that place, and what it leaves in a soul.
- Savage, merciless and proud of it. Some of you already carry a little of the pit in your blood; I can smell it.

#### Declares war
- You admire the wolf because it eats the weak. Meet the thing that eats wolves.
- Camulos trains his demons on souls like yours. I will send him a fresh pack.
- Your pack believes it is strong, [CT_NAME]. Hell will teach it the meaning of the word.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You respect only strength. Come back when you have some left.
- Wolves do not parley in the middle of a hunt, and neither do I.
- Your messenger whimpered all the way in. Send a stronger one, or none.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The pack comes to the pit. You have the right instincts; let us see whether you have the stomach.
- You leave your wounded for the wolves and call it wisdom. Hell agrees.
- Come in, northman. Here no one will call you a savage, or if they do, it is a compliment.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders tear at my borders like starving dogs. Speak, before I have you put down.
- You think yourselves cruel. You have never seen cruelty.
- Your beastmen howl at my gates every night. Say what you want and take them away.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair split of the kill.
- Done. The strong deal with the strong, and the weak are eaten. You understand.
- Acceptable. Take it back to your pack and fight over it as you like.

#### Thanks for a gift
- The pack brings tribute. You know your place before a greater beast. Good.
- I accept. You bring tribute like a wolf dragging a carcass to the pack leader.
- How fitting. The wolves feed the pit.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You keep the best meat for yourselves, as wolves always do.
- That is a share fit for the runt of the litter. I am not the runt.
- Refused. Even that clanking War Machine of yours is worth more than this.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go home and cull your weak; I will collect them as they fall.
- Your pack has bled enough to please me.
- Enough. Camulos will have plenty of your dead to train as it is.

#### Refuses peace
- No. The wolf does not stop until the prey is dead. Neither do I.
- Peace? You preach that only the strong survive. Prove it.
- Your pack is thinning. I mean to finish the cull.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? The weak do not make demands of the strong. That is your own creed, beastman.
- No. Take it by force, if your pack can.
- Nothing. A wolf that begs at hell's door ends up on a spit.

### Infernal → Elohim

#### First contact
- The Elohim. Keepers of holy places, guardians of the weak. Every one of you will look lovely in the pit.
- Your monks' purity wards off things like me, they say. Let us find out how far it reaches.
- You stood witness to the Compact, monk. Hell never signed it. Remember that.

#### Declares war
- Your shrines will be our altars. Your sacred sites will be our gates.
- I will make your monks watch their holy places burn, and then I will take the monks.
- The last time the Elohim made peace with hell, it ended in a house full of blood. This war will end worse.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Elohim treaties are written in tears, and I have no use for tears that are not mine to cause.
- I do not bargain with saints. I break them.
- Go back to your shrines, monk. Pray I do not follow you home.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The Elohim at my gate, unarmed as always. Brave, or foolish?
- Come, keeper. You tend the dying and I receive them. We are in the same trade, at different ends.
- [CT_NAME], even saints have needs. Tell me yours.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your monks sanctify the land against my taint. It washes off.
- You look at me as if you remember the last time the Elohim trusted hell. Good. Keep remembering.
- Speak, priest. Your purity makes my teeth ache.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Read every word, saint. Hell keeps its treaties to the letter, and only to the letter.
- Done. A bargain with the Elohim; the pit will be talking of it for an age.
- Acceptable. Go home to your shrines, and sleep well, if you can.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the holy ones. Do your monks know you sent it?
- I accept. Even saints know when to placate the dark.
- How kind. I will think of you fondly when your shrines are mine.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer charity; I want sacrifice.
- That is a monk's bargain: all virtue and no value.
- Refused. You can afford better; I have seen what your pilgrims leave at the shrines.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. All that came before is forgiven, as the treaties say. Every word of it binding.
- As you like. Go and tend your sacred sites. Lock your doors at night.
- Enough. The Elohim always come round to peace in the end, and hell can always wait.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You signed with hell once and paid for it. I want you to pay again.
- Peace? Your monks still fight with their bare hands. I enjoy watching.
- Your sacred sites are not yet mine. The war goes on.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Your monks carry no weapons, and you think you can carry threats?
- No. The Elohim give; they do not take. Do not forget yourselves.
- Nothing. Pray for it instead; you are good at that.

### Infernal → Grigori

#### First contact
- The Grigori, who trust no god. Wise. But the lords of the pit are not gods, and we are much closer.
- Your creed says the heavens the gods built are counterfeit. You never said that of hell, did you?
- A people who walked away from the gods' war. How sad; the war followed you.

#### Declares war
- You refuse to believe in the gods. You will believe in me.
- Your adventurers wanted heroes' deaths. They will get heroes' afterlives, and those are very long.
- No god protects the Grigori. That is precisely why I came first to you.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your famous counsel is wasted on the damned.
- I do not talk to heroes while they are still bleeding on my field.
- Go and find your own answers, as your creed teaches.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The godless come to hell's door. I have so much to show you.
- You owe the gods nothing, [CT_NAME]. Then owe me something instead.
- Come in, freethinker. Here, at least, you will find a power that keeps its promises.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your adventurers hunt my demons for sport. Speak, before I hunt yours.
- Your people call my Ashen Veil a cult of murderers. They are; they are also mine.
- Speak, Grigori. A lack of faith is not a shield.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. You trust no one, so I know you read the terms. Good.
- Done. People who need no gods make honest bargains, if dull ones.
- Acceptable. Your independence has a price; you have just paid part of it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- The godless, giving to hell. I am almost touched.
- I accept. You give to me what you would never give to a god. Interesting.
- How generous. Your adventurers will find me grateful, one day, when they arrive.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You bargain like men who have never needed a miracle.
- Too little, even from a people with no temples to keep.
- Refused. Your heroes are worth more than this. Send me one instead.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your cities and lead yourselves, while you can.
- Very well. Your heroes have earned a little rest before I collect them.
- Enough. You fight well for a people with no one to pray to.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your heroes have no god to save them, and I want them.
- Peace? You could turn from the gods. You cannot turn from me.
- Your adventurers keep coming. Let them; hell has room.

#### Rejects a demand
- You refuse the gods' commands, and you think you can command me?
- No. Rely on yourselves, as you are always telling the world.
- Nothing. Your creed teaches self-reliance. Practise it.

### Infernal → Hippus

#### First contact
- The Hippus. You rode beside Kylorin when he drove my kind out of Patria. Did you think we would forget?
- Horse lords and sell-swords. I pay very well, in coin you have never seen.
- Your horses shy from my hounds already. Wise beasts.

#### Declares war
- Your horses will scream before you do.
- My Gaersteeds will run your herds into the ground, and then they will run down your riders.
- You sold your lances to my enemies, rider. I will pay you back in fire.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your mercenaries can negotiate with my hellhounds.
- I do not talk terms with hirelings. Send whoever is paying you.
- Go back to your plains, rider, while you still have plains.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, horse lord. I am always hiring.
- Your companies fight for gold, [CT_NAME]. I offer more than gold.
- The Hippus at my gate. Your horses are trembling; you are not. Good.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your companies have been selling their lances against me. Who paid more?
- Speak, rider. Your horse will not hold still much longer in this heat.
- I know what your raiders did to my kind in the last days of Patria. Talk.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A mercenary and a demon, shaking on a deal. Count your fingers afterwards.
- Done. A mercenary's bargain, struck clean.
- Acceptable. Spend it on horses that do not bolt at the smell of brimstone.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Your clans give nothing away, so I must ask: whom are you hoping I will burn instead of you?
- I accept. Your clans may need a friend in the pit someday.
- How generous. Perhaps you will ride for me next.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That is a hireling's price for a lord's request.
- You would charge me for the dung of your own horses. No.
- Refused. You haggle like a raider with a knife at a merchant's throat. My throat is thicker than that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Ride away while your horses still have legs.
- Consider the contract ended, and the payment taken.
- Enough. Go and sell your lances somewhere else.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your companies are breaking, and I want to watch them run.
- Peace? You hunted my kind across Patria. Now be hunted.
- No one outruns the Hippus, they say. No one outruns hell either.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Mercenaries are paid for their work, not given gifts for their gall.
- No. Your lances have been for sale to my enemies; let my enemies pay you.
- Nothing. Go and raid your own cousins for it, as you always have.

### Infernal → Illians

#### First contact
- The Illians. I have walked through the mire of Mulcarn, below. It was cold and dull. Rather like you.
- Mulcarn's old priests, awake again, following a mortal who wants to be a god. How entertaining.
- Snow and silence. You will find that fire disagrees.

#### Declares war
- Your winter will melt in my fires, and your halls will run with steam.
- Mulcarn is gone, and his would-be heir is still mortal. Mortals come to me.
- Let us see whose god is stronger. Yours is gone, and mine is very much awake.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your breath freezes, and so does your argument.
- I do not bargain with snowdrifts.
- Go back to your caverns, frost-priest. They are colder than any welcome I could give.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The Illians at hell's door. Mind the heat; I would hate for anything of yours to melt.
- You want a throne in the heavens; I want souls on the ground. We need not quarrel, [CT_NAME].
- Come in from the cold. Here, everything is warm.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your snows keep putting out my fires. Speak, before I decide to melt you.
- You think you can become a god? You are still mortal. I can smell it on you.
- The White Hand has a bad habit of killing my cultists. Explain yourselves.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Fire and ice at the same table. The gods would be furious.
- Done. Keep it frozen, if you like; it will thaw when you come to me.
- Acceptable. Your ascension will need paying for, I suppose.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Tribute from the frost. It will melt down here, but I appreciate the gesture.
- I accept. When you fall from your throne of ice, I will remember this kindly.
- How generous. A god-in-waiting, sending tribute to hell.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That offer is as cold as your halls and twice as empty.
- Refused. Mulcarn's priests never did learn to bargain.
- No. You would trade me snowmelt for hellfire and call it even.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and play at being a god.
- Fine. Your snow and my fire make nothing between them but mud.
- Enough. The world is wide enough for winter and hell, for now.

#### Refuses peace
- No. I want to watch your throne of ice drip.
- Peace? Fire does not make peace with ice. It consumes it.
- Your White Hand is falling apart. I will not stop now.

#### Rejects a demand
- Gods make demands, and you are not one yet.
- No. The flames give nothing to the cold.
- Nothing. Go and freeze.

### Infernal → Khazad

#### First contact
- The Khazad. Your Stonewardens say hell burns hotter than any forge. They are right. Come and see.
- Dwarves, counting gold in the dark. There is a whole hell for that, and Mammon keeps it. You would feel at home.
- Children of stone. I have always wondered whether stone screams in the fire.

#### Declares war
- Your vaults will melt, dwarf, and the gold will run like water down into my pits.
- Kilmorph shaped you out of stone. Hell has always been very good at breaking stone.
- Your Stonewardens warned you that the foolish burn away like fool's gold. Let us see which of you is real.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your hammers are loud, but my fires are louder.
- Go back to your tunnels, dwarf. You will want them.
- Talk? You are digging your own graves, dwarf. I would hate to interrupt.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Khazad. You love gold, and I can find you more of it than your vaults can hold.
- Your forges are the finest in Erebus, [CT_NAME], save mine. Let us talk shop.
- Welcome, dwarf. You distrust magic, I know. Good. I am not offering magic; I am offering power.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Stonewardens preach against me at every hearth in the Underhome. Speak.
- You count your gold while my legions burn your borders. Count faster.
- Speak, dwarf. Your beard is beginning to smoke.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A dwarf who drives a bargain like a demon. I am impressed.
- Done. Weigh it if you must; hell does not cheat on the weight, only on the terms.
- Acceptable. Put it in your vaults. I will collect it, and you, later.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Dwarven gold, offered up to hell. I will have it melted into something with screams in it.
- I accept. Your vaults must be overflowing, or your nerve failing.
- How generous. Mammon would be jealous.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You weigh your gold with a heavy thumb, and I can see it.
- Your price is as hard as your heads. No.
- Refused. Your merchants would laugh you out of the market for this.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and count what is left in your vaults.
- Very well. Your gunners are tiresome, and stone does not burn well. Go.
- Enough. Go back below and seal your stone doors.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your vaults are not yet empty.
- Peace? I have not yet melted down your crowns.
- The Underhome kept you safe from winter. It will not keep you safe from fire.

#### Rejects a demand
- A dwarf demanding gold from hell? You have the bargain backwards.
- No. Dig it up yourselves; you are good at that.
- Nothing. Your vaults are full enough to keep you warm until I arrive.

### Infernal → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- The Kuriotates. You take in every outcast and stray in Erebus. Would you take in a demon?
- A crown over centaurs, giants, lamia and men. So many different flavours of soul in one realm.
- Your settlements stretch so far and so thin. Each one is a little door left open for me.

#### Declares war
- Centaur, giant, lamia or man, every one of your peoples screams the same in the fire.
- Your outlying settlements will burn first, and then I will come for the great cities at your core.
- All those races, all those souls. Hell has room for every one of them.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your courtiers are very polite. I am not.
- I do not haggle with a menagerie while I am hunting it.
- Your court sends an envoy of a different race each time. Send the one who surrenders.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Kuriotate. Your realm opens its doors to everyone; so does mine, though it never lets them out.
- Your lamia command real magic, [CT_NAME]. I could teach them so much more.
- The confederation comes to the pit. Do bring the centaurs next time; they fascinate me.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your realm shelters every refugee fleeing my legions. That will stop.
- Your centaurs patrol my borders as if they owned them. Speak, before I loose the hounds.
- You offer asylum to every creature in Erebus, but not to my kind? How unwelcoming.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. One crown, many peoples, one signature. Very efficient. I approve.
- Done. Spread it among your many peoples; they will squabble over it nicely.
- Acceptable. You run an orderly realm. It will make an orderly ruin.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the confederation. The giants did not carry it, I hope; they smell.
- I accept. Your settlements may stand a little longer.
- How generous. Your realm takes in everyone; now it gives to everyone too.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer what a frontier settlement could spare, not what a kingdom owes.
- That is an offer for a petty clan, not for a lord of hell.
- Refused. Your great cities are rich. I know; I have counted them.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Draw back into your core lands and count what you lost on the frontier.
- Your settlements may rebuild. I will know where to find them.
- Enough. Your centaurs fought well; I will collect them some other day.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your shell is cracking, and I can see the soft parts.
- Peace? I have not yet reached your core cities, and I so want to see them.
- Every race you sheltered will come to me in the end. Why wait?

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Your realm takes in every beggar in Erebus; I did not know it had become one.
- No. Your realm has plenty of everything; take it from your settlements.
- Nothing. Hell grants no asylum to your treasury.

### Infernal → Lanun

#### First contact
- The Lanun. Your sea god stopped answering your prayers an age ago. Hell always answers.
- You sold ships to both sides when Patria tore itself apart. A people after my own heart.
- Captains who answer to no one. You will all answer to me, in the end.

#### Declares war
- Your ships will burn to the waterline, and the drowned will come to me.
- Danalin will not save you, sailor. He has not even spoken to you in an age.
- Run before the wind, captain. My fires run faster.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I have dealt with liars for ages, captain, but even I insist they lie for longer than a tide.
- Go back to your ship, pirate, while it still floats.
- I do not sit down with sea-thieves while their crews are still shooting at mine.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, captain. You have no god who answers, and neither, strictly, do I.
- Your Overlords drive their dreamers mad, [CT_NAME]. I prefer despair. We could compare methods.
- The Lanun come to hell. I hear you will trade with anyone, and I am anyone.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your ships smuggle my prey out of my reach. That stops now.
- Speak, pirate. Your word means nothing, but say it anyway.
- Your cultists make the Drown of honest sailors. Their souls are mine all the same.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A pirate's bargain, and a fair one. Will wonders never cease.
- Done. A pirate's word and a demon's word on one page. The ink is blushing.
- Acceptable. Spend it in port, and spend it badly.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the sea-raiders. Danalin never got such tribute from you, I imagine.
- I accept. The sea has sent hell another tribute.
- How generous. I may spare one of your harbours, briefly.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That is a smuggler's offer, and I am not a customs clerk.
- You offer me the bilge and keep the treasure in the hold. I can smell the difference.
- Refused. Your word is not collateral, captain. It never was.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Take your fleets back out to sea; I prefer my enemies on dry land, where they burn.
- As you like. Your fleets may sail on, and I will watch which ports they visit.
- Enough. Salt water and hellfire never mixed well.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your harbours are burning, and I like the colour on the water.
- Peace with pirates? You would break it with the next tide.
- Your sea god is silent, captain. Nothing is coming to save you.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Go and board some fat merchant, pirate. Hell is not a merchantman.
- No. Ask the Overlords; their gifts come with madness attached, but at least they come.
- Nothing. Hell pays no tolls to the sea.

### Infernal → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- The Ljosalfar. Your priests of Leaves say there is no rebirth for those exiled to hell. Your priests are right.
- Elves of the summer court, crawling back out of your hidden groves. Your forests are so very dry.
- Your rangers once felled a Balor with plain arrows. I remember the Balor. I remember its screams.

#### Declares war
- Your ancient forests will burn, elf, and nothing will grow back.
- The Fellowship of Leaves promises renewal. Hell offers only ash.
- Your groves were nearly lost to the ice. They will be lost to the fire.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Elves talk for decades and then say nothing. I have no decades to spare.
- Go back to your trees, elf. I will be along to light them.
- I do not parley with druids. They always smell of wet leaves.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, elf. Your court values beauty. Hell has its own, if you know where to look.
- Your forests are lovely, [CT_NAME]. It would be a shame if anything happened to them.
- The Ljosalfar come to hell's door. Surprising. Even elves get desperate.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your treants pull my demons apart. I take it personally.
- Your druids pray for my destruction at every grove. Speak.
- You look at me as if I were rot in your woods. I am much worse.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Elven craftsmanship is wasted on elves anyway.
- Done. Carry it back to your hidden groves, and mind the dry leaves on the path.
- Acceptable. Even the summer court must bargain with the fires eventually.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the summer court. Your priests of Leaves would burn you for it, if they burned things.
- I accept. The forest bows to the flame at last.
- How generous. When the fires come, I will leave one ancient tree standing, so you have something to weep under.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer leaves and ask for gold.
- That is an elf's bargain: beautiful, and empty.
- Refused. Your forests are worth more to me burning.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your groves, and keep them damp.
- Very well. Your forests may grow, until I need firewood.
- Enough. Your archers have made their point, a few thousand times over.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your forests are burning, and I want to see them all go.
- Peace? You would only replant.
- Your people barely survived the death of their god. Let us see whether they survive me.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand from the forest? Go and ask your trees.
- No. Ask Cernunnos; he is new to being a god, and may still be generous.
- Nothing. Hell is not a grove for you to harvest.

### Infernal → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- The Luchuirp. You build servants without souls. How wasteful; the soul is the only part worth having.
- Gnome artificers. Your miners keep turning up pieces of Mammon's hoard in the deep shafts. Do keep digging.
- Little makers of golems. Your clockwork men cannot feel pain. Fortunately, their makers can.

#### Declares war
- I will melt your golems into slag and take the makers instead.
- Your clay soldiers do not fear me. They are the only ones in your realm who will not.
- Kilmorph hid you under the mountain from the ice. There is no mountain deep enough to hide you from fire.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Send a golem to talk next time; at least it will not whine.
- I do not bargain with tinkerers while their toys are breaking.
- Go back to your workshops, little one. Sweep up the pieces.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, builder. Hell always has work for clever hands.
- Your golems are marvels, [CT_NAME]. Imagine one with a demon inside it instead of a spell.
- The Luchuirp at hell's door. Mind your step; the hounds are taller than you.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems trample my imps into the mud. Speak, before I take them apart.
- Your Stonewardens chant against me in every forge. I hear the hammers stop.
- You bury the strange crystals your miners find instead of bringing them to me. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your work is excellent. Hell appreciates craftsmanship more than you might think.
- Done. Some day you will build me something, and you will not even know it.
- Acceptable. Kilmorph's children always knew the value of things.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Gnome-work, freely given to hell. Kilmorph will be furious, and I adore that.
- I accept. Your craftsmanship is wasted on the surface; it belongs in the deep places.
- How generous. I will keep it far from the forges, so it does not melt.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You price your work as if your golems had souls.
- That is a tinker's offer, for a tinker's customer.
- Refused. Your ancestors made wonders in the Age of Magic. Offer me one of those.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your workshops and count your broken golems.
- The Open-Skiers may keep their sky, a little longer.
- Enough. Rebuild, little ones. I like having something to break.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your golems are melting, and I want to see what their makers do next.
- Peace? I came for the makers, not their toys.
- Your goddess cannot shelter you this time. Run back underground if you like; fire follows.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Your golems never ask for anything. Learn from them.
- No. Kilmorph hands out gifts to her children. I do not.
- Nothing, gnome. Not a cog.

### Infernal → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim. Your desert is already halfway to hell. I could finish the work for you.
- Children of Lugus. You worship the sun. How sweet. Let me show you a fire that never sets.
- Desert folk with an elf's faith. Lugus' light will not reach you in the pit.

#### Declares war
- Your sun burns; so do we. Let us see which burns longer.
- Your Radiant Guard will shine brightly as they fall.
- The Empyrean promises wisdom and fairness. Hell promises neither.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your Vicars talk of justice; I have no use for it.
- Go back to your sands. I will be there shortly.
- Shield your eyes and go home, sun-priest. Down here there is nothing for your light to fall on.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, desert wanderer. You know heat; you will find hell homely.
- Your Empyrean gives an equal voice to small and great, [CT_NAME]. I give an equal fate to them.
- The Malakim at my door. Do not stare at the flames; they are not your sun.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Radiant Guard burns my demons. It hurts, a little. Speak.
- You call me darkness. I am fire; we are relatives, you and I.
- Speak, priest. Your light gives me a headache.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your Empyrean prizes fairness. Hell prizes profit. We met in the middle.
- Done. The desert taught you to drive a hard bargain; hell taught me to keep one.
- Acceptable. Lugus will not mind. Or he will, but he will not say.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the children of Lugus. Your sun must be very cross with you.
- I accept. Even the light pays tribute to the fire.
- How generous. When I come for the desert, I will begin at the far end of it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even a demon can see this is crooked, and we invented crooked.
- That is a desert offer: dry and empty.
- Refused. The sun gives freely; you should too.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your desert. It is hot enough without my help.
- Fine. Your sun may rise tomorrow. Not forever.
- Enough. Bank your Radiant Guard's light; it stings, and I have tired of it.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your sun is setting, and I want to watch.
- Peace? Your temples still stand. That will change.
- Lugus has not saved you yet. He will not.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Ask your sun. It gives itself away every morning.
- No. Lugus gives; hell takes.
- Nothing. You chose a god of light, and he gave you sand. Do not ask me to make up the difference.

### Infernal → Mercurians

#### First contact
- The Mercurians. Of course you followed us up. You always do.
- Angels who broke the Compact so you could go on killing my kind. Did you think hell would not return the favour?
- Rebels of Arawn, with prayers carved into your skin. Mortal flesh suits you. It bleeds.

#### Declares war
- You have hunted us through hell and creation alike. Today the hunt turns round.
- Your host defied its own gods to fight me. Let us see what your defiance is worth without them.
- Pray, angels, with every cut in your skin. Nobody up there is listening to you any more.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You never once spoke to my kind except with a hammer. I return the courtesy.
- Talk with an angel of Arawn? I would sooner talk with the hounds.
- Go and carve another prayer. You will need it more than words.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- An angel at my gate who has not yet drawn steel. How novel. Speak, before you remember yourself.
- You care nothing for mortals, they say. Neither do I. Perhaps we have one thing to discuss.
- The Mercurians come to bargain with hell. Your old masters would weep to see it.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You smell of holy oil and old blood. Say your piece and go back to your war.
- Your host is mistaken for demons wherever it goes. I find that hilarious.
- Speak, rebel. You have no gods behind you now, and my patience is shorter than your temper.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Hell and heaven's deserters, trading like merchants. The Compact never imagined this.
- Done. I will read every word. Angels lie too, when the cause is holy enough.
- Acceptable. Go and spend it on weapons to use against me; I expect nothing less.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the angels. Is it blessed? It is smoking a little.
- I accept, with the deepest suspicion.
- How generous. Do your carved prayers allow for gifts to the enemy?

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You bargain the way you fight: all force, no subtlety.
- That is an angel's offer. Righteous, and worthless.
- Refused. You came to fight me, not to sell to me. Remember that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. You will break it, of course. You broke the Compact for less.
- Very well. Rest your wings. The war between us does not end; it only pauses.
- Enough, for now. Even angels must bandage the wounds they carved into themselves.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You followed us out of hell to keep fighting. Then fight.
- Peace with the Mercurians? You would not know what to do with it.
- You broke heaven's oath to kill me. I will not break mine to spare you.

#### Rejects a demand
- An angel demanding from hell? Your gods would not dare, and you are not your gods.
- No. You came to take my life, not my gold. Try for the one you came for.
- Nothing. Carve that into your skin.

### Infernal → Sheaim

#### First contact
- The Sheaim. One of yours slipped out of Camulos' prisons, I hear. Hell noticed.
- Gate-openers. You and I both work at thinning the walls of creation. For very different reasons.
- You want creation to end. I want it full of mortals for me to collect. We should talk.

#### Declares war
- End creation, and where will the souls come from? You are ruining my harvest.
- Your gates lead into places I rule. Did you think I would not walk back through them?
- Armageddon is my business, gate-opener, not yours. I will not have amateurs ending the world.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You want the world to end; I want it to suffer. There is nothing to discuss.
- Go back to your rituals. I am busy.
- I do not barter with people who would burn the market down.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The Sheaim at hell's door. You know the way well enough.
- Your rituals thin the walls of creation, [CT_NAME]. I like a thin wall.
- Come in, gate-opener. Let us discuss how the world ends, and who gets to keep the pieces.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your summonings drag my servants up without asking. That is theft.
- You would end everything, and leave me nothing to torment. Speak.
- Speak, doom-sayer. I am tired of your prophecies.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Hoard it for your Armageddon if you like; I will still be collecting long after.
- Done. A deal between those who want the world ended and those who want it in pain.
- Acceptable. Your gate-magic is useful. Keep it pointed elsewhere.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Sheaim. Generosity at the end of the world. How touching, and how pointless.
- I accept. Ceridwen would not like this, I suspect.
- How generous. I will use it to keep the world going a little longer; I need it full of sinners.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. A people who expect no tomorrow should not be so stingy today.
- That is a doomsayer's offer: everything promised, nothing paid.
- Refused. I am not ending the world for that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep your gates away from my borders.
- The world may limp along a while longer. I prefer it limping.
- Enough. Go and work your rituals somewhere I am not standing.

#### Refuses peace
- No. I need the world intact, and you do not.
- Peace with the Sheaim? You would just open another gate behind my back.
- Your gates are closing, one by one. I mean to close them all.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? You want my treasure to spend unmaking the world I mean to harvest. No.
- No. Ask Ceridwen, who opened your prison. Let her pay for her own apocalypse.
- Nothing. The end of the world will not be funded by hell.

### Infernal → Sidar

#### First contact
- The Sidar. You sold pieces of your souls for endless life. Whoever bought them, I will pay more for the rest.
- Grey shades in hidden cities. You hunt the undead as abominations. I am not undead, shade. I am much worse.
- You gave up love, hate and hunger to live forever. You gave up everything that makes a soul worth torturing. Almost.

#### Declares war
- Immortal, are you? Hell is very good at testing that claim.
- Your hidden cities will burn, and what is left of your souls will come to me.
- You are hard to kill, shade. I have all the time in the world.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your voices are hollow, and I have no patience for echoes.
- No. You traded away your feelings; why would you mind being ignored?
- Your envoy drifted through my wall without knocking. It can leave the same way.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, grey one. You have stepped half out of the world already. Let me show you the other way out.
- The Sidar come out of hiding. Something must be frightening you, [CT_NAME].
- Sit, shade. You and I both find mortals tedious.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You call the undead aberrations and kill them on sight. Who are you to judge what is unnatural?
- Your grey cities keep my cultists out. Speak, before I find a way in.
- You feel nothing, they say. I can change that.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A cold bargain with a cold people. Refreshing.
- Done. You will not even enjoy it. How sad.
- Acceptable. Spend it on whatever shades spend things on.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A shade bearing gifts to hell. Mind you do not leave the rest of your soul on the table.
- I accept. Perhaps there is a little soul left in you after all.
- How generous. I will remember it when what is left of you comes down.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You let your souls go for a few extra centuries. I do not sell so cheaply.
- That is a ghost's offer: thin, and see-through.
- Refused. You have had centuries to learn to trade; it shows nowhere.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your libraries and your long, cold reading. I can wait as long as you can.
- You will outlive this treaty, shade. I may not care.
- Enough. Fade back into your hidden cities.

#### Refuses peace
- No. I want to see whether a shade can scream.
- Peace? You left your fog to fight me. Now find out how long forever really is.
- You are hard to kill, but not impossible. I have proved it twice this season.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand from a people who want nothing? How out of character.
- No. You traded your soul for time. Trade some time for gold.
- Nothing. Shades need nothing; you have said so for centuries.

### Infernal → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Svartalfar. A god who sells his miracles for a price. Esus and hell are in the same trade.
- Dark elves of the Unseelie court. You punished your own kin for worshipping the wrong god. I approve.
- Your court rules in the dark half of the year. Hell rules in the dark all the year round.

#### Declares war
- Your assassins are skilled, elf. Mine do not need to hide.
- Esus taught you to deceive. I will teach you to despair.
- Your court persecuted its own for the sake of a new god. Let us see how it fares under a new master.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Every word out of an Unseelie mouth is a knife in disguise.
- Go back to your Winter Court, elf; the snow suits your lies.
- I do not barter with liars while they are still bleeding.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Unseelie. Your court and mine have much in common: cruelty, elegance, and a taste for the dark.
- [CT_NAME], your shadowriders move unseen. I have work for unseen things.
- The Winter Court at hell's door. Sit, and lie to me; I enjoy it.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your assassins keep turning up in my cities, very dead. Send better ones, or none.
- You smile like Esus himself. Speak, and drop the smile.
- Your court lies to everyone. Do not imagine you can lie to me.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Esus would be proud of us both.
- Done. Count it in the dark if you like; it is all there, which is more than your court usually manages.
- Acceptable. A miracle, paid for in advance, just as your god likes it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Unseelie court. What is it really for?
- I accept. Your court understands that the dark must be fed.
- How generous. I will repay it with something equally sharp.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That is a trick, and not even a clever one.
- Your court's offers always have a blade in them. This one has nothing else.
- Refused. Esus would charge you more for this, and he would be right.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your court and sharpen something; you always do.
- Very well. Your court may scheme in peace, for a while.
- Enough. We are both too clever to waste ourselves on each other.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your court will learn that hell's dark is deeper than yours.
- Peace? You would stab me at the signing.
- Your shadows are thinning, elf. When the last one goes, so do you.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Your god charges for his miracles, and you expect mine for free?
- No. Your court has lied its way into enough wealth.
- Nothing. The dark gives nothing to those who live in it.

## Khazad

### Khazad → Amurites

#### First contact
- Amurites. A whole nation of spell-weavers. Our grandfathers traded their finest work to your kind for illusions that vanished by morning. We remember.
- So you are the children of Kylorin. I hope your gold is more solid than your forefather's empire.
- Mages, is it? Show me your coin first. Your conjuring can wait outside.

#### Declares war
- Your wizards can throw all the fire they like. Stone does not burn, and neither do our cannon.
- You have no siege engines, they say; your mages are your artillery. Good. Ours do not get tired.
- We'll see how your spells hold up against honest powder and good dwarven steel, [CT_NAME].

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Every word out of an Amurite mouth has a glamour on it.
- Ach, more of your clever talk. I've heard enough to last me till the mountains wear down.
- Away with ye. When we want a lecture, we'll enrol.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the scholars. Come in, but leave your wands at the door; it's a dwarven custom.
- You're a strange folk, Amurite, but you pay your debts. Sit, we'll talk.
- Welcome. Your archmages make fine customers, so long as they pay in metal and not in promises.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- I don't trust anything that glows, and your whole nation glows.
- Your hedge-wizards were seen near our mines. If they're looking for magic, there's none down there.
