- Speak plainly, Amurite. No tricks, or the guards will show you out.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! And I've had my Stonewardens check it for enchantments, so don't bother.
- A fair trade, Amurite. Solid goods, solid coin. As it should be.
- Done. Mind you, if this melts away come morning, we'll know who to visit.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Amurites? I'll have it weighed and tested before I say thank you. Ah, it's real. Thank you.
- Well now. A mage giving something away for nothing. Kylorin must be turning over in the ice.
- I'm obliged to you. It's not often your kind gives anything a dwarf can hold in his hand.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. I've seen illusions with more substance than this offer.
- Your archmages may squabble over trifles, but I'll not trade good stone for one.
- Ach, no. My grandfather's grandfather made that kind of deal with a wizard, and we've been sorry ever since.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back to your schools, and we'll go back to our forges.
- Enough. Your spells have scorched our walls, and our cannon have taught your mages some humility.
- Peace it is, but we'll be keeping a careful watch on your wizards.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your mages have burned our halls. We'll knock down a few of your towers first.
- Peace? Not while a single Amurite spell is still cast against our walls.
- Your spells crack our walls; our cannon crack your towers. I like our odds better.

#### Rejects a demand
- Conjure it yourself, if you're so clever.
- No. The Khazad were cheated by mages once. Never again.
- Not a single coin. You can transmute lead into gold, can't you? Then do it.

### Khazad → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- The Balseraphs. Masks and tricks and painted faces. Everything a dwarf hates, all in one court.
- Your court paid horse-raiders to bring it dwarven slaves once. We have not forgotten, and we never will.
- A circus that calls itself a nation. I'll be counting my fingers after every handshake.

#### Declares war
- You kept one of Kilmorph's children in a cage, diving in the mud for gold to amuse your court. Today the mud is yours.
- No more tricks, jesters. Our cannon do not laugh.
- Your mimics steal the skill of the warriors they kill. Let them try to steal a dwarf's stubbornness.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I'll not listen to a single rhyme.
- Every word your court says is a trap. Go away.
- Get your harlequin out of my hall before I lose my temper.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the court of masks. Take yours off, and we'll talk. No? Then talk anyway.
- I'll admit your festivals are a sight. Come, sit. Mind the stairs.
- Welcome, Balseraph. You'll forgive me if I keep my hand on my purse.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your taskmasters prowl near our mines looking for slaves. Call them off, or lose them.
- I know what your court does to its prisoners. Speak, and be quick.
- Your painted smiles don't fool me. Get to the point.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and I've had it read three times by three different clerks. No tricks this time.
- A fair bargain, from a court of tricksters. Wonders never cease.
- Done. If any of it is an illusion, you'll be paying twice.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift? From the Balseraphs? Let me see if it's real. Hmm. It is. Well, thank you.
- Generous of you. I'll keep it in the vault, well away from anything your court might have enchanted.
- Aye, I accept. But I'll have it checked for vipers.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That's a trinket for a fool, and I'm no fool.
- Your offers are like your masks: pretty on the outside, empty underneath.
- Ach, I can smell the greasepaint on this bargain from here. No.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back to your festival, and keep your slavers away from our hills.
- Enough. Your jesters have danced their last dance against our walls.
- Very well, peace. But every dwarf in the hills will sleep with a hand on his axe while your caravans are about.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your court laughed at our kin. We'll see who laughs last.
- Peace? Not while your taskmasters hold a single dwarf in chains.
- This is one show your court will sit through to the very end.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand? From a court of thieves and liars? No.
- Not a coin. You'd only spend it on more masks.
- Ah, no, I'll not be shoved around by a clown.

### Khazad → Bannor

#### First contact
- The Bannor. Every farm a fort, every peasant a soldier. Now that's a people who understand walls.
- Crusaders of Junil, eh? We follow Kilmorph, and she doesn't ask for unquestioning obedience. Just honest work.
- Your Halls are full of merchants from every land, I hear. Good. The Khazad are always looking for a new market.

#### Declares war
- Your Order calls its enemies damned. Well, the Khazad call ours debtors, and we always collect.
- You've fought orcs and demons for an age, crusader. Now try a dwarven siege line.
- Your fortress farms are well built. Our cannon will be pleased to test them.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I don't care to hear a sermon in the middle of a siege.
- Your Confessors can talk to the walls. We're busy.
- Ach, away with your priest-talk. Come back when you've something to pay with.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Bannor! Disciplined, honest and well armed. My kind of neighbour.
- Come in, crusader. We'll not talk religion, and we'll get on fine.
- Welcome. Your Orders buy good steel, and we make the best. Shall we talk business?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your priests keep adding names to their list of the damned. I hope ours isn't on it, for your sake.
- Your Crusaders marched a bit close to our mines last season. Speak.
- I'll hear you out, Bannor, but I'm in no mood for preaching.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! A Bannor contract, signed and sealed. As solid as one of your fortresses.
- Done. You drive a hard bargain, crusader, but a fair one.
- A fine trade. Junil's people know the value of good iron.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Junil be praised, as you'd say. And Kilmorph too, as we'd say. Thank you, crusader.
- I'm obliged. It'll go in the vault next to your last payment.
- Well now, that's generous. Your priests won't mind you giving to a dwarf, will they?

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That's a soldier's offer, all bluster and no coin.
- Your Order may demand obedience, but it can't demand a bargain.
- Ach, no. Even a crusader should know better than to try that on a dwarf.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back to your fortress farms. Our walls will be here if you need them.
- Enough. Your peasant regiments drill well, I'll grant ye. Let's not waste any more of them on our walls.
- Fair enough. Peace, and may your Order find some other enemy to fight.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your Crusaders started this. We'll finish it.
- Peace? Not while your Order is still knocking on our gates.
- Your crusade marched on our halls. It'll march home lighter, or not at all.

#### Rejects a demand
- A tithe? We tithe to Kilmorph, not to Junil.
- No. Your Order can collect from its own faithful.
- Your priests may tax the faithful. The Khazad keep faith with Kilmorph and with our ledgers, and neither owes you a copper.

### Khazad → Calabim

#### First contact
- The Calabim. Vampires, ruling over herds of men. Kilmorph made us from stone; there's no blood in us worth drinking.
- Blood-drinkers. I hear you keep your people like cattle. We keep our people in good stone halls with food on the table.
- Vampire lords. You'd best know that dwarves don't make good bloodpets. Too stubborn by half.

#### Declares war
- Your nobles live in decadent luxury on the blood of their slaves. We'll see how they fare against honest steel.
- You suck the life out of your cities. We'll knock the walls down around your ears.
- A vampire's strength is in the mind, they say. Let's see how your minds hold up to a cannonade.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I'll not trade words with a leech.
- Your envoy keeps eyeing the guards' throats. Get it out of my hall.
- We don't parley with things that feed on people. Out.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Calabim. Come in, but keep your teeth to yourselves.
- You're a strange folk, vampire, but you pay in gold, and gold's the same no matter who holds it.
- Welcome. You'll find no throats down here, only ledgers. Shall we open them?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your hunters were seen near our hills. If they want blood, they'll have to dig through rock for it.
- Your people look at our traders like drowning men at a rope. I know what you do to them. Speak.
- Speak, vampire. I don't like the look in your eye.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A vampire's coin spends the same as anyone's.
- A fair trade. Your Grand Broods have a head for business, I'll give you that.
- Done. Pleasure doing business, though not much pleasure.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Something from the Calabim with no blood on it? It's not cursed, is it?
- I'm obliged. I hope none of your herd went hungry for it.
- Well now. A vampire giving instead of taking. That's a new one.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You'll not drain me dry with a bargain like that.
- That's a leech's offer: a small bite now, and the rest drained later.
- Ach, no. I can see the teeth behind that smile.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go home to your Grand Broods and tell them dwarves are not on the menu.
- Enough. Your nobles have learned that stone halls don't bleed.
- Very well. But any hunter of yours found in our tunnels gets a stake and a shovel, peace or no.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your nobles have feasted long enough.
- Peace? Not while a single vampire still sits on a throne of blood.
- We'll not stop till your blood-farms are broken open and the herds run free.

#### Rejects a demand
- Demand? You'll get nothing from the Khazad, leech.
- No. Go drain your own people, if you need more.
- Not a single coin. Our gold is not your blood to drink.

### Khazad → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- The Clan of Embers. We fought a goblin war not long back. I hope you've brought better manners than they did.
- Orcs of Braduk. You worship a fallen fire; we work an honest one. Mind you don't confuse the two.
- You throw warriors at a problem till it goes away, I hear. Our walls don't go away.

#### Declares war
- Your raiders burn and loot. Let's see them loot a dwarven hold with the doors barred and the cannon loaded.
- You'll find no thatched villages to burn in the Underhome, orc. Only stone, and us.
- The goblins tried our tunnels once. Ask them how it went. Ah, but you can't.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You talk with an axe, so I'll answer with a hammer.
- Your envoy came in smelling of smoke and left the door open. Out.
- Grunt all you like. We'll listen when your fires are out.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- The Ember Banner, come to trade instead of raid? Let me sit down before I faint.
- Welcome, orc. You've strong backs and good iron in your hills, I'll wager.
- Come in. Your fire burns villages, ours makes steel. Perhaps there's a trade between the two.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders hit our caravans on the mountain road. Give me one reason not to send the musketeers after them.
- I can hear your goblins scratching at our gates. Speak.
- Speak, orc, and keep your hands off the merchandise.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! An orc who pays in full. I'll have that carved somewhere.
- Done. And it goes home in a cart, not in a raid. Agreed?
- A fair trade, if a smoky one.

#### Thanks for a gift
- An orc bringing gifts instead of torches. I'm obliged, and more than a bit suspicious.
- Well now. An orc giving something to a dwarf. The goblins would never believe it.
- I'm obliged. We'll forge it into something useful, which is more than it was.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That's a raider's price: you take, and I lose.
- Ach, you'd sell me back my own caravan. No.
- Not good enough. Bring me real iron, not scrap from burned villages.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go home, and keep your torches away from our caravans.
- Enough. Your spears are blunt from our walls. Go and sharpen them somewhere else.
- Right, then. Peace, and the first goblin found in our tunnels breaks it.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your raiders burned our road-houses. We'll burn your war camps.
- Peace? You'd raid again before the ink's dry.
- The goblin war ended when the goblins did. This one will end the same way.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand from the Clan? You'd do better trying to raid us. You'd still fail, mind.
- No. Orcs take; dwarves trade. You'll get nothing for nothing.
- Not a nail. Go and beg at your sacred fire.

### Khazad → Doviello

#### First contact
- The Doviello. Wolf-folk of the north. You leave your fallen for the snow; we carve ours into the rune halls. We're not much alike.
- Beastmen and war machines. Your engines are crude, friend. Ours are better, and we'll sell you one, at a price.
- You lived through the long winter by becoming the wolf. We lived through it by barely noticing.

#### Declares war
- Wolves have eaten dwarves before. Dwarves have skinned a good many wolves too.
- Your pack hunts the weak. You'll find none behind our walls.
- Bring your war machine, Doviello. We'll show you what a real siege looks like.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I don't bargain with a wolf while its teeth are in my leg.
- Howl all you like outside. The gates are stone, and they're shut.
- Your envoy's got blood on his beard. Not ours, I hope. Out.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the northmen. Rough folk, but honest in your way. Sit.
- Welcome. You respect strength; well, we've plenty, in stone and in steel.
- Come in from the cold, Doviello. Or do you prefer it out there?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders prowl our hills like a hungry pack. Call them in.
- You think only of blood. We think of the reckoning. Speak.
- Speak, beastman, and keep your hounds away from our miners.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair split. I'd not have guessed the pack could count past its kills.
- Done. Strong hands, firm deal.
- Aye, that'll do. Take it home to the pack and fight over it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- From the Doviello, for nothing? Your pack must be going soft. Don't worry; I'll tell no one.
- Well, I'm obliged. I never thought a Doviello would give me anything but a scar.
- Aye, thank you. And no, we'll not owe you a favour for it; that's not how gifts work.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer the runt's share and expect me to be grateful.
- Ach, that's a beggar's price, and you're no beggar. Try again.
- Not enough. You're used to taking from the weak, and we're not weak.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back north and hunt something else.
- Enough. Your pack's thinned out on our walls. Take what's left home.
- Hmph. Peace it is, and keep your beasts on your own side of the hills.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Wolves that come to the door get the hammer.
- Peace? You'd break it the moment your belly rumbled.
- Your pack tore at our walls. Now our cannon will tear at yours.

#### Rejects a demand
- Take it by strength, if you can. You can't.
- No. Your creed says the strong take from the weak. Look around; we're the strong ones here.
- Not a scrap, wolf. Go and hunt.

### Khazad → Elohim

#### First contact
- The Elohim. Keepers of holy places. We keep vaults. It's much the same work, though we lock our doors better.
- Pilgrims and monks. You're the most trusted folk in Erebus, they say. That's a fine thing in a trading partner.
- Your monks carry no weapons? Then you'll be needing someone to make you good strong locks.

#### Declares war
- Your shrines sit on good stone, monk, and we've a use for it.
- You defend your holy places with bare hands. We come with cannon. Think on that.
- We asked to trade, and you turned us away. Now we'll trade the hard way.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You'll talk of mercy, and I've heard it all before.
- Your monks can sit at our gates and meditate. We're not coming out.
- Not now, Elohim. Come back when your purse is open and your sermon's shut.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Elohim! Honest folk. Come in, come in.
- Welcome, pilgrim. Kilmorph's halls are holy too, in their way. Mind the steps; they're older than your order.
- The Khazad respect anyone who keeps their word, and you've kept yours for ages. Sit.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your monks keep wandering into our mines looking for holy relics. There's only ore down there.
- Speak, Elohim. I've no time for preaching today.
- You look at our forges as if they offended you. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! A deal with the Elohim is as good as carved in stone.
- Done. Your word's good, and so is ours.
- A fine trade. Your monks drive a gentle bargain, but they drive it straight.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Elohim. I'm touched, truly.
- Well, I'm obliged. Your charity's famous, and now I see why.
- Thank you. Kilmorph will remember your kindness, and so will our ledgers.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even saints have to pay a fair price.
- Ach, no. You're a holy folk, but that's not a holy bargain.
- Not enough, pilgrim. Your shrines can spare more than that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back to your shrines; we'll not trouble them again.
- Enough. Your monks fought with nothing but their fists and their faith. We'll not shame ourselves further.
- So be it. Kilmorph keep your holy places.

#### Refuses peace
- No. We've come too far to turn back now.
- Peace? Not until your shrines are under our protection.
- Your warrior monks fight well with bare hands. Not well enough.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand from the Elohim? You're meant to be the giving sort.
- No. Your monks took vows of poverty; I'd hate to tempt them.
- Not a coin. Your order lived on charity through the whole Age of Ice; ask your charity.

### Khazad → Grigori

#### First contact
- The Grigori. No gods, no masters, just your own two hands. A dwarf can respect that.
- Adventurers, eh? Every one of your heroes wants to go poking about in someone else's tunnels. Not ours, if you please.
- You've turned your backs on the gods; we turned ours on most of the world. Perhaps we'll get along.

#### Declares war
- Your heroes are mighty, they say. Let's see a hero hold up against dwarven siegecraft.
- You lead yourselves, Grigori. We'll see how well you lead yourselves under cannon fire.
- Your adventurers come looting through our holds. We'll send them home in pieces.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your famous counsel's wasted on us till the fighting's done.
- Go home and think for yourselves, as you're so fond of doing.
- Not now, Grigori. Our ears are full of the sound of hammers.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Grigori. Free folk, standing on your own feet. Come in.
- Ah, the godless! No offence meant. Sit.
- You don't pray and we don't preach. We'll get on fine.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your adventurers keep turning up in our mines with empty sacks and leaving with full ones. Speak.
- You tell our miners Kilmorph doesn't care for them. She does. Speak, and mind your tongue.
- Speak, Grigori. If it's another lecture on the gods, save your breath for the climb home.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. No god to swear by, so you swore by your own name. Good enough for me.
- Done. You bargain like a dwarf, Grigori. That's a compliment.
- A fair trade, by our reckoning and by yours.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Grigori? Well, I'm obliged, and I'll not ask which ruin your adventurers dug it out of.
- Thank you. You didn't need a god to tell you to be generous, did you?
- I accept it gladly. Your heroes are welcome to a drink in our halls.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You can do better than that, and you know it.
- Ach, that's an adventurer's offer: all promise and no plunder.
- Not good enough. You don't need a god to teach you sums.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Your free folk can go back to governing themselves, and we'll go back to minding our own.
- Enough. Your heroes fought well. Let them go home and boast of it.
- Done, then. May your adventurers find better tunnels to poke in.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your heroes are still at our gates.
- Peace? Not until your adventurers have learned to leave our holds alone.
- You rely on yourselves, Grigori. Rely on yourselves to survive this.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? You're the ones who say a free folk earns its own way.
- No. Earn it, as your creed says.
- Not a coin. Go and adventure for it.

### Khazad → Hippus

#### First contact
- The Hippus. Your raiders once took a dwarven company with nets and bolas. Then the muskets came out. Remember?
- Horse lords. They say no one outruns the Hippus. Musket balls do.
- Mercenaries, aye? We've gold and you've lances. That could be fine business, if you keep your hands off our caravans.

#### Declares war
- Your horses don't like thunder, rider. We've brought plenty.
- Your riders jeered that our feet don't reach the stirrups. We never needed stirrups; we had cannon.
- Your clans once took coin to carry off dwarven captives. Today we settle that account.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I'll not talk with a rider who's got a lance at my throat.
- Ride off. Our gates don't open for horse-thieves.
- Ach, you'll wheel round and charge the moment I open my mouth. Away.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, horse lord. Leave the beast outside; our halls weren't built for it.
- The Hippus at our gate, and not raiding! Come in, we've a contract to discuss.
- Sit, rider. Your companies want gold, and we've plenty. Let's talk.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders struck our caravans in the hills again. Speak.
- I've not forgotten what your kind did to dwarves on the open road. Talk fast.
- Speak, rider, before I start counting the horses I'm owed.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! A Hippus contract, and an honest one. I'll have the scribes frame it.
- Done. Your companies keep their word, I'll give you that.
- A fair trade. Spend it on fodder.

#### Thanks for a gift
- From the Hippus, and no invoice attached? I'll frame the empty space where it should be.
- I'm obliged. Perhaps the old grudge can rest a while.
- Thank you. Next time you pass through the hills, our gates will be open.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We hire Hippus companies at a fair rate; we don't buy their leftovers at a dear one.
- Ach, that's a horse-trader's price, and I've seen the horse. No.
- Not good enough, rider. You can't rush a dwarf into a bad deal; we don't run.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Ride home, and keep off the mountain roads.
- Enough. Our muskets have taught your horses what thunder means.
- Very well. Peace, but our watchmen will keep their eyes on the hills.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You've raided us once too often.
- Peace? Our roads aren't safe for a single cart yet. Not yet.
- No one outruns the Hippus? Fine. We'll see who outlasts.

#### Rejects a demand
- You'll have to raid us for it, and you know how that went last time.
- No. Your companies get paid for work, not for nothing.
- Not a coin, rider. Earn it with your lances.

### Khazad → Illians

#### First contact
- The Illians. Your god's winter lasted six generations up top. Down in the Underhome, we hardly noticed.
- Mulcarn's old priests. Our old kings kept us below with tales of a dread god and his legion of giants. Were those your giants?
- Winter folk. Winter never had a hold on the Underhome, and it never will.

#### Declares war
- You want the ice back. We want the sun. Our cannon will settle the matter.
- Your cold can't reach the deep halls, and our powder doesn't freeze. Come on, then.
- Stone holds the heat of the forge longer than you can hold a blizzard.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your breath freezes before it reaches my ears.
- Go back to your frozen caverns. We've caves of our own, and warmer ones.
- Ach, more talk of the long winter. We've a war to fight.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Illians. Come in and warm yourselves by the forge. Or don't, if it's not to your taste.
- Welcome. You're a cold folk, but you pay in good coin, and that warms me.
- Sit, winter-folk. We dwarves know a thing or two about deep places ourselves.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your snows keep closing the mountain passes, and our caravans can't get through. Speak.
- You'd freeze the whole world to make a god of a mortal. Not our part of it, you won't.
- Speak, Illian, and keep your frost off my beard.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair trade, even if your coin's a bit chilly to the touch.
- Done. Frozen or not, gold's gold.
- A fine bargain. Mind the ice on your way out; it's yours.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Well, I'm obliged to the Illians, and a little warmer for it.
- Thank you. We'll set it by the forge to thaw.
- I accept. Strange to have the winter bringing presents.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That's as cold an offer as I've ever seen.
- Ach, no. Your bargains are like your winters: too long and too harsh.
- Not good enough. Thaw it out and try again.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Take your blizzards home.
- Enough. Our forges have melted your snow, and your cold has cooled our tempers.
- Right. Peace, and may the passes stay clear.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You'd bring back the Age of Ice. Not while we've powder left.
- Peace? Your winter's still sitting in our passes.
- We slept through Mulcarn's winter once. We'll not sleep through yours.

#### Rejects a demand
- Go and dig it out of the ice yourselves.
- No. Your winter took enough from the world as it is.
- Not a coin. Mulcarn's gone, and his old priests make no demands of us.

### Khazad → Infernal

#### First contact
- Demons. Our Stonewardens warned us: hell burns hotter than any forge, and the foolish burn away like fool's gold.
- So you've climbed up out of the pit. We've dug deep ourselves, and never once wished to meet you.
- Hell's own legions. We'll trade, if we must, but every coin you hand us gets bitten twice.

#### Declares war
- Kilmorph's stone stood before you came, and it'll stand when you've gone back down.
- Your fires are hot, demon. Our forges are hotter, and they make cannon.
- We've dug deep enough to know what lies at the bottom. Today we fill the hole in.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I'll not deal with the pit.
- Go back where you came from. Our Stonewardens will see you on your way.
- Ach, the stink of brimstone. Out, before it gets in the beer.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Demons in my hall. Well, sit, but don't touch anything.
- Welcome, I suppose. Your gold is real, at least. I've had it checked.
- We'll talk business, demon, and nothing but business. There'll be no souls in this bargain.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your imps were seen in our deep shafts. There's nothing down there for you.
- Speak, demon, and make it quick. The smell is bothering the miners.
- Every Stonewarden in the Underhome prays against you night and day. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. But if there's a soul anywhere in the small print, the whole thing's void.
- Done. I'll be checking every coin for sulphur.
- A fair trade. Kilmorph forgive me for it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from hell? I'll have it blessed before it goes near the vaults.
- I accept it. I don't trust it, but I accept it.
- Thank you, I suppose. I'll keep it well away from the children.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There's a trap in it somewhere, and I've no wish to find it the hard way.
- Ach, I know fool's gold when I see it.
- That's a bargain for the damned, and I'm not damned yet.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Back down the hole with you, and we'll set a stone over it.
- Enough. Our cannon have made your demons think twice about stone walls.
- Peace, then. But the Stonewardens will keep their vigil.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Not until the last of your kind is back in the pit.
- Peace with demons? A dwarf never forgets a cheat, and you're the greatest cheats there are.
- Our powder's dry and our walls are high. Come and try them.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? From hell? Not a nail, not a pebble.
- No. Mammon can fill your coffers; we won't.
- Not a coin. The flames can find their own fuel.

### Khazad → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- The Kuriotates. Centaurs, giants, lamia and men all under one crown. That's a market with a lot of mouths.
- A confederation, is it? Well, the Khazad were a lot of squabbling clans once. We know how hard it is to hold together.
- Your settlements are spread thin over a great deal of land. That's a great many roads to sell paving for.

#### Declares war
- Your settlements are spread thin, Kuriotate. We'll take them one by one.
- You'll pull back into your shell, I hear. Good. Shells are what our siege engines were made for.
- Your giants are big, but they fall like anyone else under cannon fire.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I'll not haggle with a crown that sends a different race to every meeting.
- Not now. Your centaurs can trot back home.
- Ach, away with your courtly manners. We're busy.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Kuriotate. Your realm's open to all, and so is our market.
- Ah, the confederation. Sit; your giants will have to stand, I'm afraid. Low ceilings.
- Come in. Your centaurs are fine soldiers, and we make fine armour. Let's talk.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your settlements keep creeping closer to our mines. Speak.
- Your court is too clever by half. Say what you mean.
- Speak, Kuriotate, and leave the lamia's magic outside.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! A royal contract. I'll have it carved in stone.
- Done. Your administration's efficient, I'll grant you that.
- A fair trade. Your centaurs can carry it home; they've the backs for it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the confederation, carried by a centaur, no less. I'm obliged.
- Thank you. Your core cities must be rich indeed.
- I accept, and gladly. Your settlements will find our traders generous in turn.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That's an offer for a frontier settlement, not for the Khazad.
- Ach, you'd trade like a king and pay like a peasant.
- Not good enough. Your great cities can afford better.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Mend your settlements; we'll sell you the stone at a fair price.
- Enough. Your centaurs have tired themselves out on our walls.
- Fair enough. May your settlements prosper, at a respectful distance from our hills.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your settlements are still in our way.
- Peace? Not until your crown learns to respect our borders.
- Your shell's well made, I'll give you that. But siegecraft is what dwarves do best.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? We'd sooner sell to a centaur than give to a king.
- No. The Khazad are not one of your settlements.
- Not a coin. Ask your many races; one of them must have some.

### Khazad → Lanun

#### First contact
- The Lanun. Pirates and traders, they say, and no telling which you'll be on a given morning.
- Sea-folk. You sold ships to both sides when Patria tore itself apart. A dwarf can admire the profit, if not the honour.
- A captain's word is law on his own deck, I hear, and nowhere else. Then we'll want it in writing.

#### Declares war
- Your ships can't sail into the mountains, pirate. We can march down to your harbours.
- Every caravan you've robbed is written in our ledgers. Today we collect.
- The sea's yours, captain. The land is ours, and that's where you keep your harbours.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I'd sooner bargain with the barnacles on your hull; at least they stay put.
- Go back to your ship and sail away. We're not buying.
- Ach, you'd sell me the sea if you could. Not today.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Lanun! Come in, but leave your cutlass by the door.
- Welcome, captain. You've goods from every shore, and we've gold from under every mountain. Let's talk.
- Sit, captain. You've traded with every frozen tribe and every drowned port; you'll have news worth hearing.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your corsairs took another of our ore barges off the coast. Speak, and it had better be an apology.
- I know your word's worth less than the parchment it's written on. Speak anyway.
- Speak, captain. And put back the spoon you just pocketed.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! And I'll have a copy of the contract for every captain in your fleet.
- Done. And every captain who sails under you is bound by it, mind, not just the one holding the pen.
- A fair trade, and from a pirate! I'll have it carved in stone before it changes its mind.

#### Thanks for a gift
- I'll not ask where this washed up from, captain. Thank you.
- I'm obliged. Perhaps there's honour on the seas after all.
- Thank you. We'll put it in the vault, where no pirate can reach it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. I've seen sea-chests like this before: a layer of silver on top and ballast underneath.
- Ach, that's the price of a cargo that fell off someone else's ship. No.
- Not good enough, captain. Dwarves don't fall for sea-stories.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back to the sea and leave our caravans alone.
- Enough. Our cannon have sunk enough of your ships.
- Peace, aye, and our shore batteries stay loaded, in case your word drifts.

#### Refuses peace
- No. We've had Lanun treaties before; they washed off in the first rain.
- Peace? Your captains would each sign a different one and keep none.
- Your harbours are still burning, captain. We'll finish the job.

#### Rejects a demand
- A pirate making demands of a dwarf. Have you seen the size of our gates?
- No. The Khazad don't pay tribute to the sea.
- Not a coin. Your sea god's silent; ask him anyway.

### Khazad → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- The Ljosalfar. Elves of the forest, with magic that our old kings said could fell any warrior. We'll see.
- Forest folk. You love your trees; we love the stone beneath them. Let's not quarrel over the roots.
- Your archers are the best in Erebus, they say. Our cannon have a longer reach.

#### Declares war
- Your forests stand on our mountains' roots. We'll have them back.
- Your elven magic can't stop a cannonball.
- We'll fell your forest one tree at a time, and burn it in our forges.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. By the time an elf finishes a sentence, the war would be over anyway.
- Go back to your trees. We've no time for elven riddles.
- Your envoy brought a harp. A harp! Out.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the elves. Come in, and mind your head; our ceilings are low for your kind.
- Welcome, forest folk. You've fine crafts, and we've fine gold.
- Sit, elf. We may not see eye to eye, but we can trade.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your druids keep complaining about our mines. Speak.
- I don't trust your magic, elf. Speak plainly.
- Your treants have been pulling up our pit-props, root and all. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Elven craftsmanship is almost as good as dwarven.
- Done. Fine work, and fine gold.
- A fair trade. The Summer Court bargains better than I'd been told.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Elven work, given freely? I'll have it in the vault before you change your mind.
- Thank you. We'll put it in the vault next to some dwarven work, so it can learn something.
- I accept. Perhaps there's hope for elves and dwarves yet.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Elves price things as if they'd a thousand years to wait for payment. We don't.
- Ach, you'd trade me a pretty song for a mountain of ore.
- Not good enough. Your god came back from the dead, they say; surely your offer can too.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go back to your groves. We'll keep below them, and the roots can be the border.
- Enough. Your arrows have scratched our armour enough.
- So be it. May your forests grow, well away from our mines.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your rangers shot our surveyors. We'll survey your forest with cannon.
- Peace? Not while your druids curse our mines.
- Your magic's failing, elf. Our cannon aren't.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand from the elves? Shake one of your trees and see what falls out.
- No. The Fellowship of Leaves can feed its own.
- Not a coin. Elves have lived long enough to save their own.

### Khazad → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- Cousins! The Open-Skiers, back under the sun. Kilmorph kept you alive beneath the ice; it does my heart good to see the old blood still about.
- The Luchuirp. Your forefathers forgot how to dig, and the glaciers nearly took the lot of you. We never forgot.
- Heirs of Kradh-Ke-zun. Your golems are clever things, cousin, but a dwarf's own two hands never seize up in the cold.

#### Declares war
- Kin or no kin, cousin, you've crossed us. Kilmorph will forgive us both, in time.
- Your golems are fine work. It'll grieve me to break them, but break them I will.
- Even cousins quarrel, and the Khazad have never yet lost a quarrel in the family.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Kin who take up arms against kin get no hearing till the fighting's done.
- Send your golem home, cousin. It's nothing to say that I want to hear.
- Not now. Go back to your workshops and think on what you've done to your own blood.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Cousin! Come in, come in. The ale's cold and the forge is hot.
- Welcome, Luchuirp. Kilmorph's children ought to stand together, above ground and below.
- Sit down, cousin, and tell me how the golems are getting on. Still putting the plough horses out of work?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems trampled our surveyors' stakes. Is this how kin treat kin?
- You've been selling enchanted trinkets to our miners. We've had our fill of magic tricks, cousin, even from family.
- Speak, Luchuirp. Even kin can wear out their welcome.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! A bargain between Kilmorph's children; She Who Dwells Beneath would smile on it.
- Done. Your craft and our gold. There's no finer pairing in Erebus.
- A fair trade, cousin. You've not lost the old Open-Sky eye for value.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from our cousins! Kilmorph bless you for it.
- Thank you, kin. Your kindness will be carved in the Rune Hall, beside the names of our fathers.
- I'm obliged, cousin. Did one of your golems carry it all this way? Give it my thanks too.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Kin or not, a bad bargain's a bad bargain.
- Ach, cousin, you've lived in the open air too long. You've forgotten what stone is worth.
- Not good enough. Your ancestors made the finest artifacts of the Age of Magic. Offer me something a little nearer that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace, cousin. Kin shouldn't fight, and we'll not speak of it again.
- Enough. Kilmorph weeps when her children quarrel.
- Very well. Peace, and let's forget this ever happened. Except in the ledgers; nothing's ever forgotten in the ledgers.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You started this, cousin, and you'll not walk away from it so easy.
- Peace? Send your golems home first, and then we'll talk like kin.
- Kin you may be, but you've wronged us. That's a debt, and the Khazad collect every debt, even from family.

#### Rejects a demand
- Ask, cousin. Don't demand. Kin ask.
- No. You've your own mines; dig in them. Kilmorph taught your people that much again.
- Not a coin. Family helps family, but family doesn't make demands at the door.

### Khazad → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim. Desert folk who follow Lugus. Your caravans cross the sands, I hear. We've goods enough to fill every one of them.
- Children of the sun. We've lived under the mountain and you under the open sky. It'll be interesting to see what we have in common.
- Your Empyrean gives small nations the same voice as great ones. A fair principle. We'll see whether your prices are as fair.

#### Declares war
- Your Radiant Guard shines bright, but good steel and black powder win the day in the end.
- The desert's no place for siege engines, they say. We'll prove them wrong at your walls.
- Lugus may light your way, Malakim. Our cannon will light up your gates.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. I've no wish to hear about the light of Lugus while we're at war.
- Go back to your sands. Your sermon will keep, and so will our answer.
- Not now. Your Vicars can weigh the merits of the case when the guns are cold.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Malakim. Come out of the sun and into the cool of our halls.
- Ah, the desert folk. Sit; you'll find it pleasantly dark down here, for a change.
- Come in. Your caravans and our goods could make rich folk of us both.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your priests keep preaching their sun at our miners. Miners don't care for daylight. Speak.
- Speak, Malakim. And I'll have no sermons today.
- Your Radiant Guard marched past our hills last season with their spears shining. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed! Your Empyrean values fair dealing, and so do we.
- Done. A fine trade with honest folk; it doesn't happen every day.
- A fair bargain. May it travel well across the sands.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Sun-gold from the desert. I'm obliged to you, Malakim.
- Thank you. The sun shines on our halls today, and that's a rare thing.
- I accept, and gladly. Our caravans will remember your generosity at every oasis.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That's priced like water in the desert, and we're not thirsty.
- Ach, no. Your Empyrean teaches equal dealing between nations. That's not equal.
- Not good enough. The sands must hide more than this.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Go home to your desert, and may the sun keep you warm.
- Enough. Your Radiant Guard fought well; it's no shame to stop now.
- Very well. Our markets will be open to your caravans again by the next new moon.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your sun-priests started this; our gunners will finish it.
- Peace? Not while your armies stand on our hills.
- The sun sets every evening, Malakim. Yours is setting now.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? Your Empyrean preaches fairness between nations. Point to the fairness in this.
- No. Gold doesn't grow in the sun, Malakim. It's dug out of the dark, and it stays there.
- Not a coin. Your desert must have some gold buried somewhere. Dig.

### Khazad → Mercurians

#### First contact
- Angels. You broke the Compact to go on fighting demons. A dwarf can respect a grudge that long.
- The Mercurians. You care nothing for us, they say. Suits us; we care little for anyone above ground.
- Rebel angels. Mind you, we've hammers too, and we use them on demons just as gladly.

#### Declares war
- You came down to fight demons. You'll find dwarves harder.
- Wings or no wings, angel, you'll not fly over our walls.
- Your host broke the gods' own Compact. Breaking our gates will be harder work.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. An angel's sword is no pen, and I'll not sign anything at its point.
- Go and fight your demons, angel. We'll settle with you later.
- Not now. Your hammer's still wet with good dwarven blood.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the angels! Come in. Mind the low ceiling; it wasn't built for wings.
- Welcome, Mercurian. Any enemy of the pit is welcome in our halls.
- Sit, angel. You've seen hell; you'll find our forges cosy by comparison.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your host marched through our lands chasing demons and trampled our fields flat. Speak.
- You look at us as if we were demons. We're dwarves, angel, and we've the beards to prove it.
- Speak, Mercurian. And keep that hammer on your belt.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. An angel's word is good, if blunt.
- Done. Spend it on your war against the pit; I'll not complain.
- A fair trade, angel. You bargain like you fight: straight.

#### Thanks for a gift
- From an angel with blood still on its gauntlets. Well, I'm obliged all the same.
- Thank you. We'll forge it into something that hits demons hard. You'd like that.
- I accept, and gladly. When next you march on the pit, our forges will see you armed at cost.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You may be an angel, but that bargain is no blessing.
- Ach, no. You care nothing for coin, but we care a great deal.
- Not good enough. You've no use for coin, angel, so you'll not miss a little more of it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. There are demons enough for your hammers without wasting them on dwarves.
- Enough. We were never your enemy, angel. We just stood between you and something you were chasing.
- Peace, then. Go back down to hell, and give them our regards.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You marched over our dead without stopping to bury them. You'll stop now.
- Peace? Not until your host leaves our lands.
- Your wings are clipped, angel. Stand and fight.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? From an angel? Ask your gods. Oh, that's right, you left them.
- No. Even the heavens pay their debts.
- Not a coin. Go and loot hell; there's plenty down there.

### Khazad → Sheaim

#### First contact
- The Sheaim. Folk who want the world to end. Who'd lend money to the likes of you?
- Gate-openers. We dwarves spent ages sealing our doors against the world. You spend yours prying open doors to worse ones.
- You'd end creation, I hear. Then you'll pay in coin, up front. There's no credit at the end of the world.

#### Declares war
- You'd end the world. We'd sooner end you.
- Your gates will be shut, bricked over, and the bricks mortared. Dwarves know doors.
- Nobody who owes the Khazad gets to end the world before the debt's paid.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. There's no talking to folk who want everything gone.
- Back through whatever gate you came in by. We'll brick it up behind you.
- Not now. Your doom-talk curdles the ale.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Sheaim. Come in, but don't open anything.
- Welcome, I suppose. Your gold spends the same, whatever you mean to do with the world afterwards.
- Sit, gate-opener, and keep your rituals in your pocket. This is a respectable hall.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your rituals have spoiled the land near our mines; the ore comes up tainted. Speak.
- Ending the world is terrible for business, you know. Speak.
- Speak, Sheaim, and no prophecies.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Payment up front, mind.
- Done. I'll not ask what you want it for. I'd rather not know.
- A fair trade, and settled today. With your sort, I'll not wait for tomorrow.

#### Thanks for a gift
- What's the catch? With the Sheaim there's always a catch.
- Thank you, I suppose. I'll put it somewhere safe, in case the world doesn't end after all.
- I accept. It's a strange thing, a present from someone who wants everything gone.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You'll not pay me with a promise that it won't matter soon anyway.
- Ach, no. That's an offer from folk with no plans for next year.
- Not good enough. The world's still here, and so are my prices.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. And if a gate opens anywhere near our hills, we'll know whom to blame.
- Enough. We've bricked up enough of your gates for one war.
- Right, then. Peace, and may the world last a good while yet. We've investments.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Every day this war lasts is a day you're not working on your Armageddon. I like those days.
- Peace? Not while a single gate of yours stands open.
- Your rituals are faltering. We'll keep the pressure on.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? From folk who don't believe in tomorrow? Then you'll not miss what I don't give you.
- No. The Khazad don't fund the end of the world.
- Not a coin. Go and ask the void; it's got all your other hopes.

### Khazad → Sidar

#### First contact
- The Sidar. You traded pieces of your souls for long life, I hear. A bad bargain, by any dwarf's reckoning.
- Grey folk. You keep to your hidden cities and we keep to our hidden halls. We may get on.
- Shades. Our Runewardens carve the dead into stone so they're remembered. You simply decline to die.

#### Declares war
- You traded half your souls for long life. We'll see how long.
- Your hidden cities aren't so hidden from a dwarf with a map and a grudge.
- Shades are hard to kill, they say. Cannon are hard to argue with.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Come back when you're a bit more solid.
- Go back into your fog, then. We've lanterns enough to come looking.
- Not now. Talking with a shade is like haggling with a draught.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the Sidar. Come in, if you can find the door. Or walk through it, I suppose.
- Welcome, grey one. You've seen ages come and go; you'll have stories worth hearing.
- Sit. You've no taste for food any more, I hear, but the ale's good, and you can smell it at least.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your shades drift through our tunnels at night, and the miners won't go down. Speak.
- Speak, Sidar. You give me the shivers.
- You care for nothing, they say. Then why are you at my gate?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair trade, and with folk who don't even much want the goods.
- Done. Your coin's solid, at least, even if you're not.
- A fine bargain. Cold, careful and fair; I'd almost take you for a dwarf.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Sidar. Do you still remember why folk give gifts, or is it just habit?
- Thank you. We'll carve it in the Rune Hall, so it's remembered longer than you'd bother to.
- I accept. You'd no more use for it, I suppose.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You'd sell me half a soul and call it whole.
- Ach, no. A shade's offer is like a shade: thin.
- Not good enough. You've centuries of savings; dip into them.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. You've centuries to sulk about it, and we've vaults to refill.
- Enough. Your shades are hard to hit, and our gunners are getting cross.
- Fair enough. May your hidden cities stay hidden; we'll not go looking.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You started this, shade.
- Peace? You've lived a thousand years. You can wait a few more seasons for it.
- You're hard to kill. We're harder to stop.

#### Rejects a demand
- Shades who want nothing, suddenly wanting something? You've caught a fever from the living.
- No. You've no hunger, no thirst and no need. Then you've no need of this.
- Not a coin. You've endless time; earn it.

### Khazad → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Svartalfar, elves of the Winter Court. We'll trade, but we'll weigh every coin and count every spoon.
- Dark elves who pray to Esus, who sells his miracles for coin. Well, at least that's an honest arrangement.
- Your court made war on its own kin over which god to pray to. We've had feuds of our own, but never that.

#### Declares war
- Your assassins will find our halls dark, deep, and full of dwarves who don't sleep.
- Esus can't sell you a miracle big enough to stop dwarven siegecraft.
- You fight with knives in the dark. We fight with powder in the daylight. Let's see which carries further.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Every word from an Unseelie mouth has a hidden meaning, and I've no Runewarden to hand.
- Go back to your shadows. We'll find you there.
- Not now. Your envoy smiles like a cracked lock.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, the dark elves. Come in, but leave your knives at the door. All of them. Yes, that one too.
- Welcome, Svartalfar. Your coin's good, and your manners are better than they say.
- Sit. We'll talk business, and I'll count the spoons after.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your shadowriders were seen near our mines. Call them back.
- I know your court's tricks. Speak plainly, or not at all.
- Speak, elf, and wipe off that smile; it's making the guards nervous.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. I've had it read by three clerks, and none of them found a trap. Remarkable.
- Done. Esus would approve, I suppose; you did pay.
- A fair trade, from the Unseelie. I'll check the seals twice anyway.

#### Thanks for a gift
- From the Winter Court, eh? I'll have it checked for poison, curses and small print.
- Thank you. I'll keep it, but I'll not turn my back on it.
- I accept. Perhaps there's honour in the Winter Court after all, somewhere at the bottom.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. I've found the hook in it, elf. Took me two readings, but I found it.
- Ach, no. Your offers always have a knife hidden in the hem.
- Not good enough. Even Esus would want paying more for this miracle.

#### Agrees to peace
- Aye, peace. Your court can go back to stabbing itself; it's better at that.
- Enough. Your assassins keep turning up dead in our tunnels, and it's untidy.
- Peace it is. But we're changing every lock in the Underhome all the same.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your court has wronged us, and dwarves don't forget.
- Peace? I'd need to see both your hands, both your sleeves and both your boots first.
- Your court's lies have run out before our powder has.

#### Rejects a demand
- A demand? From the Winter Court? You'll have to steal it, and you'll fail.
- No. Your court has enough stolen gold already.
- Not a coin. Go and lie to someone else.

## Kuriotates

### Kuriotates → Amurites

#### First contact
- The children of Kylorin, at last. Our lamia have spoken of your schools for years; perhaps now a few of them may study there.
- Welcome, Amurites. The confederation has room for every gift, and yours is the rarest in Erebus.
- We hear your archmages quarrel like old professors. So do our magi, but every quarrel here ends at the throne.

#### Declares war
- Your adepts have tried their fire on our settlements once too often. Now let them try it on centaur lances.
- Magic for its own sake builds nothing. We go to war to end your experiments along our borders.
- You were left in peace to study, as wise rulers allow. You did not return the courtesy. Muster your mages.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your envoy may wait at the frontier settlement. The court has a war to finish first.
- No. Words from a nation of spellcasters are too easily woven into snares.
- We will not sit across a table from Kylorin's children while their fire still smokes in our fields.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Our lamia send their regards to your headmasters, friend, along with a question or two about the deeper currents.
- It is good to speak with you, [CT_NAME]. Your scholars and ours could build something that outlasts us both.
- The Amurite envoy is always welcome. Sit, and tell us what your schools are teaching this year.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Spare us the arcane flourishes. What does the Amurite council want now?
- Your archmages forget that the rest of Erebus is not their laboratory.
- We have heard what your adepts say of our lamia over their wine. Speak plainly, if your schools still teach it.

#### Accepts a deal
- Knowledge traded fairly is the best mortar an edifice could ask for. Agreed.
- A fair bargain. Let it draw the Amurite schools and our cities closer.
- Done. Even your most pedantic bureaucrat could not find a flaw in it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Generous, and unasked. The court will remember that the Amurites gave freely.
- Our magi will want to know which of your archmages to thank. Pass along our gratitude, [CT_NAME].
- A gift with no conditions attached, from a nation of scholars? You surprise us, very pleasantly.

#### Turns down a deal
- The terms favor your schools far more than our cities. Revise them, and we will listen.
- Even a first-year apprentice could see this is lopsided. We decline.
- Not this, I think. The confederation does not pay for learning with its foundations.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, then. Let your mages return to their towers and our centaurs to their pastures.
- There is more to learn from the Amurites alive than from their ashes. We accept.
- Let the fires go out. We never wanted a war with the finest minds in Erebus.

#### Refuses peace
- Your wizards would use a truce to prepare their next storm. Not yet.
- Peace, while your firebows still hold our settlements? Return them first.
- The magic you loosed on our people must be answered. The war goes on.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute is not how things are done here, not even for archmages.
- You may study our refusal at your leisure, [CT_NAME]. It will not change under examination.
- The confederation pays no tuition to the Amurite schools. Ask as a friend, and we might give.

### Kuriotates → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- A court of masks and puppets. Some who fled your carnival found asylum with us; they call it a nightmare that laughs.
- We are told your freaks were made, not born, Balseraphs. Ours came to us whole, and free.
- So the jesters of Erebus have a nation. Be welcome, and be warned: our people do not dance on strings.

#### Declares war
- Your Taskmasters have taken their last captives from our borderlands. The centaurs ride to end your carnival.
- Enough games. The confederation will pull down your big top and free every slave beneath it.
- You treat minds as toys and peoples as props. Now you will see what a free people does to its jailers.

#### Refuses to talk
- Every word from your court is a riddle with a knife in it. We will not listen.
- No harlequin dances into our halls while this war lasts.
- Speak to your own puppets, [CT_NAME]. They are the only audience you have left here.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Balseraph. You keep your word, they say, in your own peculiar fashion. That will do for us.
- Our courtiers find your envoys diverting. Let us hope the feeling stays mutual and goes no further.
- Ah, the masked court sends greetings. Unmask a little, friend; you are among allies.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your puppets were seen near our settlements again. Explain them, or call them home.
- We sheltered three of your runaway slaves this month. They told us more than enough about you.
- The confederation does not find your jests amusing today. Be brief.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed, and we have read every line twice. No offense, but one learns caution with your court.
- Even a mad court can strike a sane bargain. Done.
- A fair exchange. Our scribes will hold you to the letter of it, as you hold everyone else.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift with no punchline? We are touched, and only a little suspicious.
- We will keep it well away from mirrors, just in case. Thank you.
- Generosity from the masked court. Erebus is stranger than we thought, and kinder.

#### Turns down a deal
- There is a trick in this somewhere, and we are not clever enough to find it. So, no.
- No. We do not trade with a court that keeps the Taskmaster's whip so close at hand.
- Your terms twist more than a harlequin's dance. Straighten them out first.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, then. Return the captives you took, and keep your mimics on your own side of the border.
- Let the laughter stop for a while. The confederation accepts.
- We agree. Not because we trust you, but because our people deserve quiet.

#### Refuses peace
- Not while freaks of your making still march against us.
- Peace with a court that puppets its own nobles? Not until the strings are cut.
- You would sign whatever amuses you and tear it up when it bores you. The war goes on.

#### Rejects a demand
- We will not pay a fool's tax, Balseraph, however prettily you rhyme the demand.
- No. Find another audience for your threats; this one has stopped laughing.
- Our treasury feeds our people, not your court's hunger for spectacle.

### Kuriotates → Bannor

#### First contact
- The Bannor. Your Orders take fighters of every race, we hear. So do we, though we ask ours to build as well as fight.
- Greetings, soldiers of Junil. Our centaurs have heard of your drill and would like to see it, from a friendly distance.
- You walked out of hell and into war, and never stopped marching. Rest a while at our border; you are welcome.

#### Declares war
- Your priests have added us to their list of the damned. Very well; let them come and argue the point with our lances.
- Law without mercy is only a cage. The confederation will not live in one, and we will break yours.
- You call it a crusade. We call it the last time a Bannor column crosses our borders uninvited.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your priesthood named us enemies before your envoy said a word. We return the courtesy.
- No. Take your sermons back to the Halls of Sabathiel.
- When your Crusade halts, we will listen. Not before.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Both our peoples took in the lost and made them strong, friend. That counts for a great deal.
- It is good to see you, [CT_NAME]. How goes the long war against chaos? Ours is quieter, but never quite over.
- Bannor envoys are always punctual and always armed. We have prepared a hall suited to both.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Confessors have been preaching obedience to our centaurs. They did not take it kindly.
- The Bannor priesthood seems to think every free people is a disorder in need of correcting.
- Speak, if you must. But do not tell us again what Sabathiel wants.

#### Accepts a deal
- A fair and orderly bargain. Even your priests could not fault it.
- Let it be recorded in your Halls and in our archives alike. We are agreed.
- Done. The confederation honors its word as strictly as any of your Orders.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A generous gift, and delivered without a sermon. We are grateful, [CT_NAME].
- The Bannor give the way they fight: wholeheartedly. Thank you.
- We will share this among our settlements, so all may know the Bannor were kind to us.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. A bargain should serve two peoples, not one Crusade's war chest.
- Your terms march in close order toward your own advantage. Loosen the ranks a little.
- We cannot accept this. Your own Families would refuse it if our places were reversed.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let your soldiers go home to their fortified farms and their families.
- There is evil enough in Erebus to keep both our armies busy elsewhere. We accept.
- Agreed. We never wished to be your enemy; your priests decided that for us.

#### Refuses peace
- Your Crusade rests only long enough to sharpen its swords. Not yet.
- Peace with a people who think us damned? Not until your priests say otherwise, in writing.
- You marched on our cities with a hymn on your lips. We will not end this with one.

#### Rejects a demand
- We are not a heathen tribe to pay tithes to the Order.
- Tribute? Our people serve the crown and the confederation, not the Halls of Sabathiel.
- No. Even Junil asks obedience only of those who chose him.

### Kuriotates → Calabim

#### First contact
- The Calabim. We sent an ambassador to vampires once, and he never came home. This time we will speak from a distance.
- We know what you are, nobles of the night. Our borders are open to many peoples, but never to hunters of men.
- Greetings, Calabim. Your human herds may seek asylum with us whenever they wish. We say so plainly, at the start.

#### Declares war
- Every refugee from your blood-farms tells the same tale. We are done listening; now we ride.
- The confederation shelters what you consume. That makes us enemies, and today it makes us war.
- Our lost ambassador was the last meal you will ever take from us. Rouse your Broods.

#### Refuses to talk
- We have no wish to be charmed by that voice of yours. Speak to our lances.
- No. You dined on the last envoy we trusted to your hall.
- Nothing the Grand Broods can say will bring our dead back from your cellars.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Calabim envoy. Kindly stay on that side of the table; it is an old custom of our court.
- We speak because peace serves our people. Do not mistake it for warmth, [CT_NAME].
- Our centaurs report that your borders are quiet and orderly. That is something.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Another of your bloodpets crossed into our lands last night, begging sanctuary. We granted it.
- Your hunger shows, vampire. What do you want from us, besides what you cannot have?
- You complained that our ambassador smelled of horse. He was a centaur, and he was ours. Choose your words carefully.

#### Accepts a deal
- Trade is safer than hunger, for both of us. Agreed.
- The goods will be delivered by daylight, if you will forgive the precaution.
- A sensible bargain. We accept, and keep our distance.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Unexpected. We will look it over for teeth marks, but thank you.
- A gift from the Grand Broods. We accept it with thanks, and with our eyes open.
- Perhaps there is more to your nobility than appetite after all. Thank you.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Our people's trade is not another herd for you to bleed dry.
- We decline. Your terms drain far more than they give, as one might expect.
- We are not your cattle, to be fattened and tapped. No.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Keep to your estates and your herds, and we will keep to our cities.
- Let both our peoples bury their dead, and may yours stay buried. We accept.
- Agreed. But hear this: any of your cattle who flee to us remain free.

#### Refuses peace
- Peace with the Broods means only that you feed undisturbed. No.
- You would bargain while your herds still scream? Not yet.
- Our ambassador went to you in peace once. We will not make that mistake twice.

#### Rejects a demand
- We pay no tithes to vampires, in blood or in gold.
- Tell your Broods the confederation is not on the menu.
- No, [CT_NAME]. Hunger is not a claim.

### Kuriotates → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- Orcs of the Ember Banner. We have fought barbarians on our frontier since the confederation was young. Are you different?
- You were men of Bhall once, Clan. We judge a people by what it does, not by what it has become.
- We have heard of Braduk the Burning. Our cities prefer not to burn, but we are curious about yours.

#### Declares war
- Your raiders burned three of our settlements and left the smoke as a message. Here is our reply.
- The confederation has broken petty warbands before. The Ember Banner is only a larger one.
- You trade in fire and death. Let us see how you fare against centaurs who flinch at neither.

#### Refuses to talk
- We do not bargain with raiders while the ash is still warm.
- Go back to your fires, orc. Talk is for those who keep their word.
- No. Your warlords spoke of peace before, and struck before the ink was dry.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Clan envoy. There is meat and ale for you, and a fire, though a modest one by your standards.
- The orc who visits as a guest leaves as a friend. That is our custom.
- Our borders have been quiet, [CT_NAME]. Some of your people have learned more than the axe, it seems. It does them credit.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your goblins have been testing our watchposts. Did you think we would not notice?
- Every family your raiders burn out finds a home with us. We have a great many of them now.
- Say what you came to say, and take the stink of ash with you when you leave.

#### Accepts a deal
- Better trade than raid, for both our peoples. Agreed.
- A fair exchange. Let your clans see what our friendship is worth.
- Perhaps your priestesses will read a good omen in the flames tonight. Done.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Ember Banner? You have learned something of civilization. We are glad of it.
- Thank you. The orc who gives is rarer than the orc who takes, and far more welcome.
- We accept with thanks. Your clans may yet rise above the warbands of the wastes.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. We will not arm a people who still feed captives to a fallen goddess.
- These terms are a raid with a seal on them. We decline.
- Not good enough, orc. Bring something worth carrying home.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let the fires of Braduk burn at home, not in our fields.
- Go back to your clans, and tell them our lances are still waiting. Agreed.
- We accept. There is land enough for both of us, if you stop setting it alight.

#### Refuses peace
- You would use a truce to gather the tribes again. No.
- Not while your warbands still roam our lands. Call them home, or we will bury them here.
- Our settlers' ashes are still warm. The war goes on.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute is for the weak, your warlords say. Then you understand why we will not pay it.
- No. The confederation does not buy off raiders; it breaks them.
- Bhall herself could not frighten a coin out of our treasury, [CT_NAME].

### Kuriotates → Doviello

#### First contact
- The wolves of the north. We take in the weak and make them strong; you leave yours on the ice. We shall see whose way lasts.
- Greetings, Doviello. You survived the Age of Ice by becoming its teeth. The thaw has come; what will you become now?
- A people that eats its stragglers. We will take care not to give you any.

#### Declares war
- You honor only strength. Then honor this: our army is coming for your dens.
- The wolf culls the weak and the lame. You chose our settlements for prey, and you chose poorly.
- We have sheltered enough of the people you abandoned to know your ways. Now you will learn ours.

#### Refuses to talk
- The pack does not parley with its prey, you would say. Today, neither do we.
- No words, Doviello. Only steel, the one tongue your pack respects.
- Howl at our gates all you like. They will stay shut.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Our court has noted that the Doviello come as guests now, not raiders. Be welcome.
- Our centaurs admire your hunters. They say you run nearly as well as they do, which is high praise from them.
- It is good to speak with you, [CT_NAME]. Strength and civilization can share a border, it seems.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your hunters have been prowling around our outer settlements. Leash them.
- You smell of blood and old snow. Say your piece.
- Do not bare your teeth in our court, Doviello. Our centaurs have sharper ones on their spears.

#### Accepts a deal
- Even the wolf must trade when the hunt runs lean. Agreed.
- A fair exchange. Your pack will eat well this winter.
- Done. You bargain bluntly, and we prefer that to flattery.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift, from the pack? Your old ways would call it weakness. We call it wisdom, and thank you.
- We will remember that the Doviello shared when they might have taken.
- A wolf's gift is a rare thing. The confederation is grateful.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer us the scraps and ask for the carcass.
- We do not feed the strong at the cost of our own, Doviello.
- Even a wolf pack shares more fairly than that.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your hills and hunt elk, not our settlers.
- Lick your wounds, wolf; we will tend to ours.
- We accept. A pack is strongest when it knows where its territory ends.

#### Refuses peace
- A wolf that is spared comes back with the pack. Not yet.
- You only ask for peace because you are bleeding. Bleed a little longer.
- Our outlying families still fear the night. The war goes on until they do not.

#### Rejects a demand
- The weak pay the strong, in your creed. We are not weak.
- No. Take your growling elsewhere.
- Tribute to the Doviello? Even our children would laugh at us.

### Kuriotates → Elohim

#### First contact
- The Elohim, keepers of the holy places. Your monks have tended the broken of every age; our gates will always open to them.
- Well met, pilgrims. Your order stood witness when the Compact was forged; we would be honored to hear the tale.
- Welcome. Two peoples who shelter the lost and the hunted should know each other well.

#### Declares war
- It grieves us, Elohim, but your shrines stand on land our people cannot do without.
- Even holy men must be moved when they stand in the way of a nation's survival. We march.
- We have no quarrel with your monks, only with your borders. Forgive us if you can; we will not ask twice.

#### Refuses to talk
- We will not be swayed by your chants while our armies are in the field.
- No, pilgrim. The conscience of the crown is its own affair.
- The court is not ready for a sermon on peace. Later.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Your healers tended our wounded on the frontier, friend; we owe you thanks.
- It is always a pleasure, [CT_NAME]. How goes the reclaiming of your lost shrines?
- The Elohim honor us. Sit; our lamia have questions about the old sacred sites.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your monks lecture our settlers on the evils of war. We know them better than they think.
- Keepers of holy places should not covet our land for new ones.
- Speak, Elohim, but spare us the parables.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair trade between two peoples who keep their word.
- May it carry both our peoples safely through this age. Done.
- A good bargain. Your honesty makes trade a pleasure.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Your generosity is everything the old stories promised. Thank you.
- We will remember this kindness, [CT_NAME], whenever your pilgrims cross our lands.
- The Elohim give as their founder did, without counting. We are humbled.

#### Turns down a deal
- Kindness does not balance a ledger. We cannot accept this.
- No. We would like to help, but this asks too much of our people.
- Not on these terms, though we thank you for the courtesy of the offer.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, gladly. Go back to your shrines; we never wished to trouble them.
- Your healers will be welcome in our cities again. We accept, gladly.
- Let it end. Neither of our peoples was made for this.

#### Refuses peace
- Not yet. We must first secure what our soldiers took, however little we like it.
- Your peace would hand back everything our soldiers bled for. No.
- We regret it, Elohim, but this war must run its course.

#### Rejects a demand
- Even holy men must pay their own way. No.
- That is not how alms work, pilgrim.
- We will not be shamed into paying, [CT_NAME], however gently you ask.

### Kuriotates → Grigori

#### First contact
- The Grigori! A haven for those who would lead their own lives. In that, we are kin.
- You shelter the Luonnotar, Grigori; we shelter centaurs and lamia. The world calls us both strange.
- Welcome. We, too, judge our people by what they give, not by which god they kneel to.

#### Declares war
- Your adventurers raid our settlements and call it freedom. That ends now.
- Even a haven must answer for it when its heroes turn bandit.
- No god guards you, Grigori, by your own choice. You will have only yourselves when our lances arrive.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your adventurers can talk their way out of most things. Not this war.
- No. A people without a throne has no one who can promise us anything.
- The court will not hear you, [CT_NAME], until your heroes go home.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome! Two havens for the lost should never be strangers.
- Your adventurers are always welcome in our taverns. They tell the best stories in Erebus.
- Our scholars have been reading the Luonnotar teachings you sent, with great interest.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your free-spirited adventurers have been very free with our goods. Explain.
- You disdain the gods; must you disdain your neighbors as well?
- Speak quickly. Your people's independence does not extend into our lands.

#### Accepts a deal
- Two havens, one fair bargain. Agreed.
- Done. Let this bind our two havens a little closer.
- A fair bargain, and one we made ourselves, with no priest whispering in either ear.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift freely given by a free people. We thank you.
- Thank you. Our refugees speak well of your cities; now we see why.
- Generous, Grigori. Should your people ever need asylum, it is theirs.

#### Turns down a deal
- You prize self-reliance; rely on yourselves for the rest.
- No. Even a haven must count its coin.
- We decline. Make it fairer and we will talk again.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Havens should shelter people, not fight each other.
- Let your adventurers find other quests. We accept.
- Agreed. Let both our peoples return to the work of living their own lives.

#### Refuses peace
- Your heroes are still in our lands. Not until they leave.
- A people who answer to no god must answer to us, for now.
- The war continues, Grigori. Your adventurers began it, and our soldiers will end it.

#### Rejects a demand
- You turned your back on the gods' demands. We turn ours on yours.
- No. Lead yourselves, and pay your own way.
- Tribute, from one haven to another? You should be ashamed, [CT_NAME].

### Kuriotates → Hippus

#### First contact
- The horse lords! Our centaurs have been eager to meet you. They have firm opinions about who ought to carry whom.
- Greetings, Hippus. Your companies are famous; perhaps our treasury will become famous among them.
- Welcome. You ride horses; some of our citizens are half horse. We will get along, or we will race.

#### Declares war
- Your raiders mistook our settlements for unguarded herds. Our centaurs will correct the error.
- You sell your swords to anyone. Someone paid you to raid us, and we have come to collect the debt.
- Let us see whether the horse lords can outrun those born with four legs.

#### Refuses to talk
- Your riders have quick tongues and quicker hands. We will not talk.
- No. We are not hiring, and we are not selling.
- Ride on, Hippus. The court has nothing to say to you.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, friend! Our centaurs have saved you the best pasture outside the city.
- Our centaurs and your riders raced last spring, [CT_NAME], and nobody has yet agreed who won.
- Hippus envoys are always welcome. Your companies honor their contracts, which is more than most can say.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your companies took our enemies' coin. Explain yourself.
- Our centaurs are still offended by what your riders said about them at the border.
- Speak, horse lord, and do not try to ride your words over us.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair price, as befits a people who live by contracts.
- Our centaurs will deliver it at a gallop. Done.
- Foreign gold, honestly traded; your clans should be proud. It is a deal.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the horse lords. We are touched, and our centaurs are impressed.
- We will remember this when your companies next seek a patron. Thank you.
- Generous of you. For once, the gold flows away from the Hippus.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even mercenaries expect a fair price, and so do we.
- That bargain would not buy a lame pony. We decline.
- Not good enough. Your own clans would laugh at us for taking it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Let our centaurs and your riders race on fields, not battlefields.
- Go home; your herds need you more than this war does.
- We accept. The plains are wide enough for hooves of every kind.

#### Refuses peace
- Your riders strike and run. We will not let them run home to rest.
- Not yet. You would only sell your companies to our next enemy.
- No. Our centaurs have not finished teaching you about cavalry.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute is what you charge others for protection. We protect ourselves.
- No. Go and find someone else's caravan to rob.
- Our centaurs say no, and they put it far more colorfully than I would.

### Kuriotates → Illians

#### First contact
- The Illians. Our confederation was gathered from the ruins your winter left behind. We remember.
- Your people slept while the world thawed, Illians, and now they stir. Why?
- The lost men of Letum Frigus. Our lamia say the cold follows your envoy into the room.

#### Declares war
- We have seen the signs: frost where none should be. You would bring back the winter. Not while we stand.
- The Age of Ice nearly ended every free people in Erebus. We will end you before it returns.
- Our people survived one winter. We will not wait for another; we march on Letum Frigus.

#### Refuses to talk
- The court does not speak with those who would freeze the world.
- No. Cold words from a cold people.
- Not now. Perhaps when the snow on our fields has melted.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Illian. Come close to the fire; we keep it high for you.
- You are courteous, [CT_NAME], for a people who once ruled a frozen world.
- The confederation receives you warmly, in every sense of the word.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your priests chant to a dead god along our border. It unsettles our people.
