- The Lanun. Danalin has gone silent, and the things that answer your prayers now are much more our sort.
- Sea-traders. You sold ships to both sides when Patria fell. Will you sell to both sides at the end, too?
- Captains and corsairs. When the world ends, the sea ends with it. Chart your course accordingly.

#### Declares war
- Your ships cannot outsail the end, Lanun.
- We will burn your harbours and let the deep take whatever floats.
- A captain's word is fleeting, they say. So is a captain's fleet.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Sail away, pirate, while the wind is with you.
- We do not parley with corsairs. You would only rob the envoy.
- Your word is worth less than sea-foam. No talk.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, captain. Your crews and our cults have more in common than you would think.
- Ah, the Lanun. Have you come to trade, or to steal politely?
- Sit, [CT_NAME]. The creatures rising from your depths interest us greatly.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders have been at our coasts again. Speak.
- What do you want, pirate? Keep your hand away from your sword.
- The sea has grown dark for you, Lanun. So has our temper.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. On your word, captain, for whatever it is worth.
- Done. A fair trade, by the law of the sea.
- Agreed. Fair winds, until there are no more winds.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Lanun generosity? Did you steal it first?
- Our thanks, captain. The deep will remember you kindly, whatever lives down there now.
- Generous, Lanun. We will spare a harbour or two at the end.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That is a pirate's bargain, and we are not a fat merchant galley.
- Try that on someone who has never met a Lanun. We decline.
- Not good enough, captain. Raise your offer or raise your sails.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your waves, and to whatever crawls up from them these days.
- Peace. The sea can keep you a little longer.
- Enough. Your fleets have earned a harbour, and we have a world to end.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your harbours still stand, and your Overlords' cultists still chant in them.
- Peace? A Lanun's word turns with the tide.
- Not while a single one of your sails is still on the horizon.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to pirates? Come ashore and take it.
- No. Board us if you dare, captain.
- The Sheaim pay no toll to any captain, and no captain outranks us.

### Sheaim → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- The Ljosalfar, crawling back from your hidden groves. Your god died once already. You know how endings go.
- Elves of the Summer Court. Your forests are lovely. They will burn beautifully.
- You survived the death of Sucellus and an age of ice. Impressive. The end of the world will be harder.

#### Declares war
- Your groves are ancient. That only means they have more to lose.
- The Summer Court never truly returned, elf. We will make sure it never does.
- We have come for your forests. Call your treants; they will make fine kindling.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Go back to your trees.
- We will not talk to the Fellowship of Leaves. Your druids only mutter at saplings.
- Not now, elf. Your forest is still burning.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Ljosalfar. We admire your patience. You will need it.
- Ah, the forest elves. What does the Summer Court want from us?
- Welcome, [CT_NAME]. Leave your bow at the door; we will leave our fire there too.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your rangers watch our borders from the treetops. We see them. Speak.
- What now, elf? Has another of your groves withered?
- Your druids blame us for every blight in your woods. Most of the time they are right. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Take it back beneath your canopy.
- Done. You bargain with the patience of an ancient forest.
- We accept. Let it take root, for as long as roots have left.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Ljosalfar. You rarely give anything to those outside your groves; we are honoured.
- Generous, elf. Of all the forests of Erebus, yours will burn last.
- How kind. Your new god of the wild must be in a giving mood.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That offer is as thin as a winter branch.
- Your elders spend too long listening to trees and too little listening to us. No.
- Come back when your offer has grown a few more rings.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your hidden groves and count what is left of them.
- Very well, elf. Let your forests regrow; fire loves young wood.
- Enough. Your archers have made their point from the treetops.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your trees still stand, and that offends us.
- Peace? Your god died once, elf, and the world went on. We mean to do better.
- Not yet. There is still far too much green in your lands.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to elves? Ask your treants to dig it up for you.
- No. The Sheaim do not water other people's forests.
- Nothing, elf. Your Fellowship teaches that the forest provides. Let it.

### Sheaim → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- The Luchuirp, last heirs of the Open-Skiers. The ice crushed your golems once. Something worse is coming for them now.
- Golem-makers. Your clay servants obey without question. We find that charming, and very easy to turn.
- Your ancestors built an empire of great cities and lost it to one long winter. Imagine what the end of everything will take.

#### Declares war
- The ice ground the empire of Kradh-Ke-zun to dust. We have come to finish the work it left undone.
- Send out your golems, little ones. They will not even know when they die.
- Kilmorph sheltered your clan beneath the ice. Let us see whether she can shelter you from fire.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Go back down your tunnels and dig, as your goddess taught you.
- We will not bargain with craftsmen while their clockwork marches on our cities.
- Not a word. Let your golems negotiate; they are better at keeping quiet.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Luchuirp. Your enchanted clockwork fascinates our mages. Do not worry; we only want to look.
- Ah, the artificers. What has the forge of the Open-Skiers brought us today?
- You are welcome here, [CT_NAME]. Your people know what it is to watch a world end. We admire experience.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems have been tramping across our wards. Speak quickly, tinker.
- What do you want, Luchuirp? You have the look of someone who found a crystal they should not have touched.
- Speak, little artificer, before our mages decide to see how your golems come apart.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Fine work, as always from your forges.
- Done. Build something lovely with it before it all comes down.
- Graoin's heirs bargain as carefully as they build. Agreed.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Craftsmanship from the Luchuirp, freely given. Our thanks; your work lasts longer than most things will.
- Generous, artificer. When the end comes, your golems will be the last thing standing. Fitting.
- How kind. We will treasure it, briefly.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even a clay golem would know that offer is lopsided.
- Your terms are wound tighter than your clockwork. No.
- Not good enough, Luchuirp. Go back to your workshop and improve it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and mend your golems.
- Let it rest. Your clockwork has earned a pause, and so have our summonings.
- Enough. The surface you fought so hard to reclaim can be yours a little longer.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your forges are still burning, and only one of us may light the fires of the end.
- Peace? You spent an age in caves waiting for the sun. You can wait for this too.
- Not while your golems still march.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? Build it yourself, artificer. That is what you are for.
- No. Dig for it, as Kilmorph taught your clan beneath the ice.
- The Sheaim give nothing to golem-wrights who cannot even keep their own empire.

### Sheaim → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim, children of the desert sun. Your light is bright, but every sun burns out.
- So you are Lugus's faithful. Your god of light will make a fine torch for the end of the world.
- Desert folk, who walked through the ice to find a sun. We wonder how you will like the sky when it falls.

#### Declares war
- Your sun cannot burn the Sheaim. We have walked through fires far hotter.
- Let us see how the Empyrean judges this, desert folk. We have already judged you.
- The desert will make a fine grave. It is already empty.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Go back to your sand and your sun.
- We will not hear the Empyrean's judgments. Your god's light does not reach us here.
- Not a word, desert folk. Your sermons are as dry as your land.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Malakim. The sun shines on you even here. How irritating.
- Ah, the desert people. What does the light of Lugus want with the Sheaim?
- Enter, [CT_NAME], and take shade, if you can find any among us.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your radiant guards have been burning our acolytes. Speak.
- What do you want, Malakim? Your god's glare gives us headaches.
- Speak, desert folk, and keep your Vicars out of our temples.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Carry it home across the dunes.
- Done. Your Empyrean would weigh this case and call it fair. For once, so do we.
- Taken. Spend it quickly; the sun sets on everything eventually.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Malakim. They say you once took a dying stranger in from the wastes. Charity seems to be a habit with you.
- Generous, desert folk. Your oases will be the last to boil away.
- How kind. Your Empyrean gives an equal voice to every nation, it seems, even to ours.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That offer is as empty as the deep desert.
- Weigh it on its merits, as your judges do, and you will see why we refuse.
- Even a caravan master would blush to offer it. No.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your sun while it still rises.
- Peace. The sands may keep you a while longer.
- Enough. Your Radiant Guard fights with real conviction; we will not waste our fire on it today.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your temples still catch the morning light, and we find that offensive.
- Peace? The Empyrean judges each case on its merits. We have judged yours.
- Not yet. The light of Lugus still falls on your cities, and we mean to put it out.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? Ask Lugus to rain it down upon your dunes.
- No. Your Empyrean teaches that every nation has an equal voice. Ours says no.
- Nothing, Malakim. Not one grain of your own sand.

### Sheaim → Mercurians

#### First contact
- Angels who broke the Compact. We are delighted. You have done more to unravel creation than most of our rituals.
- The Mercurians. You hunt demons wherever they are. We summon them wherever we like. This will be interesting.
- So the rebel host has come down to Erebus. Tell us, angel, do your former lords know you are here?

#### Declares war
- You came to fight the hells. We will show you that the end of the world is worse.
- Your war against the demons ends here, angel. You will not live to see the next one.
- Every gate we open lets in something you hate. Come, and we will open a thousand.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You care nothing for mortals; why should we care for you?
- We will not talk with the rebel host. Go and carve another prayer into your flesh.
- Not a word, angel. Your hammer has spoken enough for both of us.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, angel. Do not look too closely at our summoning circles.
- Ah, the Mercurians. Our gates and your war are uneasy neighbours, are they not?
- Enter, [CT_NAME]. We promise there are no demons here, today.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- You smell of blood and holy fire. Speak, angel.
- What does the rebel host want? Be quick; we have rituals to finish.
- Speak, and keep your hammer away from our circles.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Even an angel's war needs iron, it seems.
- Done. Your host bargains the way it fights: briefly, and without courtesy.
- We accept. Spend it on your endless war against the pit.

#### Thanks for a gift
- The rebel host gives to mortals? You care so little for us that we are almost touched.
- Our thanks, angel. When the sky falls, we will save you a place to watch.
- Generous. Arawn never gave us anything, and he was once your lord, not ours.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You may terrify demons, angel, but this offer does not terrify us into taking it.
- Your host asks for more than it can carry. We decline.
- Not good enough. Carve a better offer into your arm and come back.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and fight your demons somewhere else, angel.
- Peace. The hells are still full; spend your wrath there.
- Enough. We would rather you broke your hammer on the pit than on us.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You hunt our summonings, angel, so we hunt you.
- Peace? You refused the peace of the gods themselves. You taught us how it is done.
- While holy fire still burns in our lands, there will be no peace.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the rebel host? You broke the Compact itself; why should we honour any bargain with you?
- No. Go and take it from a demon; that is what you are for.
- Nothing, angel. Prayers carved in blood buy nothing here.

### Sheaim → Sidar

#### First contact
- The Sidar. You sold pieces of your souls for a life without end. We are sorry to tell you that nothing is without end.
- Shades in hidden cities, watching the younger races. Watch closely, Grey ones. The last act belongs to us.
- You walk through other lands unseen, they say. Then you have seen our rituals, and you know what is coming.

#### Declares war
- You bought eternity with your souls. We have come to show you how short eternity can be.
- Your hidden cities will not hide from the end of the world.
- You have watched the world from the shadows long enough. Now watch it burn, and you with it.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You have all the time in the world, Sidar. Spend some of it waiting.
- Bargain with ghosts who are only half here? No.
- Not a word, shade. You would only forget it in a century.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Sidar. You at least understand that most things in this world are not worth feeling.
- Ah, the Grey. Have you come to learn something? We have much to teach about endings.
- Draw closer, [CT_NAME]. You are hard to see in this light; do stand near the braziers.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Stop drifting about our halls unseen, shade, and speak.
- What does the Grey want? Be brief, for once; some of us still count our years.
- Your watchers have been spying on our rites. We noticed. Speak.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. It will last exactly as long as you will, which is to say, until the end.
- Done. You bargain without greed. It is unsettling.
- Done. Add it to your endless hoard of knowledge.

#### Thanks for a gift
- So the Sidar remember the rest of us exist. Our thanks, shade; this is a rarer gift than the thing itself.
- Generous, shade. When the end comes, you will finally have something new to study.
- How kind. You gave away part of your soul once; this must seem a small thing beside it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You have centuries to wait for a better offer, and we can make you wait them.
- Your terms are as pale and thin as your people. No.
- Even ghosts must pay a fair price, Sidar. This is not one.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to your hidden cities and your endless study.
- Peace. Go and fade somewhere no one can see you.
- Enough. You never had much interest in this war, did you, shade?

#### Refuses peace
- No. You are very hard to kill, shade. That only means we must try harder.
- Peace? You will outlive any treaty anyway. Why should we sign one?
- Not yet. Your hidden cities are no longer hidden from us.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to ghosts? What would you even do with it?
- No. You gave up greed with your soul, or so you claim. Prove it.
- Nothing, shade. Go and haunt someone with more to give.

### Sheaim → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Svartalfar. When your god's prayers went unanswered, you declared him gone and took another. We admire such decisiveness.
- Dark elves of the Winter Court. You took the Age of Ice as a sign of your dominance. Wait until you see the end of the world.
- So the Unseelie court has come out of the cold. We hear you betray your allies. So do we, eventually; it is the end of the world.

#### Declares war
- Your assassins are subtle. Our meteors are not.
- The Winter Court has had its long season. We bring the last one.
- You hunted your own kin for praying to a dead god. We will hunt you for praying to anything at all.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your envoys carry daggers in their sleeves.
- We will not talk with the Unseelie. You would only spin another web while we spoke.
- Not a word, elf. Your silver tongue will not cool our fire.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Svartalfar. Your court is nearly as cruel as ours. We mean that as praise.
- Ah, the dark elves. What pretty schemes have you brought us today?
- Welcome, [CT_NAME]. Leave your assassins outside; ours will keep them company.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- What does the Winter Court want? Be brief, and keep your hands where we can see them.
- Your spies have been in our libraries again. Speak, before we start removing their fingers.
- Speak, elf, while we have our wine tasted for poison.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Do try not to betray this one too soon.
- Done. Esus would approve; there was certainly a price paid.
- Agreed. May it be a long winter for us both.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Svartalfar? We will have it searched for poison, and then thank you properly.
- Generous, elf. Your court surprises us, and very little does.
- Our thanks. We will remember this when the end comes, for whatever that is worth to you.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That bargain has a knife hidden in its sleeve, as every Unseelie gift does.
- You keep academies of persuasion; next time, send us one of their graduates. No.
- Not good enough. Esus makes his faithful pay for every miracle, and so do we.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your quarrel with your Summer cousins; it suits you better.
- Very well. Spin your webs elsewhere, and not near our gates.
- Enough. Your assassins and our summonings have worn each other out.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You would betray it before the first frost.
- Peace? The Winter Court keeps treaties the way it kept faith with Sucellus.
- Your shadows have not yet learned to fear our fire. They will, before we stop.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? You will have nothing free from us, elf, not even a miracle.
- No. Steal it, as is your custom. We will be watching.
- Nothing for the Unseelie. Winter always takes; this time it will go hungry.

## Sidar

### Sidar → Amurites

#### First contact
- The Amurites. Your schools are young, but their libraries already deserve a long visit. We have made several; you did not notice.
- Your laws punish those who sustain life past its natural end. By that measure every Sidar belongs on your pyres. Let us be careful with one another.
- Children of Kylorin. Mortals who live for magic, and we who live for knowledge. We may understand each other, for a while.

#### Declares war
- Your archmages would have burned us for what we are. We have decided not to wait for the attempt.
- Your schools lie under our shadow now, Amurite. We will take the libraries and leave the scholars to the fog.
- Your mages burn brightly and briefly. We have come to watch them go out.

#### Refuses to talk
- We have heard every argument your scholars can make. They were not new the first time.
- No. Your debates last a season; our patience lasts longer than your nation.
- The Grey do not bargain while a war is still young. Return in a generation.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Your scholars are among the few mortals whose company we can bear for long, [CT_NAME]. Sit.
- Welcome, Amurite. We have read much of what your schools have written. Some of it was even correct.
- Ah, the mages. Do you still execute your necromancers? Good. On that, at least, we agree.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your mages keep trying to scry our hidden cities. It is pointless, and rude. Speak.
- You regard us as a forbidden experiment, Amurite. We regard you as an unfinished one.
- Speak. Your feuding archmages have taught you to waste words; we have no use for them.

#### Accepts a deal
- Acceptable. Knowledge for knowledge is the only trade that does not decay.
- It will outlast your schools, and we will outlast it. Done.
- Agreed. Send the scrolls by daylight; our couriers are not always visible in it.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A thoughtful gift. Your scholars, at least, understand that we value what lasts.
- We shall add it to our archives. In a thousand years someone may ask where it came from, and we will still remember.
- We no longer feel gratitude as you do, Amurite, but we keep a careful record of those who have earned it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Even an apprentice of your schools would see the imbalance.
- We have weighed this offer against the long years, and it is light.
- Mortals always offer the present and ask for the future. We have far more future than you. No.

#### Agrees to peace
- We wondered how your war magic would fare against us. Now we know. Enough.
- Peace. Return to your lecture halls; we have centuries of reading to resume.
- It is finished. Your mages may tell their students they fought the Grey and lived. Few can.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your siege-mages are only now beginning to interest us.
- Your archmages would squabble over the terms for years. We would rather finish the war first.
- Peace? You still hold libraries we have not read.

#### Rejects a demand
- You would demand of us what your own schools guard so jealously? No.
- We have walked through your academies unseen for longer than you know. Do not threaten us.
- No. Bureaucracy is a mortal sickness, and we did not catch it.

### Sidar → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- The Balseraphs. Your court collects minds. Ours are mostly quiet rooms now; you will find little worth taking.
- A court of masks and laughter. We gave up laughter long ago, along with most of our souls. We do not miss it.
- We have walked through Jubilee unseen during your festivals. Your masks hide less than you think.

#### Declares war
- Your court plays with lives as a child plays with dolls. We have come to end the game.
- Death walks the streets of Jubilee tonight, unmasked. Even your harlequins will stop laughing.
- Your taskmasters went looking for slaves among our people. A shade makes a poor slave and a worse enemy.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your court twists every word, so we will give you none to twist.
- Riddles do not move us, Balseraph. Very little does.
- We will not speak with a court where every voice belongs to someone else.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Ah, Balseraph. Your court is one of the few things in Erebus that still surprises us.
- We watched your last festival from among the crowd, [CT_NAME]. You did not see us. That is as it should be.
- Welcome. Your freaks and mimics would make a fascinating study, should you ever lend us one.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your puppets keep trying to follow us into the fog. They do not come back. Speak.
- What is it, jester? Your mind magic finds little to grip in a shade.
- Speak plainly or not at all. We have no patience left for rhyme.

#### Accepts a deal
- Even a madman's bargain can be a sound one. We accept.
- Agreed. We expect you to honour it in letter, if not in spirit; we know your court's habits.
- Tell your court it amused us. It did not, but they will enjoy hearing it. Done.

#### Thanks for a gift
- An unexpected gift. Your court remains unpredictable, which is the most we can say of anyone.
- We thank you. Do not expect us to applaud; we have forgotten how.
- It will go into our long record of curious things, near the top. Our thanks.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There is a trick in this, and we have had centuries to learn the shape of tricks.
- The masks on this offer are pretty, but the face beneath is greedy. We decline.
- Word games are wasted on those who no longer want anything. No.

#### Agrees to peace
- Very well. Your circus may move on. We were weary of its noise.
- Peace. We have seen all we wished to see of your court at war.
- Go back to your festivals; we will go back to our silence. It is ended.

#### Refuses peace
- No. A peace with Jubilee is a painted stage set, and we have walked behind it.
- Your court laughs at every treaty. We will not provide it with another joke.
- Not yet. Your harlequins still caper through our valleys, and the capering is tiresome.

#### Rejects a demand
- Ah, greed. We remember it, faintly, the way one remembers a fever.
- You would extort the Grey? Your court has finally met someone its tricks cannot touch.
- No. You cannot frighten those who have already sold the part of themselves that feared.

### Sidar → Bannor

#### First contact
- The Bannor. We have watched your Crusade from its edges for a long time. It never seems to end.
- An angel led you out of hell into the daylight, they say. We paid for our own daylight with pieces of our souls.
- A people at war with chaos. You will find us very orderly, crusader; we simply do not care for your Order.

#### Declares war
- Your priests have named us unnatural. We have come to show them how natural death is.
- Death is coming to your garrison towns, crusader, and your drills will not keep it out.
- Your Confessors burned one of our walkers as a spirit of the damned. We no longer feel anger; we do not need to. We remember.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your priests would only use our words to draw up another list of the damned.
- We have heard Bannor envoys for generations. They always say the same thing.
- A truce with zealots lasts until the next sermon. We will not talk.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- You have outlived several of our acquaintances, [CT_NAME]. That counts for much with us.
- Welcome, Bannor. Your discipline is admirable, for creatures who live so briefly.
- Your Order has its uses. You keep the restless dead in their graves, and we approve of that.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Crusaders patrol our borders as though we were demons. Speak.
- What does the Order want? To save our souls? There is very little of them left to save.
- Speak, crusader. Your fervour is wasted on us; we cannot share it.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Law is useful, even to us.
- Your Families may write it into their histories. We will remember it longer than they do. Agreed.
- Acceptable. Carry it back to the Halls of Sabathiel with our compliments.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Order. Unexpected; your priests usually call us abominations.
- Your charity is sincere, Bannor, which makes it rare. We thank you.
- We will remember this, Bannor, long after your grandchildren have forgotten it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You demand obedience from your own people; do not demand it of us.
- These terms are as rigid as your drill, and they serve your Crusade, not us. We decline.
- We have watched the Bannor bargain for centuries. You always ask a little more than you give.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to your war on chaos; we were never truly part of it.
- Your Orders have fought bravely, as mortals measure bravery. Let it end.
- Go and fight the real enemies of your god, crusader; we are not among them. We accept the peace.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your priests would call it a victory and march again next spring.
- We will not make peace with a people that has never once made peace with the world.
- Not yet. Your Crusaders still march through our hidden valleys.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the Order? Junil's promises were never made to us.
- No. The Halls of Sabathiel are rich enough without our offerings.
- You would have us repent and pay for the privilege? We decline both.

### Sidar → Calabim

#### First contact
- The Calabim. You cheat death by drinking it. We paid for our years with our own souls. Do not mistake us for kin.
- So these are the Grand Broods. You are an aberration, vampire, and the Sidar do not tolerate aberrations for long.
- Vampires ruling herds of the living. We have seen your kind before. We did not approve then either.

#### Declares war
- You are a corruption of life and death alike. The Sidar have come to correct it.
- Night is falling on your estates, Calabim, and for once the dark will not be on your side.
- You have stolen too many lives to lengthen your own. We will return them to the grave, and you with them.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. We do not bargain with the dead who refuse to lie down.
- Your charm works on the hungry and the afraid. We are neither.
- Speak again, vampire, and we will answer with sunlight.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Calabim. We tolerate you, for now. Do not mistake that for friendship.
- We are at peace, vampire, and we keep our word. That is all you will have from us.
- Welcome, vampire. Keep your hunger at home; our people have very little blood to offer.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- The stench of old blood reaches us even through the fog. Speak.
- You walk, you feed, and you call it living. We call it an error. What do you want?
- Speak quickly, leech. Our patience with your kind was spent long ago.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. It is as close as we will ever come to friendship with your kind.
- Do not take this as approval. It is only trade.
- We will count it, as we count everything your Broods do. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Calabim. We will examine it carefully for anything that still breathes.
- We accept it. It does not change what you are.
- Thank you. We do not feel gratitude, but we will remember this, for a while.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There is blood on this offer, and none of it is yours.
- Your Broods bargain the way they feed: greedily, and at someone else's expense. We decline.
- That price would be paid in other people's lives. Not by us.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace, for now. You will still be an aberration tomorrow.
- Very well. Return to your estate farms; we will be watching them.
- Our opinion of you has not changed, vampire; only our plans have. It is ended.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Every vampire we destroy is one fewer error in the world.
- Peace with the Calabim? We would sooner make peace with a plague.
- Not while one of your Grand Broods still feeds.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand from us? You have taken enough from the living already.
- No. There is nothing in our veins worth drinking, and nothing in our coffers for you.
- The Grey pay no tribute to the dead.

### Sidar → Clan of Embers

#### First contact
- Orcs of the Ember Banner. Your lives are short and loud. We will try to remember you.
- Your tribes are many and quick to die. We are few and very slow to. An interesting contrast.
- The Clan of Embers. We have heard of Braduk the Burning. Fire is a poor master, orc; it consumes what it serves.

#### Declares war
- Your fires will not burn what is barely here.
- Death has come for your camps, orc. Your goddess cannot save you; she could not even save herself.
- Your raiders have trampled our quiet valleys long enough. We have come to end the noise.

#### Refuses to talk
- We do not negotiate with fire.
- No. Your warlords forget their promises by morning.
- Your words are only noise, orc, and we have heard that noise from your grandfathers.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, orc. You have kept your axes to yourself. That is all we ask.
- You are still alive, [CT_NAME]. For a leader of your kind, that is a great achievement.
- The Clan keeps the peace with us. We did not expect it, and we are rarely surprised.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your raiders have been burning the forests where we walk. Speak.
- What does the orc want? Be brief; you will not live long enough for a long conversation.
- Speak, and keep your torches away from us. Fog does not burn, but our patience might.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Do not spend it all on fire.
- Orcs bargain plainly; we find that restful. Agreed.
- We will remember this bargain far longer than you will. Done.

#### Thanks for a gift
- An orc giving gifts. We have seen a great many things, and still this one is new.
- Your people's lives are short, orc, but this was a good use of a moment.
- We will record it, so that someone remembers the Clan for something other than fire.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your offer is as crude as your forges.
- Even a raider should know a fair trade when he sees one. This is not one.
- Bring it back when it is worth our time, though you may not live that long.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your warriors were brave, briefly.
- Go back to your sacred fire and warm yourselves. Enough.
- We have lost interest in your war; we suspect you never had much. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your raiders would be back within the season.
- Not while your fires still burn in our lands.
- Peace? Your goddess fell, orc. You will follow her.

#### Rejects a demand
- Orcs demanding tribute. We have outlived far better threats.
- No. Take it, if you can find us.
- We are already standing behind you, orc. You did not notice. Think on that before you demand anything.

### Sidar → Doviello

#### First contact
- The Doviello. You live like wolves and die like them. We have watched many packs come and go.
- Your people survived the winter by abandoning their weak. We survived it by abandoning our souls. Both worked.
- They say your shamans call dead chieftains back from Camulos's vault. We simply arranged never to go.

#### Declares war
- Your pack has hunted in our valleys. Now the shadow hunts you.
- The strong survive, you say. We have survived longer than strength.
- Wolves fear fire, beastman. They should fear the fog more.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Wolves do not keep bargains, and we do not offer them.
- We will not talk to a pack in the middle of its hunt.
- Snarl all you like. We gave away the part of us that could fear you.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Doviello. You are honest about your hunger. We find that refreshing.
- The pack has kept its distance this season. We noticed, and we thank you for it.
- The north is quiet. Your doing, we suspect. Come and speak.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your hunters have been tracking our walkers. They will never find them. Speak.
- What does the wolf want? Be brief, and do not bare your teeth at us.
- Speak, beastman. Your growling does not frighten what cannot fear.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Drag it back to your pack.
- Your people bargain like hunters: quickly, and without ornament. So be it.
- Strength has its uses, even in trade. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the wolves. Rare, and remembered.
- You share the kill when it suits you, it seems. We thank you.
- Long after the last wolf of the north is gone, we will remember the Doviello for this.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. This is a wolf circling a deer it thinks is wounded. We are not wounded.
- Your terms are as raw as your hides. We decline.
- Not this. Even the Illians bargained more fairly with your forefathers.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to the cold you miss so much.
- Your pack has learned what it was hunting. Enough.
- It is over. Lick your wounds; we have none to lick.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You leave your wounded behind in the snow. So will we.
- Not while your hunters still sniff along the edges of our fog.
- Peace? A wolf asks for peace only when it is losing, and you have not lost enough.

#### Rejects a demand
- You demand tribute from us? The pack has grown arrogant.
- No. You cannot take what you cannot find.
- We have outlived many pack leaders, Doviello. We will outlive this one.

### Sidar → Elohim

#### First contact
- The Elohim, keepers of holy places. You preserve old things, as we do. Perhaps we will get along.
- Your monks keep the memory of the world in chants and stories. We keep it in ourselves.
- You tend the dying in every age. We stopped dying. Do not think less of us for it.

#### Declares war
- Your shrines are full of old secrets. We have waited long enough for you to share them.
- Not even holy ground keeps death out, monk. We have come to prove it.
- You protect the world's sacred places. We have decided to study them more closely, whether you allow it or not.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your gentle words are wasted on us; we can no longer be moved by them.
- We have heard the Elohim speak of peace for ages. You always do. We are not ready.
- Not yet. Your order is patient. So are we.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Elohim. Your monks are the only mortals who visit us without wanting something.
- You have kept your promises to us, keeper. We value that more than you know.
- Ah, the keepers. How fare the sacred sites? We have walked past several of them, quietly.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your monks look at us with pity. We do not need it. Speak.
- What does the keeper of shrines want? Be brief.
- Speak, Elohim. Your sermons on the soul are wasted on those who have sold theirs.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your order bargains honestly, which in this age is nearly a miracle.
- Tend it as you tend the sacred sites. Agreed.
- We will keep it as carefully as you keep the Compact's memory.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Elohim. Your kindness reaches even the Grey. We are grateful, in our way.
- You give warmth to those who can no longer feel it. That is either wisdom or folly, and we thank you for it.
- Long after your abbeys are dust, we will remember the Elohim for this.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You guard Finner's secrets jealously; allow us to guard our interests with the same care.
- Your monks count every soul they tend; count this offer again, keeper. We decline.
- Not this. Even the most patient of your monks would call it a poor exchange.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your shrines and your seven firs.
- Your warrior monks carry no weapons, and still they bleed us. We have learned something. Enough.
- We never wished harm on your holy places, only to read them. Let there be peace.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your shrines still hold secrets we have not read.
- Not yet. Your monks still stand between us and the places we wish to study.
- Peace? You signed a peace with demons once and buried its cost. We will not make your mistake.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Your order was founded by a king who threw away his crown; you have no need of riches.
- Tribute from the Grey? Ask Sirona; your founder's goddess may still be listening.
- You came into the world to give, keeper, not to take. Do not forget yourself now.

### Sidar → Grigori

#### First contact
- The Grigori. You turned away from the gods; we turned away from death. Neither of us asked permission.
- Your adventurers wander everywhere. Several have wandered into our fog. Most of them even wandered out again.
- Your people refuse the gods and accept their mortality. We chose the opposite road, and we are curious where yours ends.

#### Declares war
- Your adventurers have pried at our hidden cities once too often. The shadow of death follows them home.
- You teach men to lead themselves. Then lead them to their graves.
- No god protects the Grigori, by your own choice. We have come to see how well that choice holds.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your heroes have not yet learned enough from this war.
- Your creed teaches men to wait and improve what they are given. Wait, then.
- Your creed offers ideas and little more. We offer even less.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Grigori. You and we have both made our peace with the gods' indifference.
- Your people ask questions where others pray, [CT_NAME]. We approve.
- Your Luonnotar guests speak of one god above the gods. We have been listening at their doors; tell them it was interesting.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your adventurers keep stumbling into our fog uninvited. Speak.
- The godless come calling, without even a god to blame for their manners. What is it?
- Speak, Grigori. Your doubt is admirable; your border patrols are not.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A fair bargain between peoples who expect nothing from heaven.
- Your people make their own fortune, Grigori; so do we. Done.
- Spend it on your adventurers; they do so love to spend. Agreed.

#### Thanks for a gift
- No god will reward you for this gift, Grigori, which makes it worth a great deal more.
- Your creed teaches men to improve what they have been given. You have improved our season. Our thanks.
- A generous thing, from a people who owe the world nothing. We will remember it.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your heroes have made you bold in bargaining.
- Your merchants would never accept such terms from us; we will not accept them from you.
- An adventurer's offer: all promise and little gold. We decline.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and improve what you have been given; we will go back to our studies.
- Your adventurers have proven themselves, and we have measured them. Enough.
- Neither of us serves a god who demanded this war, so neither of us must continue it.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You say the true heaven is closed. Our door is closed as well.
- Not yet. There are still too many of your adventurers in our hidden valleys.
- Peace? Your heroes would only use it to look for new ways into our cities.

#### Rejects a demand
- No. Your people make their own fortunes; make this one too.
- You refuse the gifts of the gods and then demand ours? Your philosophy has a gap in it.
- The Grigori ask nothing of higher powers. Do not start with us.

### Sidar → Hippus

#### First contact
- The Hippus. No one outruns the Hippus, they say. We have never felt the need to run.
- Horse lords. Your lives are spent at the gallop. Ours are spent at a walk, and they last far longer.
- Your clans raided one another for generations before your mercenary companies were formed. We watched. It was very loud.

#### Declares war
- Your riders cannot charge what they cannot see.
- Death rides faster than any horse, Hippus. Even your best mounts will not outpace it.
- Your contracts have brought your lances to our borders once too often. We are answering them.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. A mercenary's word belongs to whoever pays next.
- We will not haggle over a war, Hippus. We are not your employers.
- Gallop home. We will speak when the dust has settled, perhaps in a generation.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Hippus. You still ride, we see. Good.
- Your companies have honoured their contracts near our lands, [CT_NAME]. We noticed, and we approve.
- Ah, the horse lords. Your herds are beautiful. We remember when such things moved us.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your riders have been trampling the valleys where we walk. Speak.
- The sellsword at our door again. Name your price, then go.
- Speak, horse lord, and keep your lances lowered.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your people know the worth of a contract; so do we.
- Ride home with it before it loses its shine. Done.
- A clean exchange, quickly made, as your people prefer. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Hippus, with no contract attached? We are almost surprised.
- It is a rare mercenary who gives anything away. We thank you.
- Long after your horses' great-grandchildren are dust, we will remember your clans for this.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You charge for speed, and we have never needed haste.
- Your companies charge for every mile. We can wait for a fairer rate. We decline.
- Not this. You ask a mercenary's pay for a peasant's errand.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your lances have earned their rest, and whoever hired them has earned a refund.
- Go back to your herds and your hills. Enough.
- We would rather your companies rode elsewhere, for someone else's coin. Let it end.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your riders have not yet learned that speed cannot save them.
- Not while your lances still glint in our valleys.
- Peace? You signed with our enemies last spring, and you will sign with them again.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? You sell your lances for gold; we do not buy silence.
- No. Gold is wasted on riders who cannot find what they would raid.
- You may raid us, if you can find us. You will not.

### Sidar → Illians

#### First contact
- The Illians. They call your people living ghosts of Letum Frigus. We know what a ghost is, Illian, and you are not one.
- Once your scholars and priests received tribute from every nation. Now you dream of it again. We have seen many such dreams.
- When the Illians wake, they say, the world sleeps. We do not sleep at all.

#### Declares war
- You would make yourself a god, Illian. We have come to remind you how mortal you still are.
- Even ice melts in time, Illian, and your frozen halls are no exception. We have come.
- Your winter is an old error. We are here to correct it.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your ambition is not something we negotiate with.
- We will not hear the White Hand. Your priesthood had its age.
- Not yet, Illian. Your snows have not yet melted from our valleys.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Illian. You remember the old ages, as we do. Few others bother.
- You stand in the cold as easily as we stand in the fog, [CT_NAME]. We find that interesting.
- Ah, the lost men. Your scholars once knew a great deal. Do they still?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your dreams of godhood are loud enough to reach our hidden cities. Speak.
- Your priests of the White Hand were never patient. Speak, then.
- Speak, Illian. Your cold does not touch us, and neither do your threats.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Even the old men of Letum Frigus can bargain fairly.
- Carry it back through your rings of ice. Done.
- Your people were scholars once; they still know the value of a thing. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Illians, who once received gifts from every nation. The world has turned; we noticed.
- We will keep it safe through whatever winter you intend. Our thanks.
- Few gifts reach us from so deep in the cold. We are grateful.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That offer is as barren as the ice around your broken mountain.
- Your terms assume we are cold and desperate. We are neither. We decline.
- Not this. Your ambition has made your envoys greedy.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your snows and your dreams.
- Your climb toward heaven is not ours to stop today. Enough.
- Let the ice and the fog keep a respectful distance. Peace.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You still reach for the heavens, and we would rather see you fall.
- Not while your snows still lie over our valleys.
- Peace? The world sleeps when the Illians wake. We prefer you asleep.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the White Hand? Mulcarn is gone, Illian, and he is not coming back.
- No. You came out of that chamber with your people's obedience. Find gold there too.
- We paid no tribute when your priests ruled the ice. We will not begin now.

### Sidar → Infernal

#### First contact
- Demons, walking in Erebus. Hell attacks every part of a soul, we are told. There is very little of ours left to attack.
- So the walls of creation have been breached. We have outlived many disasters; we expect to outlive you.
- Your master forges the weak into instruments of hate. We put hate aside long ago, with the rest of our burdens.

#### Declares war
- You do not belong in creation, demon. We have come to return you to the pit.
- Your obsidian gates will not keep death out, demon. Even your kind can be unmade here.
- Your legions carve cities from dirt that does not want them. We have come to give the dirt back.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Every bargain with hell is a hook, and we have no wish to be caught on one.
- We will not speak with the pit while its fires are burning our valleys.
- Your words are fire, demon, and fire is wasted on fog.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Infernal. We are at peace. Do not ask us to enjoy it.
- You have kept your legions on your side of the border, and we keep ours unseen. It works, demon.
- Welcome, demon. You will find nothing here to torment; we feel almost nothing at all.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- The brimstone reaches us before you do. Speak.
- What does hell want with a people who have so little soul to offer?
- Speak, demon. Threats require fear to work, and we sold ours long ago.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. We have had centuries to learn how hell words a contract; this one is clean, for once.
- Do not mistake trade for friendship. Agreed.
- Spend it on your ash and your fire. Done.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from hell. We will examine it very carefully for hooks.
- It must have cost you something to give without taking. We are curious what. Our thanks.
- For a demon, that was generous. We remember everything, and we will remember this.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There is a hook in this, and it is set for souls.
- Hell bargains the way it tortures: slowly, and for its own pleasure. We decline.
- Not this. Even the Ashen Veil's cultists get better terms from you.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to your obsidian halls.
- Hell may keep its legions, so long as it keeps them away from us. Enough.
- We outlasted your fury; we will outlast your peace as well. So be it.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You do not belong in creation, and we are not finished proving it.
- Not while your legions stand on our side of the walls.
- Peace with the pit? We would sooner trust a corpse that walks.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to hell? We already gave away most of our souls; there is nothing left for Agares.
- No. Take it from your master's coffers.
- The Grey give nothing to the pit, demon, now or ever.

### Sidar → Khazad

#### First contact
- The Khazad. You carve your ancestors' deeds into the Rune Halls so they are not forgotten. We simply do not forget.
- The Khazad, who trust neither magic nor strangers. We are both. Let us see how you manage.
- You slept beneath the hills while Mulcarn's winter passed. Others walked above, unseen. Both of us survived it.

#### Declares war
- Your stone walls are thick, dwarf. The shadow of death passes through stone.
- Your vaults are deep, but nothing is deep enough to hide from us.
- Your powder and your hammers are strong. We are very hard to hit.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your siege engines are still aimed at our walls.
- We will not haggle in the middle of a war, Khazad, however good your appraisers are.
- Your people learned to distrust outsiders. Today we have learned the same lesson from you.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Khazad. Your halls are old and quiet. We find them restful.
- Your Hand Seers keep records almost as long as our memories, [CT_NAME]. We respect that.
- Ah, the dwarves. What have your forges made this season? We are always curious about things built to last.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your miners keep digging toward our hidden cities. Speak.
- Speak, dwarf. Your distrust is understandable; your rudeness is not.
- You treat us like an illusion that will vanish once the bargain is struck. We are still here. What do you want?

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Count it twice; we already have.
- A dwarven bargain is an honest bargain. Agreed.
- Lock it in your vaults; it will keep there almost as long as it would with us. Done.

#### Thanks for a gift
- Gold freely given, from a dwarf. We will set this day firmly in our memory.
- Your people remember every old insult; it seems you remember kindness too. We thank you.
- Your ancestors' pillars should record this gift. Ours will.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. That is a merchant's first offer, and we have all the time we need to wait for the second.
- Your people were cheated once by tricksters from outside. Do not try to cheat us in return. We decline.
- Not this, dwarf. Your appraisers know it is short.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your halls, and carve this war into your pillars; we will remember it without them.
- Your hammers have struck hard, and we have nothing more to gain. Enough.
- Let your deep halls and our hidden cities keep their silence. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your stone walls still stand, and so do your siege engines.
- Not yet. Your people once sealed themselves away for generations. Do so again, and we may reconsider.
- Peace? You would carve it into a pillar as our defeat. We will not give you the pleasure.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the Khazad? You have more gold than any people in Erebus.
- No. A dwarf demanding gold for nothing? You learned the wrong lesson from those who once cheated you.
- We have no coffers for you to plunder, dwarf, and no doors for you to knock on.

### Sidar → Kuriotates

#### First contact
- The Kuriotates. You do not age, we hear. We know the look of one who has stopped growing older, and we wonder what you paid.
- A confederation of men, centaurs and stranger folk. You give asylum to the rare peoples of Erebus. We are rarer than most.
- Your borders are wide and loose, and we have walked them often. You did not notice. Your settlements are pleasant.

#### Declares war
- Your borders are porous, Kuriotate. Fog passes through them easily.
- You collect rare peoples, Kuriotate. We do not care to be collected.
- Great cities fall too, Kuriotate, and yours are so few that each one will be missed.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your envoys may wait as long as we wish, and we can wish for a very long time.
- Draw back into your shell, as you always do in war. We will speak when you come out of it.
- Not yet. Your centaurs still ride in our valleys.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Kuriotate. Your court is one of the few that holds our interest.
- Your confederation shelters the outcast and the strange, [CT_NAME]. We are both.
- Ah, the great cities. How do you fare? Still young, we see.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your lamia have been trying to see through our fog. Speak.
- Speak, Kuriotate. Your courtesy is admirable; your border settlements are not.
- What does the confederation want? There is a hiss in your voice today.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your royal administration is orderly. We approve.
- You will still be young enough to remember this bargain in a century, we expect. So will we. Done.
- Your settlements may pass it from hand to hand, as they do everything. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- The great cities send gifts to the hidden ones. Our thanks, and our compliments to the centaurs who carried it.
- Your openness to strange peoples extends even to us. We thank you.
- You understand patience, Kuriotate; that is why we will remember this.

#### Turns down a deal
- Your royal administrators ask too much, and they know it. No.
- You play a long game, but so do we, and we have played it longer. We decline.
- Not this. Offer it to one of your client peoples; they may be obliged to accept it.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Your shell held; we do not need to test it further.
- Your centaurs fought well, and we would rather study them than kill them. Enough.
- You and we will remember this war long after your people have forgotten it. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your outer settlements are still in our way.
- Not yet. You are patient. So are we, and we will win that contest.
- Peace? You would only use it to draw your borders over our hidden valleys again.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? We are not one of your protectorates, Kuriotate.
- Tribute from the Grey to an ageless child? We know too well what agelessness costs. No.
- The Grey do not pay for asylum, least of all to those who cannot find us.

### Sidar → Lanun

#### First contact
- The Lanun. Your seas have grown dark, and your god no longer answers. We have watched it happen.
- Pirates and captains. Your word is fleeting, they say. Ours is very slow, and very long.
- Your priests' disciples make the Drown, we hear: warriors raised dead from the sea. We do not care for the dead who will not rest.

#### Declares war
- Your Drown are an abomination, Lanun. We have come to end them, and those who made them.
- Your harbours lie in our shadow now, captain. Even the sea cannot hide you.
- Your ships cannot sail where we walk.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. A captain's word changes with the tide.
- We will not bargain with pirates in the middle of a raid.
- Not yet. Your fleets still haunt our shores.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, captain. Your ships have kept away from our coasts; we noticed.
- You are still afloat, [CT_NAME]. We are glad; our friends tend to sink before we notice them.
- Ah, the Lanun. Your sea-tales are among the few that still interest us.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your longships have been circling our coasts again. Speak.
- Draw your cutlass if it comforts you, captain; it will pass through us. Now, what do you want?
- Speak, captain. Your Overlords' dreamers babble about the Grey, we hear. Do not believe all of it.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. A captain answers only to one he has given his word to. Count us among them, for this.
- Your crews may toast it; we will simply remember it. Done.
- It is a fair trade, even by the sea's flexible sense of honour. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Lanun? We will not ask which ship it came from.
- We thank you, captain. So many crews were lost in the ice; it is good to see one come back generous.
- The sea forgets everything it swallows. We do not. This will be remembered.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You bargain as you sail, captain: one eye on the horizon and one hand on our purse.
- Your terms shift like the tide; by the time you sail home they will have shifted again. We decline.
- Not this. Even the Aifons beneath your waves would call it a poor exchange.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Back to your waves, and to whatever answers your prayers there now.
- Your fleets have grown tired of searching for a shore they cannot see. Enough.
- The sea is wide, captain; sail it somewhere else. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your Drown still shamble on our shores.
- Not while your ships keep bringing the dead to our lands.
- Peace? Your word is fleeting and ours is not. Unequal treaties end badly.

#### Rejects a demand
- You would levy a toll on fog, captain? No.
- No. You cannot board a ship you cannot see.
- Your captains may conscript anyone they please, but not the Grey, and not our gold.

### Sidar → Ljosalfar

#### First contact
- The Ljosalfar. Your god died and your people nearly followed. We understand clinging to a life that ought to have ended.
- Elves of the Summer Court, back from your hidden groves. You live long, for mortals. Not long enough to bore us yet.
- Your groves are old, elf. We have walked in them quietly and listened to the trees whisper about you.

#### Declares war
- Your forests hide much, elf, but they cannot hide you from the fog.
- Death comes even beneath the ancient canopy, elf, and it walks quietly.
- You came back from the brink once, when your god fell. We have come to show you the brink again.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Elves nurse grudges for centuries. We will wait a few, and then perhaps we will talk.
- We will not speak with the Fellowship of Leaves while its arrows are still in the air.
- Not yet. Set your treants on us if you like; we will wait for them to tire.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Ljosalfar. You are nearly as patient as we are, and so our conversations are never hurried.
- Your groves were green when we last passed through them, [CT_NAME]. We were glad.
- Of all the mortal peoples, the elves are the slowest to die. We appreciate that in a neighbour.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your rangers watch our walkers from the treetops. They see nothing. Speak.
- The Summer Court has fallen silent before, elf. Perhaps it should again. What do you want?
- Speak. Your treants make very poor guards against those who are not quite there.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your folk bargain with the patience of trees, and we with the patience of stones.
- Let it grow slowly, as your forests do. Done.
- It will last as long as an elven promise, which is longer than most. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Ljosalfar. You rarely give to outsiders; we take careful note.
- Your forests survived the death of a god, and your kindness survived with them. We thank you.
- We will keep it as your druids keep the ancient forests: carefully, and for a very long time.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You are patient enough to make a better offer, and we are patient enough to wait for it.
- Your elders will have to deliberate again, elf. We decline.
- Not this. Even a sapling would see how thin this offer is.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to your groves and let them heal.
- Your archers have reminded us why your people survived the ice. Enough.
- Elves and the Grey both have time to forget this war. Only one of us ever forgets anything. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your arrows have not yet run out, and neither has our patience.
- Not yet. Your groves still crowd our hidden paths.
- Peace? Your Fellowship would plant a forest over our cities while we slept. Fortunately, we do not sleep.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the elves? The forest provides, your Fellowship says. Let it.
- No. You ask as though your Summer Court's season had returned. It has not.
- We will give the Ljosalfar nothing but our silence, which we have in abundance.

### Sidar → Luchuirp

#### First contact
- The Luchuirp. Your golems serve without souls and seem content. We have some sympathy for them.
- Heirs of the Open-Skiers. Your empire fell beneath the ice and one clan rebuilt it. We admire persistence.
- Golem-makers. You give clay a kind of life; we gave away a kind of life. Perhaps we should compare notes.

#### Declares war
- Your golems cannot fight what they cannot strike.
- Clockwork rusts, artificer. We do not. Your workshops will learn the difference.
- Your clay soldiers have marched into our hidden valleys. We will send them home as clay.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Send your golems to negotiate; at least they cannot lie.
- We will not talk to artificers while their machines are still marching.
- Not yet. Your forges still burn for this war.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Luchuirp. Your golems fascinate us. They have no souls, and they do not seem to miss them either.
- You came back to the surface after an age in the dark, [CT_NAME]. We do the same, now and then.
- Ah, the artificers. Clockwork and enchantment together; few mortals manage either.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your golems keep tramping through our fog. They frighten nothing. Speak.
- What does the tinker want? Be brief; your workshop will miss you.
- Speak, Luchuirp. You look at us as though we were a cursed crystal from the deep mines. Perhaps we are.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your craftsmanship deserves a fair price.
- Done. Your clan survived the ice by bargaining carefully with fate; we see it still does.
- It will last longer than most things mortals make, and yours last longer than most. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Luchuirp. Fine work, as always; we will study how it was made.
- Your golems will last a long time; so will our memory of this. We thank you.
- Your people lost an empire to the ice and still learned to give. We have seen many fail that lesson.

#### Turns down a deal
- Even a golem could see this bargain leans one way. We decline.
- Go back to your workbench, artificer; this offer needs more polishing.
- No. Your terms are as rigid as a golem's orders, and about as wise.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and oil your golems' joints; ours never need it.
- Your clockwork fought well, for things that cannot want anything. Enough.
- The open sky is yours, little artificers; we prefer its shadows anyway. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your forges still turn out soldiers for this war.
- Not yet. Your golems still walk our valleys.
- Peace? Your people waited an age beneath the ice. You can wait a little longer.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? Your forges are far better at making things than we are at giving them.
- No. Your golems never tire; set them to digging.
- The Grey do not fund workshops, however clever their golems.

### Sidar → Malakim

#### First contact
- The Malakim. Your sun is very bright. We are not always visible in it, which makes these meetings awkward.
- Desert people of Lugus. Your Empyrean judges each case on its merits. We wonder how it will judge us.
- Your people took a dying stranger in from the ice and found a faith. Mortals still surprise us, now and then.

#### Declares war
- Your sun cannot burn what is barely there.
- Death walks at noon too, Malakim, and casts no shadow on your sand.
- Your Radiant Guard hunts shadows. Today the shadows hunt back.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your Empyrean deliberates on everything; let it deliberate on this war for a while.
- We will not stand in your daylight to bargain; it thins us.
- Not yet. Your Vicars still preach against us in our own valleys.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Malakim. We will stand in the shade, if you do not mind.
- Your Empyrean gives an equal voice to small nations, [CT_NAME]. We are very small, and we thank you.
- Ah, the desert folk. Your light is harsh, but your judges are fair.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your Vicars call us unnatural. Speak.
- What does the sun want with the shadows? Be brief.
- Speak, Malakim. Your god's glare does not make your words any clearer.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Your Empyrean would call it fair, and so do we.
- Done. May your caravans reach the oases before the heat does.
- Desert traders bargain honestly; water teaches them to. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Malakim. Your charity reaches even those who avoid your sun.
- Lugus's light is not for us, but your kindness is. We thank you.
- After the dunes have shifted a thousand times, we will still remember the Malakim for this.

#### Turns down a deal
- Desert traders weigh water by the drop. Weigh this offer the same way, and you will see why we refuse.
- Your terms are as harsh as the deep desert. We decline.
- Not this. Your oases are generous; your envoys are not.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Return to your sun; we will return to the shade.
- Your Radiant Guard has made its point, and its point was very bright. Enough.
- Your Empyrean may record that the Grey accepted its judgment, this once.

#### Refuses peace
- No. Your Vicars still preach that we are shadows to be burned away.
- Not yet. Your sun still beats on our valleys.
- Peace? Your Empyrean has not yet heard our case. We will present it in your cities.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? Ask Lugus to shine some gold down on you.
- No. Your Empyrean teaches equality between nations, and equals do not pay tribute.
- The desert has taught you thirst, Malakim. It has not taught us generosity.

### Sidar → Mercurians

#### First contact
- The Mercurians. You once served Arawn, lord of the dead. We arranged never to enter his vault. Perhaps that troubles you.
- Angels who broke the Compact. You are often mistaken for demons, we hear. We are often mistaken for ghosts. We should not mistake each other.
- Your host cares little for mortals. Good. We are not entirely mortal, and we care little for you.

#### Declares war
- You served death's lord, and we cheated him. One of us must answer for it.
- Death has come for your host, angel. Your old master would approve.
- You see a demon in everything that is not you. We are not demons, but we will fight like them.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You care nothing for mortal words. Why should we care for yours?
- We will not talk with an angel who would not even keep the gods' own Compact.
- Not yet. Your hammers have not tired.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, angel. You hunt demons and we hunt the walking dead. Our wars may run side by side.
- Your host has left our hidden cities alone, angel. We are grateful, in our way.
- Ah, the rebel host. You are nearly as detached from mortals as we are.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your soldiers look at us as though we came from the pit. We did not. Speak.
- What does the rebel host want? Be brief; it is the only skill your envoys have.
- Speak, angel. Prayers carved into flesh do not impress those who keep no gods.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Spend it on your war against the hells.
- Angels bargain plainly; we approve. Done.
- It will serve your crusade better than it serves our vaults. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Mercurians. We are surprised; you care so little for anyone.
- Arawn's former servant, giving to those who escaped him. There is a jest in that somewhere. Our thanks.
- We will remember this longer than you will remember us, angel.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. Your host asks as though the world owed it something for the war it chose.
- Not even angels get those terms from the Grey. We decline.
- Not this. Your soldiers fight better than your envoys bargain.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go and find your demons; we are not them.
- Your war is with the hells, not with us. Enough.
- Let death's angels and death's deserters go their separate ways. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. You hunt what you hate. So do we.
- Not yet. Your host still mistakes us for its enemies, and we are teaching it otherwise.
- Peace? You refused the peace of the gods themselves. Do not lecture us about treaties.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the rebel host? Ask Arawn; you know where his vault lies.
- No. Take it from a demon; you seem to enjoy that.
- The Grey owe nothing to death, or to death's angels.

### Sidar → Sheaim

#### First contact
- The Sheaim. You wish to end creation; we spent our souls to stay in it. We will not be good neighbours.
- So you are the gate-openers. You bind the spirits of the dead into unholy shapes, we hear. We have seen worse, but not often.
- Your people come from every nation, united only by a longing for the end. We prefer to watch the world go on.

#### Declares war
- We paid dearly to remain in this world. We will not let you end it.
- Those who would kill everything must expect death to visit them first. Even you.
- You twist the spirits of the dead into unholy forms. We have come to free them, and to end you.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. You do not want peace; you want an ending.
- We will not talk to those who would close the world like a finished book.
- Not yet. Your gates still stand open.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Sheaim. We are at peace, though we do not understand you, and we understand most things.
- Your rituals fascinate us, [CT_NAME], the way a flame fascinates a moth that has learned better.
- Welcome. Tell us what you have learned of the other planes; we will tell you nothing in return, as usual.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your rites have been tearing at the edges of the world near our cities. Speak.
- What does the apocalypse want today? Be brief; even we have limits.
- Speak, gate-opener. Your doom is not ours.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. This bargain will outlast your apocalypse; we will see to it.
- Try not to spend it on the end of the world. Done.
- Knowledge of the planes is worth much to us, whatever you mean to do with yours. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Sheaim. We will examine it for broken bindings.
- It is strange, to receive gifts from those who want everything gone. We thank you all the same.
- We will remember this after your Armageddon has failed.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. You offer us things you intend to destroy.
- Your terms are as twisted as your rituals. We decline.
- Not this. A bargain is a promise about the future, and you have promised the future to the void.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your rituals; we will be watching them very carefully.
- Your summonings have tired us, and we do not tire easily. Enough.
- Do not mistake our peace for indifference to your purpose. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. While you live, the world is in danger, and we live in the world.
- Not yet. Your planar gates are still breathing smoke into the world.
- Peace? A truce would only give your rituals time to ripen.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute? You mean to unmake the world, gold included. Why should we hurry it along?
- No. You would only burn it with everything else.
- The Grey give nothing to the apocalypse.

### Sidar → Svartalfar

#### First contact
- The Svartalfar. Your assassins are skilled, and we are very hard to kill. That may save us both some trouble.
- Elves of the Winter Court. You declared your god gone and took Esus instead. We understand; gods are useful only while they answer.
- You do not betray all of your allies, we hear. Only most. We have outlived many betrayals.

#### Declares war
- Your assassins have tested our patience. Now the shadow of death tests yours.
- You thrive in the dark, Svartalfar. So do we, and we have had far longer to learn it.
- Your Winter Court never finishes its wars. Neither do we, once one has begun.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your envoys carry daggers. Ours carry nothing; there is nothing in us to stab.
- We will not talk while your shadows creep about our cities.
- Not yet, elf. Your court's words are too sweet to be trusted in wartime.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- Welcome, Svartalfar. Your court is cruel, but it is never dull.
- Your assassins have kept away from us, elf. We are grateful; we would hate to waste them.
- Ah, the dark elves. You walk in shadows, and so do we. It is a wonder we do not meet there more often.

#### Greeting (hostile)
- One of your assassins was found in our streets. We returned the body. Speak.
- What does the Winter Court want? Be brief, and keep your knives sheathed.
- Speak, elf. Your poisons are wasted on those who barely breathe.

#### Accepts a deal
- Agreed. Betray it if you must, elf; we will be watching when you try.
- Esus would call it a fair price for a small miracle. Done.
- We will remember the terms, should you happen to forget them. Acceptable.

#### Thanks for a gift
- A gift from the Winter Court. Poison is wasted on us, so we assume this one is sincere.
- The Winter Court is generous; that is either kindness or a plot, and we will learn which. Our thanks.
- Your court gives rarely, and never without reason. We look forward to the reason.

#### Turns down a deal
- No. There is a knife in this bargain, and we have learned to look for them.
- Your academies teach persuasion, but this is not persuasive. We decline.
- Not this. Your court has had a long winter to prepare a better offer.

#### Agrees to peace
- Peace. Go back to your quarrel with your Summer cousins; it seems to please you more.
- Your assassins have found us too hard to kill, and we have found you too hard to find. Enough.
- We will be watching your shadows as closely as you watch ours. It is done.

#### Refuses peace
- No. A Svartalfar treaty would be broken before the first frost; we have watched it happen.
- Not yet. Your shadows still move in our cities.
- Peace? Your court renounced its own god when he stopped answering. We expect no better for a treaty.

#### Rejects a demand
- Tribute to the Winter Court? Esus makes his faithful pay for their miracles. Pay for yours.
- No. Twelve assassins in our halls would find only fog.
- Demand from the Grey? Your court has mistaken patience for weakness before, elf, and buried those who made the mistake.

## Svartalfar

### Svartalfar → Amurites

#### First contact
- The Amurites. Ours was the arcane half of the elven realm when your ancestors were still shivering in furs. Kylorin taught you well, for a human.
- Children of Kylorin. You license your necromancers with permits and committees. In the Winter Court, the only licence is survival.
- A nation run like a school. Do tell us which of your archmages is next to be poisoned; we so enjoy faculty politics.

#### Declares war
- Your archmages stonewall one another at every turn. We will save them the trouble and silence them all.
- Diplomacy with scholars is nothing but footnotes. We prefer a sharper instrument.
- Your mages will make excellent subjects. The Unseelie studied the darker spheres while your people were still learning to light a fire.

#### Refuses to talk
- Submit a petition to our council. It meets every winter, and this winter is going to be very long.
- No. Your envoy may present his thesis to the knives in our antechamber.
- Talk? You have nothing to teach us, and we have no wish to tutor you.

#### Greeting (friendly)
- [CT_NAME]. Your schools produce such clever, ambitious people. We have recruited several. Do not be alarmed.
- Welcome, Amurite. You at least understand that magic need not bow to the gods' squeamishness.
- Ah, the scholars. Those necromancy permits must be such a bother. Shall we discuss alternatives?

#### Greeting (hostile)
- Your scryers keep peering into our court. Each one we catch goes home without eyes. State your business.
- You disapprove of us, mage. Your disapproval is noted, filed, and of no consequence.
- Speak, Amurite, and be brief. Your lectures are notorious even in the Winter Court.

#### Accepts a deal
- A fair exchange of learning. How civilized; we hardly recognize ourselves.
- Agreed. Do let your archmages quarrel over it afterwards; we will enjoy the spectacle.
- We accept. Trade is slower than theft, but your wards are so tiresome to pick.

#### Thanks for a gift
- How thoughtful. Your schools teach manners after all.
- A gift from the Amurites. We shall find a use for it, and perhaps one for you.
- Generous, scholar. The Winter Court remembers its benefactors, and now and then it even spares them.

#### Turns down a deal
- That offer would fail the most lenient of your examinations. Try again.
- No. You price your knowledge the way your archmages guard their chairs: jealously and absurdly.
- Did you imagine the Unseelie court could not count? We decline.

#### Agrees to peace
- Very well. Return to your squabbling faculties; we will return to our webs.
- Peace, Amurite. Your fire-mages have earned a reprieve, and we have a long memory for their faces.
- Enough. A war between two courts of magic only flatters the priests.

#### Refuses peace
- Peace? Your archmages have not yet finished dying in the order we arranged.
- No. Your schools still hold libraries we have not looted.
- The Winter Court does not sign treaties with students. Graduate to surrender, and we will talk.

#### Rejects a demand
- You would demand tribute from your betters? Return to your classroom.
- No. Your council of archmages may vote on it for a decade; our answer will not change.
- We keep academies of our own, mage. None of them teach us to yield to threats.

### Svartalfar → Balseraphs

#### First contact
- The court of Jubilee. Masks, songs and slaves. You would have done well in the Unseelie halls, Balseraph.
- A mad court and a cruel one, face to face at last. Whichever of us wins, the dancing will be exquisite.
- Your mimics steal the skills of those they kill. We admire thrift in all its forms.

#### Declares war
- The masquerade is over, Balseraph. Take off your masks; we want to see your faces when you fall.
- Harlequins against assassins. You will find our performers do not take bows.
- Your court is merry. Ours is patient. Patience always outlives the joke.

#### Refuses to talk
- No. Your court speaks in riddles, and ours answers in knives.
- We will not trade rhymes with a jester while our cities burn.
